## Hunting Foreign Group Membership with Bloodhound-python

Aliases: —  
Tags: abuse, attack, bloodhound, dns, domain, host, ldap, sudo, upload  
Category: Active Directory / Attacking Domain Trusts - Cross-Forest Trust Abuse - from Linux  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux  
Service: DNS, LDAP  
Ports: 53, 389, 636, 3268, 3269

### Remember this attack when

- Since only Domain Local Groups allow users from outside their forest, it is not uncommon to see a highly privileged user from Domain A as a member of the built-in administrators group in domain B when dealing with a bidirectional forest trust relationship.
- If we are testing from a Linux host, we can gather this information by using the Python implementation of BloodHound.

### Prerequisites

- Since only Domain Local Groups allow users from outside their forest, it is not uncommon to see a highly privileged user from Domain A as a member of the built-in administrators group in domain B when dealing with a bidirectional forest trust relationship.
- In this case, we would need to edit our resolv.conf file to run this tool since it requires a DNS hostname for the target Domain Controller instead of an IP address.

## Hyper-V Administrators

Aliases: —  
Tags: domain, exploit, password, powershell, service  
Category: Active Directory / Hyper-V Administrators  
OS: Windows  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- If Domain Controllers have been virtualized, then the virtualization admins should be considered Domain Admins.
- If the operating system is vulnerable to CVE-2018-0952 or CVE-2019-0841, we can leverage this to gain SYSTEM privileges.

### Prerequisites

- ---- The Hyper-V Administrators group has full access to all Hyper-V features.
- It is also well documented on this blog, that upon deleting a virtual machine, vmms.exe attempts to restore the original file permissions on the corresponding .vhdx file and does so as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, without impersonating the user.
- We can delete the .vhdx file and create a native hard link to point this file to a protected SYSTEM file, which we will have full permissions to.

### Enumeration / Detection

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### Exploitation

```shell-session
C:\Program Files (x86)\Mozilla Maintenance Service\maintenanceservice.exe
```

```cmd-session
C:\htb> takeown /F C:\Program Files (x86)\Mozilla Maintenance Service\maintenanceservice.exe
```

```cmd-session
C:\htb> sc.exe start MozillaMaintenance
```

### What success looks like

- ---- The Hyper-V Administrators group has full access to all Hyper-V features.
- We can update this exploit (a proof-of-concept for NT hard link) to grant our current user full permissions on the file below: Taking Ownership of the File After running the PowerShell script, we should have full control of this file and can take ownership of it.

<a id="technique-impacket-toolkit"></a>
## Impacket Toolkit

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, exploit, hash, host, password, rpc, service, shell  
Category: Active Directory / Credentialed Enumeration - from Linux  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: RPC  
Ports: 111, 135

### Remember this attack when

- Impacket is a versatile toolkit that provides us with many different ways to enumerate, interact, and exploit Windows protocols and find the information we need using Python.
- The tool is actively maintained and has many contributors, especially when new attack techniques arise.
- The downside of this is that if a vigilant defender checks event logs and looks at event ID 4688: A new process has been created, they will see a new process created to spawn cmd.exe and issue a command.

### Prerequisites

- Impacket is a versatile toolkit that provides us with many different ways to enumerate, interact, and exploit Windows protocols and find the information we need using Python.
- We will utilize the credentials for the next few actions.
- Using psexec.py To connect to a host with psexec.py, we need credentials for a user with local administrator privileges.

### Enumeration / Detection

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### Exploitation

```bash
psexec.py inlanefreight.local/wley:'transporter@4'@172.16.5.125  
```

```bash
wmiexec.py inlanefreight.local/wley:'transporter@4'@172.16.5.5  
```

### What success looks like

- Earlier in the poisoning section, we grabbed a hash for the user wley with Responder and cracked it to obtain the password transporter@4.
- Once established, communication happens over a named pipe, providing an interactive remote shell as SYSTEM on the victim host.
- wmiexec.py Wmiexec.py utilizes a semi-interactive shell where commands are executed through Windows Management Instrumentation.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Credentialed Enumeration - from Linux` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- Note that this shell environment is not fully interactive, so each command issued will execute a new cmd.exe from WMI and execute your command.
- The downside of this is that if a vigilant defender checks event logs and looks at event ID 4688: A new process has been created, they will see a new process created to spawn cmd.exe and issue a command.

<a id="technique-kerberoasting-overview"></a>
## Kerberoasting Overview

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, domain, hash, hashcat, host, kerberos, mssql, password, service, shell, ticket  
Category: Active Directory / Kerberoasting - from Linux  
OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: kerberos, mssql  
Ports: 88, 1433

### Remember this attack when

- This is also possible across forest trusts if authentication is permitted across the trust boundary.
- Domain accounts running services are often local administrators, if not highly privileged domain accounts.
- Finding SPNs associated with highly privileged accounts in a Windows environment is very common.

### Prerequisites

- Kerberoasting is a lateral movement/privilege escalation technique in Active Directory environments.
- All you need to perform a Kerberoasting attack is an account's cleartext password (or NTLM hash), a shell in the context of a domain user account, or SYSTEM level access on a domain-joined host.
- Domain accounts running services are often local administrators, if not highly privileged domain accounts.

### Enumeration / Detection

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### Exploitation

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### What success looks like

- All you need to perform a Kerberoasting attack is an account's cleartext password (or NTLM hash), a shell in the context of a domain user account, or SYSTEM level access on a domain-joined host.
- However, the ticket (TGS-REP) is encrypted with the service account’s NTLM hash, so the cleartext password can potentially be obtained by subjecting it to an offline brute-force attack with a tool such as Hashcat.
- If the password for a domain SQL Server service account is cracked, you are likely to find yourself as a local admin on multiple servers, if not Domain Admin.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Kerberoasting - from Linux` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

<a id="technique-kerberoasting-with-getuserspns-py"></a>
## Kerberoasting with GetUserSPNs.py

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, crack, credential, domain, hash, host, kerberos, password, shell, smb, sudo, ticket  
Category: Active Directory / Kerberoasting - from Linux  
OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: SMB, kerberos  
Ports: 88, 139, 445

### Remember this attack when

- A prerequisite to performing Kerberoasting attacks is either domain user credentials (cleartext or just an NTLM hash if using Impacket), a shell in the context of a domain user, or account such as SYSTEM.
- If we can retrieve and crack one of these tickets, it could lead to domain compromise.
- It is always worth investigating the group membership of all accounts because we may find an account with an easy-to-crack ticket that can help us further our goal of moving laterally/vertically in the target domain.

### Prerequisites

- A prerequisite to performing Kerberoasting attacks is either domain user credentials (cleartext or just an NTLM hash if using Impacket), a shell in the context of a domain user, or account such as SYSTEM.
- We must also know which host in the domain is a Domain Controller so we can query it.
- To do this, we will need a set of valid domain credentials and the IP address of a Domain Controller.

## Kerbrute - Internal AD Username Enumeration

Aliases: —

### Remember this attack when

- This repository contains many different user lists that can be extremely useful when attempting to enumerate users when starting from an unauthenticated perspective.

## Lateral Movement

Aliases: —  
Tags: acl, bloodhound, domain, evasion, host, ldap, password, port, rdp, service, shell, smb, ssh, sudo, upload, winrm  
Category: Active Directory / Lateral Movement  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: LDAP, RDP, SMB, SSH, winrm  
Ports: 22, 139, 389, 445, 636, 3268, 3269, 3389, 5985, 5986

### Remember this attack when

- This means that any user in the domain can RDP in and, if they can escalate privileges, could potentially steal sensitive data such as credentials.
- This is worth noting as a finding; we can call it Excessive Active Directory Group Privileges and label it medium-risk.
- If the entire group had local admin rights over a host, it would definitely be a high-risk finding.

### Prerequisites

- --- After pillaging the host DEV01, we found the following set of credentials by dumping LSA secrets: hporter:Gr8hambino!
- This means that any user in the domain can RDP in and, if they can escalate privileges, could potentially steal sensitive data such as credentials.
- This is worth noting as a finding; we can call it Excessive Active Directory Group Privileges and label it medium-risk.

<a id="technique-llmnr-nbt-ns-poisoning-linux"></a>
## LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning (Linux)

Aliases: LLMNR poisoning, NBT-NS poisoning, Responder, LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning - from Linux, Quick Example - LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning, Responder In Action  
Tags: attack, crack, dns, domain, hash, hashcat, host, http, password, poison, port, relay, service, smb, sudo  
Category: Active Directory / LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning - from Linux  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: DNS, HTTP, SMB  
Ports: 53, 80, 139, 445

### Remember this attack when

- The host then broadcasts out to the entire local network asking if anyone knows the location of \\\\printer01.inlanefreight.local.
- This hash can then be cracked offline or used in an SMB Relay attack if the right conditions exist.
- As shown earlier in the module, the -A flag puts us into analyze mode, allowing us to see NBT-NS, BROWSER, and LLMNR requests in the environment without poisoning any responses.

### Prerequisites

- We will perform these actions with the goal of acquiring valid cleartext credentials for a domain user account, thereby granting us a foothold in the domain to begin the next phase of enumeration from a credentialed standpoint.
- This section and the next will cover a common way to gather credentials and gain an initial foothold during an assessment: a Man-in-the-Middle attack on Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution (LLMNR) and NetBIOS Name Service (NBT-NS) broadcasts.
- Depending on the network, this attack may provide low-privileged or administrative level password hashes that can be cracked offline or even cleartext credentials.

### What success looks like

- We obtained some basic user and group information, enumerated hosts while looking for critical services and roles like a Domain Controller, and figured out some specifics such as the naming scheme used for the domain.
- Depending on the network, this attack may provide low-privileged or administrative level password hashes that can be cracked offline or even cleartext credentials.
- This hash can then be cracked offline or used in an SMB Relay attack if the right conditions exist.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning - from Linux` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- We can use the -v flag for increased verbosity if we are running into issues, but this will lead to a lot of additional data printed to the console.
- We must run the tool with sudo privileges or as root and make sure the following ports are available on our attack host for it to function best: Any of the rogue servers (i.e., SMB) can be disabled in the Responder.conf file.
- NetNTLMv2 hashes are very useful once cracked, but cannot be used for techniques such as pass-the-hash, meaning we have to attempt to crack them offline.

### What success looks like

- Let's start Inveigh with LLMNR and NBNS spoofing, and output to the console and write to a file.
- We can see that we immediately begin getting LLMNR and mDNS requests.
- GIF showcasing the usage of the Inveigh PowerShell module in a PowerShell terminal.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning - from Windows` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- The options with a [+] are default and enabled by default and the ones with a [ ] before them are disabled.
- The running console output also shows us which options are disabled and, therefore, responses are not being sent (mDNS in the above example).
- NBT-NS cannot be disabled via Group Policy but must be disabled locally on each host.

### Variants

- LLMNR poisoning, NBT-NS poisoning, Inveigh, LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning - from Windows, Using Inveigh, C# Inveigh (InveighZero), Remediation

<a id="technique-local-administrator-password-reuse"></a>
## Local Administrator Password Reuse

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, domain, hash, host, password, smb, spray, sql  
Category: Active Directory / Internal Password Spraying - from Linux  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: SMB  
Ports: 139, 445

### Remember this attack when

- If you obtain administrative access and the NTLM password hash or cleartext password for the local administrator account (or another privileged local account), this can be attempted across multiple hosts in the network.
- When working with local administrator accounts, one consideration is password re-use or common password formats across accounts.
- If we find a desktop host with the local administrator account password set to something unique such as $desktop%@admin123, it might be worth attempting $server%@admin123 against servers.

### Prerequisites

- If you obtain administrative access and the NTLM password hash or cleartext password for the local administrator account (or another privileged local account), this can be attempted across multiple hosts in the network.
- It is worth targeting high-value hosts such as SQL or Microsoft Exchange servers, as they are more likely to have a highly privileged user logged in or have their credentials persistent in memory.
- We may obtain valid credentials for a user in domain A that are valid for a user with the same or similar username in domain B or vice-versa.

### Enumeration / Detection

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### Exploitation

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ sudo crackmapexec smb --local-auth 172.16.5.0/23 -u administrator -H 88ad09182de639ccc6579eb0849751cf | grep +

SMB         172.16.5.50     445    ACADEMY-EA-MX01  [+] ACADEMY-EA-MX01\administrator 88ad09182de639ccc6579eb0849751cf (Pwn3d!)
SMB         172.16.5.25     445    ACADEMY-EA-MS01  [+] ACADEMY-EA-MS01\administrator 88ad09182de639ccc6579eb0849751cf (Pwn3d!)
SMB         172.16.5.125    445    ACADEMY-EA-WEB0  [+] ACADEMY-EA-WEB0\administrator 88ad09182de639ccc6579eb0849751cf (Pwn3d!)
```

### What success looks like

- If you obtain administrative access and the NTLM password hash or cleartext password for the local administrator account (or another privileged local account), this can be attempted across multiple hosts in the network.
- It is worth targeting high-value hosts such as SQL or Microsoft Exchange servers, as they are more likely to have a highly privileged user logged in or have their credentials persistent in memory.
- Local Admin Spraying with CrackMapExec The output above shows that the credentials were valid as a local admin on 3 systems in the 172.16.5.0/23 subnet.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Internal Password Spraying - from Linux` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- It is always worth looking for this issue during penetration tests, even if it is not part of our path to compromise the domain, as it is a common issue and should be highlighted for our clients.
- One way to remediate this issue is using the free Microsoft tool Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) to have Active Directory manage local administrator passwords and enforce a unique password on each host that rotates on a set interval.

### Variants

- No separately named variant was identified in the cited CPTS subsection.

### Useful commands

## Net Commands

Aliases: —  
Tags: domain, host, password  
Category: Active Directory / Living Off the Land  
OS: Windows  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- Net commands can be beneficial to us when attempting to enumerate information from the domain.
- Keep in mind that net.exe commands are typically monitored by EDR solutions and can quickly give up our location if our assessment has an evasive component.
- Some organizations will even configure their monitoring tools to throw alerts if certain commands are run by users in specific OUs, such as a Marketing Associate's account running commands such as whoami, and net localgroup administrators, etc.

### Prerequisites

- We can list information such as: - Local and domain users - Groups - Hosts - Specific users in groups - Domain Controllers - Password requirements We'll cover a few examples below.

## Network Information

Aliases: —  
Tags: dns, domain, host, pivot, rdp, tunnel, winrm  
Category: Active Directory / Living Off the Land; Situational Awareness  
OS: Windows  
Service: DNS, RDP, winrm  
Ports: 53, 3389, 5985, 5986

### Remember this attack when

- | |route print | Displays the routing table (IPv4 & IPv6) identifying known networks and layer three routes shared with the host.
- We can determine if it is active and filtering traffic.
- We may find that the host is dual-homed and that compromising the host may allow us to move laterally into another part of the network that we could not access previously.

### Prerequisites

- This could help us with lateral movement after obtaining credentials.
- This network information may help directly or indirectly with our local privilege escalation.
- It may lead us down another path to a system that we can access or escalate privileges on or reveal information that we can use for lateral movement to further our access after escalating privileges on the current system.

### What success looks like

- Two more important commands provide us with a ton of valuable data and could help us further our access.
- Any networks that appear in the routing table are potential avenues for lateral movement because they are accessed enough that a route was added, or it has administratively been set there so that the host knows how to access resources on the domain.
- We may find that the host is dual-homed and that compromising the host may allow us to move laterally into another part of the network that we could not access previously.

<a id="technique-nopac-samaccountname-spoofing"></a>
## NoPac (SamAccountName Spoofing)

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, bypass, domain, exploit, host, kerberos, ldap, payload, service, shell, ticket, upload  
Category: Active Directory / Bleeding Edge Vulnerabilities  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: LDAP, kerberos  
Ports: 88, 389, 636, 3268, 3269

### Remember this attack when

- A great example of an emerging threat is the SamTheAdmin vulnerability, also called noPac or referred to as SamAccountName Spoofing released at the end of 2021.
- This vulnerability encompasses two CVEs 2021-42278 and 2021-42287, allowing for intra-domain privilege escalation from any standard domain user to Domain Admin level access in one single command.
- Here is a quick breakdown of what each CVE provides regarding this vulnerability.

### Prerequisites

- This vulnerability encompasses two CVEs 2021-42278 and 2021-42287, allowing for intra-domain privilege escalation from any standard domain user to Domain Admin level access in one single command.
- | 42287 is a vulnerability within the Kerberos Privilege Attribute Certificate (PAC) in ADDS.
- Once done, we must request Kerberos tickets causing the service to issue us tickets under the DC's name instead of the new name.

### What success looks like

- This vulnerability encompasses two CVEs 2021-42278 and 2021-42287, allowing for intra-domain privilege escalation from any standard domain user to Domain Admin level access in one single command.
- By default, authenticated users can add up to ten computers to a domain.
- Once done, we will have access as that service and can even be provided with a SYSTEM shell on a Domain Controller.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Bleeding Edge Vulnerabilities` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- Once done, we must request Kerberos tickets causing the service to issue us tickets under the DC's name instead of the new name.
- When a TGS is requested, it will issue the ticket with the closest matching name.
- NoPac uses many tools in Impacket to communicate with, upload a payload, and issue commands from the attack host to the target DC.

### Variants

- No separately named variant was identified in the cited CPTS subsection.

## Pass the Ticket (PtT) from Linux — Additional CPTS Example

Aliases: —  
Tags: abuse, domain, forward, kerberos, password, port, rdp, service, smb, ssh, ticket, winrm  
Category: Active Directory / Pass the Ticket (PtT) from Linux  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: RDP, SMB, SSH, kerberos, winrm  
Ports: 22, 88, 139, 445, 3389, 5985, 5986

### Remember this attack when

- In that case, we could try to find Kerberos tickets to impersonate other users and gain more access to the network.
- This variable can identify if Kerberos tickets are being used or if the default location for storing Kerberos tickets is changed.
- However, when you change your password, you must recreate all your keytab files.

### Prerequisites

- In that case, we could try to find Kerberos tickets to impersonate other users and gain more access to the network.
- It is not a requirement to be joined to the domain to use Kerberos tickets from a Linux machine.
- These ccache files are protected by specific read/write permissions, but a user with elevated privileges or root privileges could easily gain access to these tickets.

### Enumeration / Detection

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

- In that case, we could try to find Kerberos tickets to impersonate other users and gain more access to the network.
- These ccache files are protected by specific read/write permissions, but a user with elevated privileges or root privileges could easily gain access to these tickets.
- Keytab files commonly allow scripts to authenticate automatically using Kerberos without requiring human interaction or access to a password stored in a plain text file.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- In this scenario, our attack host doesn't have a connection to the KDC/Domain Controller, and we can't use the Domain Controller for name resolution.

<a id="technique-pass-the-certificate"></a>
## Pass-the-Certificate

Aliases: AD CS NTLM Relay Attack (ESC8), Shadow Credentials (msDS-KeyCredentialLink)  
Tags: attack, bloodhound, dcsync, domain, host, http, https, imap, kerberos, ldap, mssql, password, port, relay, rpc, service, shell, smb, smtp, ticket, winrm  
Category: Active Directory / Pass the Certificate  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: HTTP, HTTPS, IMAP, LDAP, RPC, SMB, SMTP, kerberos, mssql, winrm  
Ports: 25, 80, 88, 111, 135, 139, 143, 389, 443, 445, 465, 587, 636, 993, 1433, 3268, 3269, 5985, 5986

### Remember this attack when

- A certificate authority configured to allow web enrollment typically hosts the following application at /CertSrv: Microsoft Active Directory Certificate Services webpage for inlanefreight-CA01-CA.
- Note: If you encounter error stating "Error detecting the version of libcrypto" , it can be fixed by installing the oscrypto library.
- In BloodHound, the AddKeyCredentialLink edge indicates that one user has write permissions over another user's msDS-KeyCredentialLink attribute, allowing them to take control of that user.

### Prerequisites

- This attack requires the targeted machine account to have the Printer Spooler service running.
- Shadow Credentials refers to an Active Directory attack that abuses the msDS-KeyCredentialLink attribute of a victim user.
- In BloodHound, the AddKeyCredentialLink edge indicates that one user has write permissions over another user's msDS-KeyCredentialLink attribute, allowing them to take control of that user.


### What success looks like

- Once we successfully obtain a TGT, we're back in familiar Pass-the-Ticket (PtT) territory.
- The command below generates an X.509 certificate and writes the public key to the victim user's msDS-KeyCredentialLink attribute: In the output above, we can see that a PFX (PKCS12) file was created (eFUVVTPf.pfx), and the password is shown.
- We will use this file with gettgtpkinit.py to acquire a TGT as the victim: With the TGT obtained, we may once again pass the ticket: In this case, we discovered that the victim user is a member of the Remote Management Users group, which permits them to connect to the machine via WinRM.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Pass the Certificate` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- Note: If you encounter error stating "Error detecting the version of libcrypto" , it can be fixed by installing the oscrypto library.

### Variants

- AD CS NTLM Relay Attack (ESC8), Shadow Credentials (msDS-KeyCredentialLink)

<a id="technique-pass-the-hash"></a>
## Pass-the-Hash

Aliases: PtH, PTH, Pass the Hash (PtH), Pass the Hash with Mimikatz (Windows), Pass the Hash with PowerShell Invoke-TheHash (Windows), Pass the Hash with Impacket (Linux), Pass the Hash with NetExec (Linux), Pass the Hash with evil-winrm (Linux), Pass the Hash with RDP (Linux), UAC limits Pass the Hash for local accounts  
Tags: attack, credential, domain, exploit, hash, host, kerberos, netcat, password, powershell, rdp, service, shell, smb, winrm  
Category: Active Directory / Pass the Hash (PtH)  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: RDP, SMB, kerberos, winrm  
Ports: 88, 139, 445, 3389, 5985, 5986

### Remember this attack when

- Mimikatz has a module named sekurlsa::pth that allows us to perform a Pass the Hash attack by starting a process using the hash of the user's password.
- /run - The program we want to run with the user's context (if not specified, it will launch cmd.exe).
- When using Invoke-TheHash, we have two options: SMB or WMI command execution.

### Prerequisites

- The attacker doesn't need to decrypt the hash to obtain a plaintext password.
- As discussed in the previous sections, the attacker must have administrative privileges or particular privileges on the target machine to obtain a password hash.
- This lab contains two machines, you will have access to one (MS01), and from there, you will connect to the second machine (DC01).

### Enumeration / Detection

### What success looks like

- Hashes can be obtained in several ways, including: - Dumping the local SAM database from a compromised host.
- This lab contains two machines, you will have access to one (MS01), and from there, you will connect to the second machine (DC01).
- This tool is a collection of PowerShell functions for performing Pass the Hash attacks with WMI and SMB.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Pass the Hash (PtH)` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- If we run into this issue on a real-world engagement, a great recommendation for the customer is to implement the Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS), which randomizes the local administrator password and can be configured to have it rotate on a fixed interval.
- If SMB is blocked or we don't have administrative rights, we can use this alternative protocol to connect to the target machine.
- Note: There is one exception, if the registry key FilterAdministratorToken (disabled by default) is enabled (value 1), the RID 500 account (even if it is renamed) is enrolled in UAC protection.

## Pass-the-Ticket (Linux)

Aliases: PtT, Pass-the-Ticket, Pass the Ticket (PtT) from Linux, Identifying Linux and Active Directory integration, Finding Kerberos tickets in Linux, Finding KeyTab files, Finding ccache files, Abusing KeyTab files, KeyTab Extract, Obtaining more hashes, Abusing KeyTab ccache, Using Linux attack tools with Kerberos, Impacket, Evil-WinRM, Miscellaneous, Linikatz  
Tags: abuse, attack, chisel, crack, credential, domain, hash, hashcat, host, john, kerberos, password, port, rdp, service, shell, smb, ssh, sudo, ticket, wget, winrm  
Category: Active Directory / Pass the Ticket (PtT) from Linux  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: RDP, SMB, SSH, kerberos, winrm  
Ports: 22, 88, 139, 445, 3389, 5985, 5986

### Remember this attack when

- In that case, we could try to find Kerberos tickets to impersonate other users and gain more access to the network.
- We can identify if the Linux machine is domain-joined using realm, a tool used to manage system enrollment in a domain and set which domain users or groups are allowed to access the local system resources.
- realm - Check if Linux machine is domain-joined The output of the command indicates that the machine is configured as a Kerberos member.

### Prerequisites

- In that case, we could try to find Kerberos tickets to impersonate other users and gain more access to the network.
- It is not a requirement to be joined to the domain to use Kerberos tickets from a Linux machine.
- As an attacker, we are always looking for credentials.

### What success looks like

- In that case, we could try to find Kerberos tickets to impersonate other users and gain more access to the network.
- We can identify if the Linux machine is domain-joined using realm, a tool used to manage system enrollment in a domain and set which domain users or groups are allowed to access the local system resources.
- realm - Check if Linux machine is domain-joined The output of the command indicates that the machine is configured as a Kerberos member.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Pass the Ticket (PtT) from Linux` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- In this scenario, our attack host doesn't have a connection to the KDC/Domain Controller, and we can't use the Domain Controller for name resolution.

<a id="technique-pass-the-ticket-windows"></a>
## Pass-the-Ticket (Windows)

Aliases: PtT, Pass-the-Ticket, Pass the Ticket (PtT) from Windows, Pass the Ticket (PtT) attack, Harvesting Kerberos tickets from Windows, Pass the Key aka. OverPass the Hash, Pass the Ticket (PtT), Pass The Ticket with PowerShell Remoting (Windows), Mimikatz - PowerShell Remoting with Pass the Ticket, Rubeus - PowerShell Remoting with Pass the Ticket  
Tags: attack, domain, dump, hash, http, https, john, kerberos, ldap, password, port, powershell, service, ticket  
Category: Active Directory / Pass the Ticket (PtT) from Windows  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: HTTP, HTTPS, LDAP, kerberos  
Ports: 80, 88, 389, 443, 636, 3268, 3269

### Remember this attack when

- It can be: Service Ticket (TGS) to allow access to a particular resource.
- Note: If you pick a ticket with the service krbtgt, it corresponds to the TGT of that account.
- This option can be used to dump all tickets (if running as a local administrator).

### Prerequisites

- We need a valid Kerberos ticket to perform a Pass the Ticket (PtT) attack.
- It can be: Service Ticket (TGS) to allow access to a particular resource.
- Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT), which we use to request service tickets to access any resource the user has privileges.

### What success looks like

- It can be: Service Ticket (TGS) to allow access to a particular resource.
- Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT), which we use to request service tickets to access any resource the user has privileges.
- Mimikatz - Extract Kerberos keys Now that we have access to the AES256HMAC and RC4HMAC keys, we can perform the OverPass the Hash aka.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Pass the Ticket (PtT) from Windows` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- Exported tickets (sekurlsa::tickets /export) do not work correctly due to the wrong encryption.

### Variants

- PtT, Pass-the-Ticket, Pass the Ticket (PtT) from Windows, Pass the Ticket (PtT) attack, Harvesting Kerberos tickets from Windows, Pass the Key aka. OverPass the Hash, Pass the Ticket (PtT), Pass The Ticket with PowerShell Remoting (Windows), Mimikatz - PowerShell Remoting with Pass the Ticket, Rubeus - PowerShell Remoting with Pass the Ticket

<a id="technique-passwdnotreqd-field"></a>
## PASSWDNOTREQD Field

Aliases: —  
Tags: domain, password  
Category: Active Directory / Miscellaneous Misconfigurations  
OS: Windows  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- If this is set, the user is not subject to the current password policy length, meaning they could have a shorter password or no password at all (if empty passwords are allowed in the domain).
- A password may be set as blank intentionally (sometimes admins don’t want to be called out of hours to reset user passwords) or accidentally hitting enter before entering a password when changing it via the command line.
- It is worth enumerating accounts with this flag set and testing each to see if no password is required (I have seen this a couple of times on assessments).

### Prerequisites

- Just because this flag is set on an account, it doesn't mean that no password is set, just that one may not be required.
- It is worth enumerating accounts with this flag set and testing each to see if no password is required (I have seen this a couple of times on assessments).

### Enumeration / Detection

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb> Get-DomainUser -UACFilter PASSWD_NOTREQD | Select-Object samaccountname,useraccountcontrol

samaccountname                                                         useraccountcontrol
--------------                                                         ------------------
guest                ACCOUNTDISABLE, PASSWD_NOTREQD, NORMAL_ACCOUNT, DONT_EXPIRE_PASSWORD
mlowe                                PASSWD_NOTREQD, NORMAL_ACCOUNT, DONT_EXPIRE_PASSWORD
ehamilton                            PASSWD_NOTREQD, NORMAL_ACCOUNT, DONT_EXPIRE_PASSWORD
$725000-9jb50uejje9f                       ACCOUNTDISABLE, PASSWD_NOTREQD, NORMAL_ACCOUNT
nagiosagent                                                PASSWD_NOTREQD, NORMAL_ACCOUNT
```

### Exploitation

<a id="technique-password-spraying"></a>
## Password spraying

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, password, smb, spray  
Category: Active Directory / Spraying, Stuffing, and Defaults  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: SMB  
Ports: 139, 445

### Remember this attack when

- For example, if it is known that administrators at a particular company commonly use ChangeMe123!
- when setting up new accounts, it would be worthwhile to spray this password across all user accounts to identify any that were not updated.

### Prerequisites

- Confirm the access, service configuration, and target-specific values shown in the cited CPTS source before running the commands.

### Enumeration / Detection

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ netexec smb 10.100.38.0/24 -u <usernames.list> -p 'ChangeMe123!'
```

### Exploitation


<a id="technique-password-spraying-considerations"></a>
## Password Spraying Considerations

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, brute, domain, john, password, spray  
Category: Active Directory / Password Spraying Overview  
OS: Cross-platform / not specified  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- One example is brute-forcing attempts to identify the password for an account using a long list of passwords.
- It’s common to find a password policy that allows five bad attempts before locking out the account, with a 30-minute auto-unlock threshold.
- If you don’t know the password policy, a good rule of thumb is to wait a few hours between attempts, which should be long enough for the account lockout threshold to reset.

### Prerequisites

- Confirm the access, service configuration, and target-specific values shown in the cited CPTS source before running the commands.

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### What success looks like

- However, it may be possible to obtain the domain password policy with internal access, significantly lowering this risk.
- We can err on the side of caution and either choose to do just one targeted password spraying attempt using a weak/common password as a "hail mary" if all other options for a foothold or furthering access have been exhausted.

<a id="technique-petitpotam-ms-efsrpc"></a>
## PetitPotam (MS-EFSRPC)

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, dcsync, domain, host, http, https, imap, kerberos, ldap, mssql, port, rpc, smb, smtp, sudo  
Category: Active Directory / Bleeding Edge Vulnerabilities  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: HTTP, HTTPS, IMAP, LDAP, RPC, SMB, SMTP, kerberos, mssql  
Ports: 25, 80, 88, 111, 135, 139, 143, 389, 443, 445, 465, 587, 636, 993, 1433, 3268, 3269

### Remember this attack when

- PetitPotam (CVE-2021-36942) is an LSA spoofing vulnerability that was patched in August of 2021.
- The flaw allows an unauthenticated attacker to coerce a Domain Controller to authenticate against another host using NTLM over port 445 via the Local Security Authority Remote Protocol (LSARPC) by abusing Microsoft’s Encrypting File System Remote Protocol (MS-EFSRPC).
- This technique allows an unauthenticated attacker to take over a Windows domain where Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) is in use.

### Prerequisites

- First off, we need to start ntlmrelayx.py in one window on our attack host, specifying the Web Enrollment URL for the CA host and using either the KerberosAuthentication or DomainController AD CS template.
- We can see this by typing klist (using the klist command requires installation of the krb5-user package on our attack host.
- Running klist Confirming Admin Access to the Domain Controller Finally, we could use the NT hash for the built-in Administrator account to authenticate to the Domain Controller.

### What success looks like

- The flaw allows an unauthenticated attacker to coerce a Domain Controller to authenticate against another host using NTLM over port 445 via the Local Security Authority Remote Protocol (LSARPC) by abusing Microsoft’s Encrypting File System Remote Protocol (MS-EFSRPC).
- This technique allows an unauthenticated attacker to take over a Windows domain where Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) is in use.
- There is also a PowerShell implementation of the tool Invoke-PetitPotam.ps1.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Bleeding Edge Vulnerabilities` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- In the attack, an authentication request from the targeted Domain Controller is relayed to the Certificate Authority (CA) host's Web Enrollment page and makes a Certificate Signing Request (CSR) for a new digital certificate.

### Variants

- No separately named variant was identified in the cited CPTS subsection.

<a id="technique-pingcastle"></a>
## PingCastle

Aliases: —  
Tags: bloodhound, domain, ldap, password, port, powershell, smb  
Category: Active Directory / Additional AD Auditing Techniques  
OS: Windows  
Service: LDAP, SMB  
Ports: 139, 389, 445, 636, 3268, 3269

### Remember this attack when

- Thinking about security for a second, if you do not have an active inventory of the hosts in your enterprise, PingCastle can be a great resource to help you gather one in a nice user-readable map of the domain.
- Note: If you are having issues with starting the tool, please change the date of the system to a date before 31st of July 2023 using the Control Panel (Set the time and date).
- PingCastle Interactive TUI The default option is the healthcheck run, which will establish a baseline overview of the domain, and provide us with pertinent information dealing with misconfigurations and vulnerabilities.

### Prerequisites

- Even better, PingCastle can report recent vulnerability susceptibility, our shares, trusts, the delegation of permissions, and much more about our user and computer states.
- Viewing The Report Throughout the report, there are sections such as domain, user, group, and trust information and a specific table calling out "anomalies" or issues that may require immediate attention.

### Enumeration / Detection

## PowerShell Constrained Language Mode

Aliases: —  
Tags: powershell  
Category: Active Directory / Enumerating Security Controls  
OS: Windows  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- PowerShell Constrained Language Mode locks down many of the features needed to use PowerShell effectively, such as blocking COM objects, only allowing approved .NET types, XAML-based workflows, PowerShell classes, and more.

### Prerequisites

- PowerShell Constrained Language Mode locks down many of the features needed to use PowerShell effectively, such as blocking COM objects, only allowing approved .NET types, XAML-based workflows, PowerShell classes, and more.

### Enumeration / Detection

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb> $ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

ConstrainedLanguage
```

### Exploitation

```powershell-session

ConstrainedLanguage
```

### What success looks like

- PowerShell Constrained Language Mode locks down many of the features needed to use PowerShell effectively, such as blocking COM objects, only allowing approved .NET types, XAML-based workflows, PowerShell classes, and more.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Enumerating Security Controls` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- CPTS did not state a distinct failure condition in this subsection; verify placeholders, reachability, permissions, syntax, and the cited source context.

<a id="technique-powerview"></a>
## PowerView

Aliases: —  
Tags: bloodhound, domain, kerberos, ldap, powershell, service, ticket  
Category: Active Directory / Credentialed Enumeration - from Windows  
OS: Windows  
Service: LDAP, kerberos  
Ports: 88, 389, 636, 3268, 3269

### Remember this attack when

- Much like BloodHound, it provides a way to identify where users are logged in on a network, enumerate domain information such as users, computers, groups, ACLS, trusts, hunt for file shares and passwords, perform Kerberoasting, and more.
- It requires more manual work to determine misconfigurations and relationships within the domain than BloodHound but, when used right, can help us to identify subtle misconfigurations.
- Adding the -Recurse switch tells PowerView that if it finds any groups that are part of the target group (nested group membership) to list out the members of those groups.

### Prerequisites

- It requires more manual work to determine misconfigurations and relationships within the domain than BloodHound but, when used right, can help us to identify subtle misconfigurations.
- Now we know who to target for potential elevation of privileges.

<a id="technique-printer-bug"></a>
## Printer Bug

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, dcsync, domain, host, ldap, password, relay, service, smb  
Category: Active Directory / Miscellaneous Misconfigurations  
OS: Windows  
Service: LDAP, SMB  
Ports: 139, 389, 445, 636, 3268, 3269

### Remember this attack when

- To leverage this flaw, any domain user can connect to the spool's named pipe with the RpcOpenPrinter method and use the RpcRemoteFindFirstPrinterChangeNotificationEx method, and force the server to authenticate to any host provided by the client over SMB.
- This attack can be leveraged to compromise a Domain Controller in a partner domain/forest, provided you have administrative access to a Domain Controller in the first forest/domain already, and the trust allows TGT delegation, which is not by default anymore.
- We can leverage the Get-SpoolStatus function from SecurityAssessment.ps1 (available on the target system) as preserved in this repository or this tool to check for machines vulnerable to the MS-PRN Printer Bug.

### Prerequisites

- This attack can be leveraged to relay to LDAP and grant your attacker account DCSync privileges to retrieve all password hashes from AD.
- The attack can also be used to relay LDAP authentication and grant Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD) privileges for the victim to a computer account under our control, thus giving the attacker privileges to authenticate as any user on the victim's computer.
- This attack can be leveraged to compromise a Domain Controller in a partner domain/forest, provided you have administrative access to a Domain Controller in the first forest/domain already, and the trust allows TGT delegation, which is not by default anymore.

### Enumeration / Detection

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb> Import-Module .\SecurityAssessment.ps1
PS C:\htb> Get-SpoolStatus -ComputerName ACADEMY-EA-DC01.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL

ComputerName                        Status
------------                        ------
ACADEMY-EA-DC01.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL   True
```

### Exploitation

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb> Import-Module .\SecurityAssessment.ps1
PS C:\htb> Get-SpoolStatus -ComputerName ACADEMY-EA-DC01.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL

ComputerName                        Status
------------                        ------
ACADEMY-EA-DC01.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL   True
```

### What success looks like

- This attack can be leveraged to compromise a Domain Controller in a partner domain/forest, provided you have administrative access to a Domain Controller in the first forest/domain already, and the trust allows TGT delegation, which is not by default anymore.

## PrintNightmare

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, domain, exploit, host, meterpreter, payload, service, shell, smb, sudo  
Category: Active Directory / Bleeding Edge Vulnerabilities  
OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: SMB  
Ports: 139, 445

### Remember this attack when

- PrintNightmare is the nickname given to two vulnerabilities (CVE-2021-34527 and CVE-2021-1675) found in the Print Spooler service that runs on all Windows operating systems.
- Many exploits have been written based on these vulnerabilities that allow for privilege escalation and remote code execution.
- Using this vulnerability for local privilege escalation is covered in the Windows Privilege Escalation module, but is also important to practice within the context of Active Directory environments for gaining remote access to a host.

## Privilege Escalation — Active Directory

Aliases: —

### Remember this attack when

- Following the steps in the SeImpersonate and SeAssignPrimaryToken section in the Windows Privilege Escalation module, we can work to escalate our privileges to SYSTEM, which will result in an initial foothold in the Active Directory (AD) domain and allow us to begin enumerating AD.
- We'll try escalating privileges using the PrintSpoofer tool and then see if we can dump any useful credentials from the host's memory or registry.
- An easier way would be to modify the DNN Allowable File Extensions once again to allow the .exe file format.

<a id="technique-protected-users-group"></a>
## Protected Users Group

Aliases: —  
Tags: domain, host, password, service  
Category: Active Directory / Hardening Active Directory  
OS: Windows  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- Adding users to Protected Users prevents user credentials from being abused if left in memory on a host.
- - CredSSP will not cache plaintext credentials in memory even if Allow delegating default credentials is set within Group Policy.
- - Windows Digest will not cache the user's plaintext password, even if Windows Digest is enabled.

### Prerequisites

- This group can be used to restrict what members of this privileged group can do in a domain.
- Adding users to Protected Users prevents user credentials from being abused if left in memory on a host.
- - CredSSP will not cache plaintext credentials in memory even if Allow delegating default credentials is set within Group Policy.

### Enumeration / Detection

### What success looks like

- Along with ensuring your users cannot cause harm to themselves, we should consider our policies and procedures for domain access and control.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Hardening Active Directory` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- - Members cannot authenticate using NTLM authentication or use DES or RC4 keys.
- - Members cannot renew a TGT longer than the original 4-hour TTL.
- Note: The Protected Users group can cause unforeseen issues with authentication, which can easily result in account lockouts.

## Protocol Specific Attacks — Active Directory

Aliases: —  
Tags: discover, domain, hijack, password, powershell, rdp, service  
Category: Active Directory / Attacking RDP  
OS: Windows  
Service: RDP  
Ports: 3389

### Remember this attack when

- If a user is connected via RDP to our compromised machine, we can hijack the user's remote desktop session to escalate our privileges and impersonate the account.
- So, for example, the following command will open a new console as the specified SESSIONID within our current RDP session: If we have local administrator privileges, we can use several methods to obtain SYSTEM privileges, such as PsExec or Mimikatz.
- With this new account, we can attempt to discover what kind of privileges it has on the network, and maybe we'll get lucky, and the user is a member of the Help Desk group with admin rights to many hosts or even a Domain Admin.

### Prerequisites

- Let's imagine we successfully gain access to a machine and have an account with local administrator privileges.
- If a user is connected via RDP to our compromised machine, we can hijack the user's remote desktop session to escalate our privileges and impersonate the account.
- RDP Session Hijacking As shown in the example below, we are logged in as the user juurena (UserID = 2) who has Administrator privileges.

### Enumeration / Detection

<a id="technique-remote-desktop"></a>
## Remote Desktop

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, bloodhound, credential, domain, host, rdp, winrm  
Category: Active Directory / Privileged Access  
OS: Windows  
Service: RDP, winrm  
Ports: 3389, 5985, 5986

### Remember this attack when

- Typically, if we have control of a local admin user on a given machine, we will be able to access it via RDP.
- If we gain control over a user through an attack such as LLMNR/NBT-NS Response Spoofing or Kerberoasting, we can search for the username in BloodHound to check what type of remote access rights they have either directly or inherited via group membership under Execution Rights on the Node Info tab.
- We could also check the Analysis tab and run the pre-built queries Find Workstations where Domain Users can RDP or Find Servers where Domain Users can RDP.

### Prerequisites

- Checking Remote Access Rights using BloodHound Node info for WLEY@INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL showing execution rights, including Group Delegated RDP Privileges set to 1.
- This can also be helpful for the blue team to periodically audit remote access rights across the environment and catch large-scale issues such as all Domain Users having unintended access to a host or audit rights for specific users/groups.

### Enumeration / Detection

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb> Get-NetLocalGroupMember -ComputerName ACADEMY-EA-MS01 -GroupName "Remote Desktop Users"

ComputerName : ACADEMY-EA-MS01
GroupName    : Remote Desktop Users
MemberName   : INLANEFREIGHT\Domain Users
SID          : S-1-5-21-3842939050-3880317879-2865463114-513
IsGroup      : True
IsDomain     : UNKNOWN
```

### Exploitation

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb> Get-NetLocalGroupMember -ComputerName ACADEMY-EA-MS01 -GroupName "Remote Desktop Users"

SID          : S-1-5-21-3842939050-3880317879-2865463114-513

IsDomain     : UNKNOWN
```

### What success looks like

- Typically, if we have control of a local admin user on a given machine, we will be able to access it via RDP.
- Enumerating the Remote Desktop Users Group From the information above, we can see that all Domain Users (meaning all users in the domain) can RDP to this host.
- If we gain control over a user through an attack such as LLMNR/NBT-NS Response Spoofing or Kerberoasting, we can search for the username in BloodHound to check what type of remote access rights they have either directly or inherited via group membership under Execution Rights on the Node Info tab.

<a id="technique-roles-and-services"></a>
## Roles and Services

Aliases: —  
Tags: abuse, crack, forward, host, password, ssh  
Category: Active Directory / Pillaging  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: SSH  
Ports: 22

### Remember this attack when

- If we gain access to a backup system, we may be able to review backups, search for interesting hosts and restore the data we want.
- Restic checks if the environment variable RESTICPASSWORD is set and uses its content as the password for the repository.
- If this variable is not set, it will ask for the password to initialize the repository and for any other operation in this repository.

### Prerequisites

- Typically backup systems need an account to connect to the target machine and perform the backup.
- Most companies require that backup accounts have local administrative privileges on the target machine to access all its files and services.
- If we gain access to a backup system, we may be able to review backups, search for interesting hosts and restore the data we want.

### Enumeration / Detection

### What success looks like

- Most companies require that backup accounts have local administrative privileges on the target machine to access all its files and services.
- If we gain access to a backup system, we may be able to review backups, search for interesting hosts and restore the data we want.
- restic - Back up a Directory with VSS Note: If the user doesn't have the rights to access or copy the content of a directory, we may get an Access denied message.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Pillaging` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

### Remember this attack when

- It is highly versatile; we just have to find the correct command to issue for what we want to accomplish.
- An example of using rpcclient from an unauthenticated standpoint (if this configuration exists in our target domain) would be: The above will provide us with a bound connection, and we should be greeted with a new prompt to start unleashing the power of rpcclient.

## Scenario 2

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, domain, password  
Category: Active Directory / Password Spraying Overview  
OS: Linux  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- Typically, I can only identify 40-60% of valid accounts using a list such as jsmith.txt.

### Prerequisites

- Eventually, I was able to follow a complicated attack chain involving Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD) and the Shadow Credentials attack to ultimately gain control over the domain.

### Enumeration / Detection

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### Exploitation

```bash

#!/bin/bash

for x in {{A..Z},{0..9}}{{A..Z},{0..9}}{{A..Z},{0..9}}{{A..Z},{0..9}}
    do echo $x;
done
```

### What success looks like

- In this example, I significantly increased my chances of a successful password spraying attack by starting the attack with ALL domain accounts in my target list.
- From here, I obtained valid passwords for a few accounts.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Password Spraying Overview` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- CPTS did not state a distinct failure condition in this subsection; verify placeholders, reachability, permissions, syntax, and the cited source context.

### Variants

- No separately named variant was identified in the cited CPTS subsection.


<a id="technique-share-hunting"></a>
## Share Hunting

Aliases: —  
Tags: bloodhound, domain, forward, host, mssql, password, rdp, service, smb, sql  
Category: Active Directory / Lateral Movement  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: RDP, SMB, mssql  
Ports: 139, 445, 1433, 3389

### Remember this attack when

- There have been many times on penetration tests where I have had to turn to digging through file shares to find a piece of information, such as a password for a service account or similar.
- I have found myself digging through file shares often during penetration tests when I am stuck.
- Digging through the script we find another set of credentials: account:L337^p@$$w0rD Checking in BloodHound, we do not find an account user, so this may just be an old password.

### Prerequisites

- Turning back to the Penetration Tester Path content, we remember that both the Credentialed Enumeration from Windows and the Credentialed Enumeration from Linux sections covered hunting file shares with Snaffler and CrackMapExec respectively.
- I have often been able to access departmental shares (such as IT) with low privileged credentials due to weak NTFS permissions.
- File share permissions are very difficult to maintain, especially in large organizations.

### Enumeration / Detection

<a id="technique-sid-history-abuse-cross-forest"></a>
## SID History Abuse - Cross Forest

Aliases: —  
Tags: abuse, attack, domain, token  
Category: Active Directory / Attacking Domain Trusts - Cross-Forest Trust Abuse - from Windows  
OS: Windows  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- If a user is migrated from one forest to another and SID Filtering is not enabled, it becomes possible to add a SID from the other forest, and this SID will be added to the user's token when authenticating across the trust.
- If the SID of an account with administrative privileges in Forest A is added to the SID history attribute of an account in Forest B, assuming they can authenticate across the forest, then this account will have administrative privileges when accessing resources in the partner forest.

### Prerequisites

- If a user is migrated from one forest to another and SID Filtering is not enabled, it becomes possible to add a SID from the other forest, and this SID will be added to the user's token when authenticating across the trust.
- If the SID of an account with administrative privileges in Forest A is added to the SID history attribute of an account in Forest B, assuming they can authenticate across the forest, then this account will have administrative privileges when accessing resources in the partner forest.

<a id="technique-smb-null-session-to-pull-user-list"></a>
## SMB NULL Session to Pull User List

Aliases: —  
Tags: domain, host, ldap, password, smb  
Category: Active Directory / Password Spraying - Making a Target User List  
OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: LDAP, SMB  
Ports: 139, 389, 445, 636, 3268, 3269

### Remember this attack when

- If you are on an internal machine but don’t have valid domain credentials, you can look for SMB NULL sessions or LDAP anonymous binds on Domain Controllers.
- Either of these will allow you to obtain an accurate list of all users within Active Directory and the password policy.
- If you already have credentials for a domain user or SYSTEM access on a Windows host, then you can easily query Active Directory for this information.

### Prerequisites

- If you are on an internal machine but don’t have valid domain credentials, you can look for SMB NULL sessions or LDAP anonymous binds on Domain Controllers.
- If you already have credentials for a domain user or SYSTEM access on a Windows host, then you can easily query Active Directory for this information.
- This user list will not be as complete, but it may be enough to provide you with access to Active Directory.

### Enumeration / Detection

<a id="technique-smbmap"></a>
## SMBMap

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, domain, host, smb, upload  
Category: Active Directory / Credentialed Enumeration - from Linux  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux  
Service: SMB  
Ports: 139, 445

### Remember this attack when

- It can be used to gather a listing of shares, permissions, and share contents if accessible.
- This can be especially useful when pillaging shares for useful information.
- Try this against other shares on the Domain Controller and see what you can find.

### Prerequisites

- It can be used to gather a listing of shares, permissions, and share contents if accessible.
- Like CME, we can use SMBMap and a set of domain user credentials to check for accessible shares on remote systems.
- SMBMap To Check Access The above will tell us what our user can access and their permission levels.

<a id="technique-snaffler"></a>
## Snaffler

Aliases: —  
Tags: bloodhound, domain, host, ssh  
Category: Active Directory / Credentialed Enumeration - from Windows  
OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: SSH  
Ports: 22

### Remember this attack when

- Snaffler in Action We may find passwords, SSH keys, configuration files, or other data that can be used to further our access.

### Prerequisites

- Snaffler is a tool that can help us acquire credentials or other sensitive data in an Active Directory environment.
- Snaffler requires that it be run from a domain-joined host or in a domain-user context.
- Now that we have a wealth of data about the INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL domain (and hopefully clear notes and log file output!), we need a way to correlate it and visualize it.

### Enumeration / Detection

```bash  
Snaffler.exe -s -d inlanefreight.local -o snaffler.log -v data
```

### What success looks like

- Snaffler can produce a considerable amount of data, so we should typically output to file and let it run and then come back to it later.
- It can also be helpful to provide Snaffler raw output to clients as supplemental data during a penetration test as it can help them zero in on high-value shares that should be locked down first.
- Snaffler in Action We may find passwords, SSH keys, configuration files, or other data that can be used to further our access.

### What to do next

<a id="technique-sniffing-ldap-credentials"></a>
## Sniffing LDAP Credentials

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, domain, host, ldap, netcat, port  
Category: Active Directory / Miscellaneous Misconfigurations  
OS: Cross-platform  
Service: LDAP  
Ports: 389, 636, 3268, 3269

### Remember this attack when

- When the device attempts to test the LDAP connection, it will send the credentials to our machine, often in cleartext.
- Accounts used for LDAP connections are often privileged, but if not, this could serve as an initial foothold in the domain.

### Prerequisites

- Many applications and printers store LDAP credentials in their web admin console to connect to the domain.
- Sometimes, these credentials can be viewed in cleartext.
- Other times, the application has a test connection function that we can use to gather credentials by changing the LDAP IP address to that of our attack host and setting up a netcat listener on LDAP port 389.

<a id="technique-sql-server-admin"></a>
## SQL Server Admin

Aliases: —  
Tags: acl, attack, bloodhound, domain, host, mssql, password, port, service, sql  
Category: Active Directory / Privileged Access  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: mssql  
Ports: 1433

### Remember this attack when

- It is common to find user and service accounts set up with sysadmin privileges on a given SQL server instance.
- Another way that you may find SQL server credentials is using the tool Snaffler to find web.config or other types of configuration files that contain SQL server connection strings.
- BloodHound, once again, is a great bet for finding this type of access via the SQLAdmin edge.

### Prerequisites

- It is common to find user and service accounts set up with sysadmin privileges on a given SQL server instance.
- We may obtain credentials for an account with this access via Kerberoasting (common) or others such as LLMNR/NBT-NS Response Spoofing or password spraying.
- Another way that you may find SQL server credentials is using the tool Snaffler to find web.config or other types of configuration files that contain SQL server connection strings.

### Enumeration / Detection

```cypher
MATCH p1=shortestPath((u1:User)-[r1:MemberOf*1..]->(g1:Group)) MATCH p2=(u1)-[:SQLAdmin*1..]->(c:Computer) RETURN p2
```

### What success looks like

- We may obtain credentials for an account with this access via Kerberoasting (common) or others such as LLMNR/NBT-NS Response Spoofing or password spraying.
- BloodHound, once again, is a great bet for finding this type of access via the SQLAdmin edge.
- Viewing our Options with Access to the SQL Server We could then choose enablexpcmdshell to enable the xpcmdshell stored procedure which allows for one to execute operating system commands via the database if the account in question has the proper access rights.

<a id="technique-the-credential-theft-shuffle"></a>
## The Credential Theft Shuffle

Aliases: —  
Tags: credential, dcsync, domain, password  
Category: Active Directory / Skills Assessment - Password Attacks  
OS: Windows  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- The target behavior or access described in the cited `Skills Assessment - Password Attacks` section is present.

### Prerequisites

- The Credential Theft Shuffle, as coined by Sean Metcalf, is a systematic approach attackers use to compromise Active Directory environments by exploiting stolen credentials.
- The process begins with gaining initial access, often through phishing, followed by obtaining local administrator privileges on a machine.
- Attackers then extract credentials from memory using tools like Mimikatz and leverage these credentials to move laterally across the network.

<a id="technique-why-are-aces-important"></a>
## Why are ACEs Important?

Aliases: —  
Tags: abuse, acl, attack, bloodhound, domain, exploit, host, password, service  
Category: Active Directory / Access Control List (ACL) Abuse Primer  
OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- These can be great for us as penetration testers as many organizations are unaware of the ACEs applied to each object or the impact that these can have if applied incorrectly.
- They cannot be detected by vulnerability scanning tools, and often go unchecked for many years, especially in large and complex environments.
- During an assessment where the client has taken care of all of the "low hanging fruit" AD flaws/misconfigurations, ACL abuse can be a great way for us to move laterally/vertically and even achieve full domain compromise.

### Prerequisites

- Some example Active Directory object security permissions are as follows.
- Flowchart showing WriteDacl and WriteOwner permissions with associated actions like Grant Rights, GenericWrite, and AddMember, including Linux and Windows tools for each action.
- We will run into many other interesting ACEs (privileges) in Active Directory from time to time.

### Enumeration / Detection

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### Exploitation

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### What success looks like

- Attackers utilize ACE entries to either further access or establish persistence.
- If we have this access over a user, we could assign them an SPN and perform a Kerberoasting attack (which relies on the target account having a weak password set).
- Finally, if we have this access over a computer object, we could perform a resource-based constrained delegation attack which is outside the scope of this module.

### What to do next

### Remember this attack when

- The --da (enumerate domain admins group members ) option and the -PU ( find privileged users) options.
- To identify more potential users, we can run the tool with the -PU flag and check for users with elevated privileges that may have gone unnoticed.
- This output gives an example of the dangers of nested group membership, and this will become more evident when we work with BloodHound graphics to visualize this.

### Prerequisites

- The --da (enumerate domain admins group members ) option and the -PU ( find privileged users) options.
- To identify more potential users, we can run the tool with the -PU flag and check for users with elevated privileges that may have gone unnoticed.
- This is a great check for reporting since it will most likely inform the customer of users with excess privileges from nested group membership.

<a id="technique-windows-authentication-process"></a>
## Windows Authentication Process

Aliases: —  
Tags: credential, domain, kerberos, ldap, password, rpc, service  
Category: Active Directory / Windows Authentication Process  
OS: Cross-platform, Windows  
Service: LDAP, RPC, kerberos  
Ports: 88, 111, 135, 389, 636, 3268, 3269

### Remember this attack when

- If the system has been assigned to a workgroup, it handles the SAM database locally and stores all existing users locally in this database.
- However, if the system has been joined to a domain, the Domain Controller (DC) must validate the credentials from the Active Directory database (ntds.dit), which is stored in %SystemRoot%\ntds.dit.
- When enabled, SYSKEY partially encrypts the SAM file on disk, ensuring that password hashes for all local accounts are encrypted with a system-generated key.

### Prerequisites

- The Windows client authentication process involves multiple modules responsible for logon, credential retrieval, and verification.
- Additionally, the LSA subsystem provides services for access control, permission checks, and the generation of security audit messages.
- These credential providers are COM objects implemented as DLLs.

### Enumeration / Detection

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### Exploitation

```powershell-session
PS C:\Users\[Username]\AppData\Local\Microsoft\[Vault/Credentials]\
```

### What success looks like

- Additionally, the LSA subsystem provides services for access control, permission checks, and the generation of security audit messages.
- The LSA contains the Negotiate function, which selects either the NTLM or Kerberos protocol after determining which protocol is to be successful.
- It is used to authenticate both local and remote users and uses cryptographic protections to prevent unauthorized access.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Windows Authentication Process` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- CPTS did not state a distinct failure condition in this subsection; verify placeholders, reachability, permissions, syntax, and the cited source context.

### Useful commands


<a id="technique-winrm-active-directory"></a>
## WinRM — Active Directory

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, bloodhound, credential, domain, hash, host, http, kerberos, password, port, powershell, rdp, shell, winrm  
Category: Active Directory / Privileged Access  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: HTTP, RDP, kerberos, winrm  
Ports: 80, 88, 3389, 5985, 5986

### Remember this attack when

- Like RDP, we may find that either a specific user or an entire group has WinRM access to one or more hosts.
- Adding the Cypher Query as a Custom Query in BloodHound Interface for creating a custom query to find WinRM users with dangerous rights.

### Prerequisites

- Like RDP, we may find that either a specific user or an entire group has WinRM access to one or more hosts.
- This could also be low-privileged access that we could use to hunt for sensitive data or attempt to escalate privileges or may result in local admin access, which could potentially be leveraged to further our access.
- Viewing Evil-WinRM's Help Menu We can connect with just an IP address and valid credentials.

### Enumeration / Detection

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb> Get-NetLocalGroupMember -ComputerName ACADEMY-EA-MS01 -GroupName "Remote Management Users"

ComputerName : ACADEMY-EA-MS01
GroupName    : Remote Management Users
MemberName   : INLANEFREIGHT\forend
SID          : S-1-5-21-3842939050-3880317879-2865463114-5614

IsDomain     : UNKNOWN
```

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb> $cred = new-object System.Management.Automation.PSCredential ("INLANEFREIGHT\forend", $password)
PS C:\htb> Enter-PSSession -ComputerName ACADEMY-EA-MS01 -Credential $cred

[ACADEMY-EA-MS01]: PS C:\Users\forend\Documents> hostname
ACADEMY-EA-MS01
[ACADEMY-EA-MS01]: PS C:\Users\forend\Documents> Exit-PSSession
PS C:\htb> 
```

### Exploitation

```cypher
MATCH p1=shortestPath((u1:User)-[r1:MemberOf*1..]->(g1:Group)) MATCH p2=(u1)-[:CanPSRemote*1..]->(c:Computer) RETURN p2
```

<a id="technique-workaround-1-pscredential-object"></a>
## Workaround #1: PSCredential Object

Aliases: —  
Tags: credential, domain, host, kerberos, password, rdp, ticket, winrm  
Category: Active Directory / Kerberos "Double Hop" Problem  
OS: Windows  
Service: RDP, kerberos, winrm  
Ports: 88, 3389, 5985, 5986

### Remember this attack when

- If we check with klist, we see that we only have a cached Kerberos ticket for our current server.
- If we try again without specifying the -credential flag, we once again get an error message.
- If we RDP to the same host, open a CMD prompt, and type klist, we'll see that we have the necessary tickets cached to interact directly with the Domain Controller, and we don't need to worry about the double hop problem.

### Prerequisites

- We can also connect to the remote host via host A and set up a PSCredential object to pass our credentials again.
- After connecting to a remote host with domain credentials, we import PowerView and then try to run a command.
- So now, let's set up a PSCredential object and try again.

<a id="technique-workaround-2-register-pssession-configuration"></a>
## Workaround #2: Register PSSession Configuration

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, credential, domain, host, http, kerberos, powershell, rdp, service, ticket, winrm  
Category: Active Directory / Kerberos "Double Hop" Problem  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: HTTP, RDP, kerberos, winrm  
Ports: 80, 88, 3389, 5985, 5986

### Remember this attack when

- We've seen what we can do to overcome this problem when using a tool such as evil-winrm to connect to a host via WinRM.
- What if we're on a domain-joined host and can connect remotely to another using WinRM?
- If we check for cached tickets using klist, we'll see that the same problem exists.

### Prerequisites

- Here we have another option to change our setup to be able to interact directly with the DC or other hosts/resources without having to set up a PSCredential object and include credentials along with every command (which may not be an option with some tools).
- Once this is done, we need to restart the WinRM service by typing Restart-Service WinRM in our current PSSession.
- We can now run tools such as PowerView without having to create a new PSCredential object.

### Enumeration / Detection

### What success looks like

- Due to the double hop problem, we can only interact with resources in our current session but cannot access the DC directly using PowerView.
- We can see that our current TGS is good for accessing the HTTP service on the target since we connected over WinRM, which uses SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol) requests in XML format to communicate over HTTP, so it makes sense.
- After we start the session, we can see that the double hop problem has been eliminated, and if we type klist, we'll have the cached tickets necessary to reach the Domain Controller.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Kerberos "Double Hop" Problem` → re-enumerate with the gained access.
